Заголовок: NATO kicks off 11-nation Starlift satellite launch program
Полный текст:
Notably, four countries that were original participants of the space effort were left out of today’s announcement — France, Hungary, Luxembourg and the United States.

BELFAST — NATO has begun implementing the multinational Starlift space project, which aims to secure military satellite launch services, the alliance said today.
The alliance shared that 10 members (Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, and the United Kingdom), alongside South Korea, committed to funding the program through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA). The agreement came on the sidelines of a meeting of NATO’s National Armaments Directors at the end of October, according to today’s statement.
First announced in 2024, NATO stresses that Starlift “aims to help participating countries work with commercial launch providers and spaceports to make access to space more resilient, responsive and cost-effective.”
Additionally, the initiative is set to support armed forces with a launch service that will assist with securing slots on commercial rockets, structured around flight from a series of spaceports across NATO territory and South Korea.
The statement did not disclose program costs or partner nations’ financial contributions. Notably, four countries that were original participants of Starlift were left out of today’s announcement — France, Hungary, Luxembourg and the United States. The statement did not share the reason for those nations’ dropping off, nor did NATO meet a request for comment by press time.
Other core parts of the program include a forum for developing and testing responsive space operations, such as urgent satellite launches and a plan to improve launch logistics through experimentation.
Europe has a number of launch sites at its disposal, including Norway’s Andøya Spaceport and the UK’s Spaceport, Cornwall. South Korea is studying the construction of a second launch site to expand local capabilities and reduce dependence on foreign services, according to Aviation Week.

Заголовок: Farnborough International Airshow 2028 already 93% booked as record sell-out approaches
Полный текст:
Farnborough International Airshow 2028 is heading towards its earliest sell-out in history, following a record-breaking 2026 event.

Just four months after the last Farnborough International Airshow (FIA), organisers have revealed that 93% of exhibition and chalet space for the 2028 event has already been sold or reserved.

The level of demand puts the UK airshow on course for the earliest sell-out in its 78-year history, with organisers adding another 1,900 square metres of exhibition space.

Further expansion is also being considered, following the introduction of a sixth exhibition hall and additional chalet facilities for the sold-out 2026 event.

When is the next Farnborough International Airshow?

The next FIA will take place from 17-21 July 2028, bringing together leading manufacturers, airlines, defence contractors and aerospace technology companies from around the world.

Photo: FIA

Why is Farnborough Airshow 2028 filling up so quickly?

The surge in bookings follows a record-breaking 2026 show, which welcomed 141,580 visitors – an increase of 41% compared to the 2024 airshow.

The five-day event generated more than $84.7 billion in commercial deals , including 353 firm aircraft orders and 904 firm engine orders.

As Aerospace Global News reported, Boeing emerged ahead of Airbus in the commercial aircraft order race, securing 186 firm orders compared with its European rival’s 157.

Major announcements also came from Embraer, GE Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney.

Aircraft orders were only part of the story: Farnborough also showcased developments in military aviation, autonomous systems and electric aircraft – including a public eVTOL transition flight by Vertical Aerospace .

Global aerospace companies have a major presence at Farnborough

Although held in the UK, Farnborough has become an important international event for aerospace and defence manufacturers from around the world.

Boeing, Lockheed Martin and Bell Textron were among the major US companies represented, alongside emerging aerospace technology developers. The event also provides the opportunity for global manufacturers to meet customers, announce aircraft orders and demonstrate new technoloies.

Farnborough’s growing defence presence has become another major attraction, with companies including Anduril Industries showcasing developments in autonomous and military systems during the 2026 event.

Farnborough organisers predict earliest-ever sell out

Gareth Rogers, CEO of Farnborough International , said: “The exceptional demand for Farnborough International Airshow 2028 demonstrates how much businesses value the event as an opportunity to connect with international customers, showcase innovation on a global scale and develop new partnerships for future collaboration.

“With 93% of exhibition and chalet space already sold and reserved just four months after our last edition, we are on track for the earliest sell-out in our show’s history, a clear vote of confidence in Farnborough’s role as a global platform for aerospace, defence and space.”

For more information, visit the Farnborough International Airshow website.

Заголовок: Azul opens Amazon crew shuttle with 19-seat Cessna SkyCourier
Полный текст:
Azul Conecta has begun flying its first 19-seat Cessna SkyCourier under a four-year contract to transport Petrobras workers in Brazil’s Amazonas state.

Azul Conecta ’s first Cessna 408 SkyCourier is flying Petrobras workers in Brazil’s Amazonas state. Azul will also sell tickets on two weekly flights linking Manaus, Coari and Carauari.

The 19-seat twin turboprop, registered PS-ENE, entered service on 3 November 2026. Azul Conecta chief executive Vitor Cordeiro told CNN Brasil that the airline expects its second SkyCourier in the first half of 2027. Azul is looking at other routes for the aircraft.

Azul plans public flights via Coari

Azul won a four-year contract to fly Petrobras workers with a flight taxi service following a tender. The flights serve Porto Urucu, Coari and Carauari. The Petrobras contract helped make the SkyCourier purchase possible, Cordeiro told Brazil’s UOL .

Photo: Azul

Petrobras has produced oil and gas at Urucu since 1988. Its gas processing plant is in the municipality of Coari. The company uses the Coari River terminal to ship crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas produced at Urucu.

Azul plans to sell seats on two of the aircraft’s weekly flights. On Fridays, it will fly from Carauari to Manaus via Coari. On Mondays, it will fly the reverse route from Manaus to Carauari, with a stop in Coari. Manaus will be the operating base for pilots, mechanics and ground staff.

A step up from the Grand Caravan

The SkyCourier gives Azul Conecta more than twice the capacity of its nine-seat Cessna Grand Caravans .

“We already have markets that are mature enough to go beyond nine seats,” Cordeiro told UOL. Some of those routes still draw too few passengers for a 72-seat ATR 72.

Azul looked at three aircraft before choosing the SkyCourier, according to UOL, including the Let L-410 Turbolet and De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter.

Photo: Cessna

Cordeiro told UOL that Azul can go longer between some maintenance tasks on the Cessna, which is helpful in Manaus, located far from Brazil’s main maintenance centres. Azul already operates Textron’s Caravans, and its experience with the manufacturer also influenced the decision.

Azul flies the Caravan to Barcelos, where visiting anglers often bring bulky fishing gear. Cordeiro told UOL the SkyCourier has more room for that equipment. The passenger SkyCourier has a 5.27-cubic-metre baggage hold rated for up to 680 kg, according to Textron Aviation’s specifications .

Cordeiro also pointed to the wider cabin, large passenger door and steps as passenger benefits compared to smaller aircraft. Cordeiro told CNN Brasil that Azul was still working out what it costs to fly the SkyCourier. He said it had used less fuel than the airline expected in its early operations.

An aircraft designed for passengers and freight

Brazil’s civil aviation regulator ANAC certified the SkyCourier in 2023 .

“The Cessna SkyCourier’s high payload capacity, short takeoff and landing capability, and cost-efficiency make it a great choice for operators in Brazil,” Lannie O’Bannion, senior vice president, Global Sales and Flight Operations, said at the time of the announcement. “The aircraft’s versatility and performance equip customers in the region with smart solutions for their unique missions and circumstances.”

Photo: Cessna

In 2025, Brazilian charter operator Cleiton Táxi Aéreo took delivery of the first SkyCourier in South America . Its aircraft came with a gravel kit for unpaved runways and a conversion kit that lets the operator switch between 19 passenger seats, nine seats with room for cargo, and an all-cargo layout. Brazil’s aviation regulator approved a mixed passenger-and-cargo configuration that year.

Заголовок: ISS astronauts 3D print human cells and tissues | Space photo of the day for Nov. 17, 2026
Полный текст:
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins works in the Life Sciences Glovebox on the ISS. (Image credit: Jessica Watkins/NASA)

Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station . Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space.

What is it?

Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research.

Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.

In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared .

Why is it incredible?

This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online .

This experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth.

When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments.

On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.

Заголовок: Did The First Quarks and Gluons Experience Brownian Motion? Sometimes.
Полный текст:
The quark-gluon plasma of the early universe experienced Brownian motion, but a new theory predicts how a particle moving at close to the speed of light is likely to be pushed and pulled by a fluid as it flies through it. The result shows that Brownian statistics doesn't always apply.

There are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe. One is to peer into the deepest, darkest regions of space. The other is to study the most dense energetic fluid we can create in particle accelerators. A new study looks at how this fluid can behave.
The fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos. In those earliest moments quarks churned among the sea of strong-force carrier particles, similar to the way dust particles dance in a swirl of atomosphere molecules. Only after the Universe expanded a bit did this fluid solidify into the nuclei we see today. By slamming particles together at near light speeds, we can recreate a bit of that early plasma fluid, but only for the briefest moments of time. So we study the fluid primarily by the particles generated by these collisions. In this new study the team simulated how the fluid behaves when a heavy particle passes through it. In the lab this can be done by slamming a proton into a heavy nucleus.
Particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion. First observed by Robert Brown as the jiggly motion of pollen in water, it occurs when smaller particles collide with a larger particle over time. The barrage of kicks nudges the larger particle around a jiggly random path. The smaller particles also collide with each other in a similar way. On a large scale this creates many of the features of thermodynamics, such as the flow of heat and the ideal gas relation of temperature and pressure.
One of the features of Brownian motion is that the distribution of particle speeds is Gaussian. Most of the particles have speeds close to the average, but there are some particles that are much faster and some that are much slower. The distribution is symmetrical; for every 10 particles moving twice as fast as the average, there should be about 10 moving half as fast. This makes sense because collisions are random.
How the Gaussian particle distribution is shifted for higher-energy collisions. Credit: Du Plessis et al.
Although a dense plasma of charged gluons is very different from a drop of water molecules, they both follow this Gaussian distribution. After all, they are both a sea of randomly colliding molecules. You would expect then that when heavy particles move through the plasma, the result would be Gaussian. All the heavy particles would be slowed down passing through the plasma, but some would slow a bit more and others a bit less because of the random collisions. This new study found that for heavy quarks in a quark-gluon plasma this is only partially true.
At slower speeds the result is precisely what we would expect. Collisions are random, and heavy quarks would have a Gaussian speed distribution. But if the heavy quarks are moving at near-light speed, such as a proton in a particle collider, then the distribution is biased. The quark is much more likely to be kicked in a way that slows it down and much less likely to get a kick that speeds it up. This skews the distribution away from Gaussian.
This means that when we study quark-gluon plasmas in a particle accelerator, we must take this bias into account. Using this result, we can better understand the fluid as a whole, and this could help us understand the connection between the hot dense state of the Big Bang and the Universe we see today.
- Du Plessis, Jean F., and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld. "Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm." Physical Review Letters 137.19 (2026): 192302. ↩

Заголовок: China Signals Its Intention to Land on Jupiter's Moon Callisto
Полный текст:
China is outlining plans to place a small lander on the surface of Jupiter's moon Callisto, the outermost of the four Galilean moons. It's an ambitious plan, and would be only the second time anything's landed on a Solar System body beyond Mars. But the payoff would be huge, even if the lander only carries its two proposed instruments.

The China National Space Administration (CNSA) has been talking about a mission to the Jovian system since 2018. It's named Tianwen-4, and it will build on the success of other recent missions like Chang'e 6, which collected the first sample from the lunar far side in 2024.
Tianwen-4 obviously isn't a sample return mission. But according to recent developments, it will attempt another extremely challenging mission profile: a landing on Callisto.
The CNSA announced a new opportunity for payloads for its Tianwen-4 mission to Jupiter.
"The primary objectives of the Tianwen-4 mission are to achieve Jovian orbiting, as well as orbiting and landing exploration of Callisto, and to advance scientific research on the Jovian system," the announcement reads. To improve the mission's performance and success, the CNSA is asking for instrument proposals from within China and from outside partners.
The orbiter itself will carry 10 instruments, and the payload will include multiple cameras, imagers, and spectrometers, as well as a particle detector and a magnetometer. But the announcement also addresses the needs of a Callisto Lander.
"The lander is planned to carry 2 scientific payloads: Callisto Surface Composition Analyzer and Callisto Lander Magnetometer," it reads.
The surface composition analyzer will be a Raman spectrometer. Raman spectrometers can analyze the composition of rocks with the light from a laser, and are becoming a standard part of planetary missions. NASA's Perseverance rover uses an ultraviolet Raman spectrometer to measure fine-scale mineralogy and to detect organic matter. The ESA's upcoming Rosalind Franklin rover will have one, and JAXA's Martian Moons Explorer carries one in its IDEFIX rover.
Callisto's surface is heterogenous on a small scale. There are small bright patches that seem to be pure water ice and there are other patches that appear to be a mixture of rock and ice. These are intermixed with larger, darker areas that are not ice. But spectral identification is uncertain. The Tianwen-4 lander and its Raman spectrometer should be able to determine the compositions of these components. There's also lots of carbon on the surface, and the instrument should be able to tell if its primordial carbon or altered carbon.
This mosaic of Callisto images from the Voyager 1 mission shows a large-scale feature named Valhalla. It's an old impact crater with concentric rings expanding outward. They extend outward for about 1,500 km, and a bright central point, probably the original impact basin, is about 600 km across. Image Credit: NASA/JPL
While Jupiter's other moons like Ganymede, and especially Europa, have strong evidence for subsurface oceans, Callisto's composition and structure is less certain. It appears to be partially differentiated, and magnetometer readings are ambiguous regarding an ocean. But if the Tianwen-4 lander's Raman spectrometer can determine if some of its surface composition is aqueously altered, that would be evidence in favour of an ocean.
The lander's other instrument will be a surface magnetometer. By combining its data with the data from the orbiter's magnetometer, ionospheric signals and signals from the moon's surface can be separated. That will reveal more about its interior, especially regarding its potential subsurface ocean.
It would be nice to have a better understanding of Callisto, since it and the other Galilean moons are expected to have formed in-situ, unlike some other Solar System moons. Some of those appear to be captured objects. So understanding Callisto is an avenue to understanding Jupiter itself, the dominant planet in our system.
Callisto's internal structure is uncertain, but it seems to be differentiated, with multiple ice layers and a rock and metal core. It may also have a saltwater ocean, but is far from certain. Image Credit: By Kelvinsong - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31643955
Landing on any of the Galilean moons is challenging, but Callisto might be the least challenging. It's probably not the best scientific destination among them, but it is the most accessible. For one thing, it's outside Jupiter's extremely powerful radiation belts, where radiation is strong enough to degrade sensitive instruments after short exposure times. Think of NASA's Juno spacecraft and its wide orbit. It only makes short dives into the radiation belts. Even then, Juno protects its most sensitive parts inside a titanium vault.
Callisto is furthest from Jupiter compared to the other three Galilean moons, so its gravity well is shallower. Less precious propellant is required to land there. Tianwen-4 can also use gravity assists at Callisto to prepare for orbital insertion.
Callisto is further away from Jupiter than the other Galilean moons. The other three are deeper inside its magnetic fields and powerful radiation belts, which makes visiting them much more hazardous. The radiation dose on Callisto's surface is weaker and won't take such a heavy toll on sensitive electronics. Image Credit: By B. Smithin Szalay, J. R., Smith, H. T., Zirnstein, E. J., McComas, D. J., Begley, L. J., Bagenal, F., et al. (2022). Water-group pickup ions from Europa-genic neutrals orbiting Jupiter. Geophysical Research Letters, 49, e2022GL098111.
Another reason Callisto is the preferred moon for a surface mssion is the its surface. Callisto's surface is ancient, cratered, and stable. It's a geologically quiet place compared to Io, for instance. It doesn't suffer from the same tidal heating and constant volcanic upheaval that Io suffers from. There are no mountains or volcanoes, only ancient crater on top of ancient crater. This makes hazard avoidance easier, since orbital images are unlikely to have changed from the time they were captured to the time the lander arrives there.
But Callisto is still challenging. It's an airless moon, and that creates its own difficulties. Atmospheric breaking isn't an option. The time delay also ranges from about 35 to 50 minutes, so round-trip communication is double that. That means the landing must be autonomous.
The best surface images come from the Galileo mission, and that spacecraft imaged most of Callisto at poor resolution. Only some small areas are imaged at higher resolutions of tens of meters per pixel.
This image of Callisto is made from data from Galileo and Voyager 1 and 2. It emphasizes how heavily cratered the moon's ancient surface is, and how uniform it is. There are a few smooth areas, and no mountains of volcanoes. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/DLR
But the mission plan calls for Tianwen-4 to orbit Callisto at an altitude of 300 km. Galileo got to within 138 km of the moon, but that was 25 years ago. Camera technology has advanced since then, and Tianwen-4 will carry a pair of visible light imaging cameras. One of them, the wide-angle camera (JWAC), is dedicated to mapping Callisto's surface and topography. Tianwen-4's proposed mapping orbit is 300 km in altitude. From that height, the JWAC operates at about 90 meters per pixel.
In 2020, the CNSA outlined a timeline for the Tianwen-4 mission that would see it launch in September of 2029. To preserve precious propellant, the spacecraft will perform a slingshot flyby of Venus in April 2030, then a pair of slingshots with Earth in 2031 and 2033.
In 2035 it will reach Jupiter and enter an orbit around the gas giant, also making flybys of irregular moons. That's phase one. Phase two starts with two gravity assists with Callisto, then in February 2038, it will enter an orbit around the moon. At some point after that, the Callisto lander will be released.
This plan was first outlined in 2020, so it will likely be changed. The instrumentation on the orbiter could be changed, too, and that includes its mapping camera and its resolution. But with their call for instrument proposals, the CNSA is making one thing clear: they intend to land on Callisto.

Полный текст:
Philippine Airlines (PAL) has finalised its order with Boeing for 15 787-10 Dreamliner aircraft , with options to purchase five more as the carrier gains greater visibility on booking demand for its long-haul flights.

The order is the Filipino flag carrier’s largest ever widebody purchase, and fulfills a commitment announced in July 2026.

Philippine Airlines adds largest member of 787 family

The 787-10 is the largest member of the 787 family and can seat up to 375 passengers in a two-class configuration.

It adds to a growing list of widebody types within the PAL fleet. The carrier currently operates the Airbus A350 and A330, and Boeing 777.

Photo: Airbus/Philippine Airlines

Boeing said the wide-bodies would support the airline’s fleet modernisation and expansion plans, adding capacity and efficiency to its medium- and long-haul network.

The original agreement was announced during the Farnborough International Airshow in July.

Modernising and expanding PAL’s fleet

Lucio C. Tan III, President and Chief Operating Officer of PAL Holdings, said: “The Boeing 787-10 will play an important role in our plans to modernise and expand our fleet. Its advanced technology, greater passenger capacity, and improved fuel efficiency will help us serve more passengers, improve our product offering, and operate more efficiently.

“As we look at our network and the markets we want to serve, we see considerable opportunities for growth.

“We want to provide our passengers with more choices, better connections, and a consistently better travel experience. Having the right aircraft and engines is essential to achieving these objectives.”

The deal was PAL’s first Boeing aircraft order since 2007, and PAL is the only Philippine carrier operating Boeing aircraft for commercial passenger flights.

First 787 deliveries not expected until 2030s

The aircraft will be powered by GE Aerospace’s GEnx-1B engines.

“Today’s signing is an important milestone in our partnership with Philippine Airlines, which spans more than five decades. The GEnx has a proven record of reliability and durability, including in demanding operating environments, and we look forward to supporting PAL as these 787-10s enter service,” said GE Aerospace Group Vice President for Global Sales Mahendra Nair.

PAL is expecting the delivery of its Boeing 787-10 orders between 2031 and 2034.

“Philippine Airlines is investing in its future, and the 787 Dreamliner is the right fit for that growth strategy,” said Boeing Senior Vice President of Global Sales and Marketing Brad McMullen.

“With its range, efficiency, and passenger comfort, the 787-10 will open new opportunities for PAL to expand its global network and provide travelers with more seamless connections to and from the Philippines.”

Philippine Airlines doubles Airbus A350-1000 order

Also at the FIA , PAL signed a memorandum of understanding with Airbus for nine of its A350-1000 aircraft.

The deal doubled the airline’s total orders for the stretched A350 variant to 18 aircraft. It already operates two A350-900s.

PAL has said the three-class A350-1000s would primarily be used to connect its hub in Manila with destinations in the United States.

The flag carrier has already received four of its existing nine aircraft order.

Заголовок: Senate docs reveal new B94 nuclear bomb. But what is it?
Полный текст:
Experts believe the B94 will eventually be a penetrating replacement for the B83.

WASHINGTON — A draft spending bill released by the Senate Appropriations Committee last week revealed a new nuclear bomb designation known as the B94, which experts believe could be capable of penetrating deep into the earth before detonating.
The B94 was first spotted by experts online, who identified the designation buried in a fiscal 2027 spending plan for the Department of Energy. The DOE includes the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), a semi-autonomous agency that oversees the production and safety of nuclear weapons.
Explanatory text for the draft bill published by the committee [PDF] shows roughly $77 million budgeted for the B94, after no money was allocated for the program in FY26. The B94 is listed under “stockpile modernization” alongside other ongoing nuclear weapons programs such as the W87-1 warhead that officials plan to mount atop the forthcoming LGM-35A Sentinel ballistic missile.
The Senate document does not explain the novel weapon name, though arms control expert Jeffrey Lewis opined on X that the B94 is likely a fresh designation for the air-launched Nuclear Delivery System (NDS-A) program previously identified in budget documents. The B94, Lewis said, “appears to be a replacement” for the B83-1 thermonuclear gravity bomb that the Biden administration moved to retire.
Representatives for Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, committee Vice Chair Patty Murray and the NNSA did not respond by press time to requests for comment.
James Acton, co-director of the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Breaking Defense the B94 is “clearly a new capability” that appears to be an air-delivered gravity bomb capable of destroying deeply buried targets. If that is the case, Acton agreed the weapon would likely serve as a replacement for the B83.
“Effectively, what this capability would be doing would be increasing somewhat the number of targets that could be destroyed,” Acton said, reasoning that several subterranean targets are currently out of reach by American weapons.
But Acton, for his part, questioned the weapon’s expected efficacy, drawing from a National Academies report published in 2005 to argue that “once targets are below about 700 meters in depth, they’re simply not destroyable with reliability by any kind of penetrator” — though he noted that penetrating technologies have likely improved in the decades since. He stated that a higher blast yield generally helps reach more deeply buried targets, but it’s not currently clear what kind of yield the B94 may boast.
Additionally, he criticized the vacuum of information around the B94, reasoning that a new nuclear weapon deserves transparency and explanation of a larger strategy similar to what’s been promulgated by previous administrations.
“One could go on forever identifying new missions for nuclear weapons and inventing new requirements, and I view that as an essentially endless process, if not guided by some kind of broader strategy,” he said. He then raised doubts about the B94’s justification, since “there’s just going to be too many targets” it won’t be able to reach.
“I think we’re witnessing both qualitative and quantitative arms racing, and I think if the administration wants to make the case for this weapon, it should give us a clear strategy and allow us and give us enough information to really debate this capability,” he said.

Заголовок: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966
Полный текст:
It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.

Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

'One of the most loved and memorable nights of my life'

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

"I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever."

A bright Leonid fireball captured during the meteor storm of 1966 above Wrightwood, California. (Image credit: NASA via Getty Images)

'Students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors, to watch'

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

"The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

"We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event."

Four views of the Leonid meteor storm of 1966. Captured from the Kitt Peak National Observatory near Tucson, Arizona. (Image credit: Aura/Noao/Nsf (Photo By Getty Images))

'It looked like every star in the sky was falling'

"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!"

'We watched them all night'

"I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep."

'It took your breath away'

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away"

A lone Leonid meteor streaks through the sky above Payson, Arizona in 2017. (Image credit: mdesigner125 via Getty Images)

'I assumed they would all be as interesting'

"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

"My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

"He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

"I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

"That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting."

Image from the more recent Leonid meteor storm in 1999 captured as part of NASA's Leonid Multi-Instrument Aircraft Campaign (Leonid MAC). (Image credit: NASA)

'I guess the party is over'

Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas .

"Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'

"Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars."

Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'"

What caused the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966?

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm .

Will we ever see another meteor storm like 1966?

This image is a composition of 33 Leonids captured overnight from Nov. 18 to 19, 2001. (Image credit: Courtesy of Koen Miskotte)

The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

[Дополнительно: Astronomy Magazine]
This 25-minute exposure on the night of Nov. 17, 1966, shows just a few of the thousands of Leonids that rained down on North American. Credit: Tom Kirby and Tom Pope, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons 17, 1966, the Leonids put on one of the greatest meteor shows in recorded history, during which eyewitnesses reported a sky that seemed to “rain shooting stars.” Observers in North America witnessed a peak of thousands of meteors per minute; Kitt Peak National Observatory reported 40 meteors per second. This peak occurred around 12:00 Universal Time, and lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes. As the requisite rate of 1,000 meteors per hour was not just met but superseded dozens of times over, the event was firmly classified as a true meteor storm. Заголовок: Space Cargo Unlimited Unveils REV1 Reentry Vehicle
Полный текст:
Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled its new reusable reentry vehicle—called REV1—at Space Tech Expo in Bremen, Germany today.

Developed in partnership with Thales Alenia Space, REV1 is designed to increase the total mass Space Cargo Unlimited can bring to orbit and back. The vehicle is targeting a first flight in 2030.

“We have always believed that microgravity can become a new environment for industry, but that potential depends on building the right infrastructure.” Space Cargo Unlimited CEO Nicolas Gaume said in a statement.

What’s inside: REV1 is designed around Space Cargo Unlimited’s BentoBox in-space testing and manufacturing platform.

The company has a one-ton BentoBox mission planned to fly on SpaceX’s Starfall reentry vehicle NET 2028, and is also working with Thales Alenia Space to fly future missions on REV1 at the same scale.

• REV1 will offer 1,200 liters of pressurized internal volume.

• It will deliver 2.5 kW of continuous power.

• REV1 is also designed to spend up to six months on orbit depending on the mission.

The vehicle has a two-module reusable architecture, with one reentry module intended to bring payloads back to Earth while the other remains in space.

• REV1 is being designed to allow for late integration of time sensitive payloads—such as biological samples.

• The vehicle is built with vibration and load mitigation capabilities to protect samples during launch and reentry.

• REV1 will also include real-time sensor feedback, as well as onboard autonomy and edge computing capabilities to help customers make the most of their in-space experiments.

Traffic jam: The unveiling comes amid a booming year for Space Cargo Unlimited, which has booked at least 10 missions on various reentry vehicles. Building its own reentry vehicle, however, gives it more flexibility and access.

“With BentoBox, we are developing the space factory that can fly across a fleet of vehicles. REV1 is being designed from the inside out to take this BentoBox capability even further,” Gaume said. “Our ambition is to bring space closer to industry and, ultimately, create value for the customers of our customers.”

Заголовок: Friend or foe becomes the question as skies fill with potential adversaries
Полный текст:
[Sponsored] Quickly and accurately identifying friendly forces requires IFF attuned to drones.

Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) technology has been around for decades, but as threats and platforms rapidly evolve, IFF must be adaptable to distinguish allied forces from potential threats and operate in contested and denied environments.
Breaking Defense spoke with Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems, about how IFF technology is changing, how it can be used across both U.S. and allied forces, and how it must adapt to meet future threats.
Breaking Defense: IFF technology has been around for a long time. How is it critical to joint forces operations today?
Guanu: IFF is a question-and-answer system. It uses a waveform, which is electrical energy, to transmit data. If you’re a platform and you’re unsure of another platform’s friend status, you ask a question – which is called an interrogation – and the unknown platform responds via secure communications to positively identify itself. Interrogators ask the question, transponders answer the question, and combined interrogator transponders do both. We have these systems on aircraft, ships, land, and radar platforms.
When you look back on history, the introduction of radar was revolutionary. However, radar only showed that something was out there, not whether it was friendly. There needed to be some way of identifying friendly forces where you weren’t spoofed by the enemy. IFF was introduced in World War II and continues to be a critical system.
IFF works alongside radars, data links, sensors and many other systems. For instance, if an adversary attempts to attack our assets from the air, IFF allows our defensive measures to engage threats without endangering friendly forces.
Since that time, warfare has expanded into multiple domains, not only land and sea and air, but space and cyber. Today’s adversaries are more agile and with new technology the speed of conflict has increased dramatically.
When you bring in unmanned systems and associated swarms it adds further complexity beyond what our forces have had to deal with in the past. The Department of War’s Joint All Domain Command and Control strategy (JADC2) strategy helps manage this by connecting assets across domains.
IFF underpins the C2 part of the strategy. This allows joint forces to sense and make sense of data. Is it friend or foe? Then you need to act. You need to be able to do that in split seconds, or you’re not ahead of the adversaries.
With changing threats, such as the proliferation of drones, how is IFF evolving to meet that challenge?
Modern warfare demands technological advances including enhanced cryptology, faster processing, and detection at greater ranges. IFF must be easily upgradeable to meet future threats.
Migrating to software-based IFF skills and card-based solutions is key to providing agility. Our IFF systems use a modular design and open system architecture that allows new capabilities to be integrated through software updates rather than hardware changes. This reduces obsolescence and accelerates enhancements without modifying fleet infrastructure.
Additionally, as unmanned air systems (UAS) expand in threat environments, new technologies are needed to equip the platforms that don’t overload the already crowded IFF frequency band. We are developing this technology and working with the IFF community to define enhancements to Mode 5 to address these changes to the combat environment.
How can IFF be used across both U.S. and allied forces? What are the challenges to ensuring that IFF is being used effectively across joint forces and across all domains?
If you look at IFF or at these missions, say across the U.S. and its coalition, what are the things that you want? You want interoperability and standardization for U.S. and allied operations. Mode 5, the latest secure IFF waveform, is a NATO standard and supports worldwide interoperability.
The challenges associated with ensuring the effective use of Mode 5 across joint forces come from the significant number of different nations, platforms and manufacturers deploying unique IFF systems. In the U.S., the Air Traffic Control Radar Beacon System (ATCRBS), Identification Friend or Foe (IFF), and Mark XII Systems (AIMS) office ensures compatibility across U.S. and NATO forces.
Certifying equipment at both the box level and platform level is critical to overall system performance. The recent AIMS box-level certification of our AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder is a major milestone. The new CIT provides advanced, multi-function capabilities while supporting the latest crypto and cybersecurity resilience requirements. The AIMS certification means the product is ready for use and can serve as a drop-in replacement for current systems.
In addition to having the same tools and waveform, everyone must operate under a consistent concept of operations (CONOPS), otherwise interoperability breaks down and then challenges can occur.
What are the benefits of a combined system and how does it differ from a standalone interrogator or transponder?
Ships typically use interrogators as a key element of their combat ID system to identify airborne objects while aircraft generally carry transponders to respond to questions.
A combined interrogator transponder (CIT) provides both capabilities in one box. This is essential for tactical aircraft that need to engage and where space for equipment is limited on the platform.
By combining both functions, CITs reduce size, weight and power demands and require only a single supporting infrastructure. Whether a platform uses an interrogator, transponder, or both depends on the mission and CONOPS.
How do you work around concerns about things such as jamming and spoofing?
IFF is a radio frequency (RF)-based solution, which can be subject to electronic warfare (EW) attacks. There’s constant evolution with RF so staying ahead of threats is crucial.
We are one of the key co-architects of the secure Mode 5 waveform, and our systems employ anti-jam techniques to operate in this contested environment.
We’re constantly maturing our technology, to support the latest crypto, anti-jam and cybersecurity resilient requirements. At a recent AIMS User Working Group, we successfully demonstrated our latest transponder’s resilience by introducing live RF jamming during the demo.
How long has BAE Systems been involved with IFF? What are your key areas of focus in IFF as you look forward?
BAE Systems has more than 80 years of IFF experience. Since Mode 5’s introduction in the mid-2000s, we have delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator-transponder systems and 16,000 transponders across 140 platform types in more than 40 countries. Our systems support U.S. and coalition forces and air defense, weapons systems, air traffic control, and range instrumentation.
We develop solutions to outpace modern threats. We’ve seen a huge improvement in capability driving advanced performance while reducing size, weight and power. Modular firmware and software-defined architectures enable upgrades and integration into next-generation platforms.
Adversaries are agile so we must be faster by anticipating threats, developing counter technology and fielding updates quickly. Our next-generation products are designed as drop-in upgrades. With robust hardware processing capability, we can constantly update firmware and software after deployment to provide a new capability to address new threats.
Our enhancements, such as anti-jam and cyber resilience features, continue to lead in the industry. We’re listening to our customers. The future of IFF is a system that’s easily upgradeable, integrated, affordable and effective.
I’m proud to be part of the team at BAE Systems and our mission: “We Protect Those Who Protect Us.” We remain committed to delivering systems that meet today’s requirements and can rapidly adapt to tomorrow’s challenges.

The Pacific archipelago of Micronesia is preparing to welcome a new carrier in the form of One Pacific Airways, which will launch regional services using an Embraer ERJ145LR aircraft.

According to AeroRoutes, the airline is due to launch commercial operations on 30 November.

Its schedule includes a twice-weekly return service between the capital Pohnpei and Kosrae, and an island hopping service connecting Pohnpei with Chuuk, then Koror, Yap, Chuuk and returning to Pohnpei.

One Pacific Airways relies on a sole ERJ145LR

One Pacific Airways plans to use its sole Embraer ERJ-145LR to connect these island communities across the Pacific.

The 50-seat, 26-year-old regional jet, painted a vibrant red, has a maximum range of approximately 2,870km and a cruising speed of 833km/h, making it suited to linking destinations across the geographically dispersed region.

The aircraft offers a smaller-capacity alternative to larger narrowbodies, allowing the airline to serve these low density routes while providing a comfortable passenger experience.

Working with Nauru Airlines for Pacific connectivity

One Pacific Airways, whose parent company is South Pacific Airways, is also in talks with Nauru Airlines, the flag carrier of Nauru – the third-smallest country in the world – to explore opportunities for the two airlines to work together commercially and operationally.

One Pacific Airways founder and president, Chih Yuan Wang, said the discussions were focused on how to maximise opportunities to benefit both carriers.

“We see opportunities for the two airlines to work together in a practical and commercially focused way,” Wang said.

“Our discussions have been focused on identifying areas where we can complement each other and create better connectivity and commercial opportunities.”

A proposed route map for One Pacific Airways featuring airline partners

Challenges of flying in the South Pacific

Like any airline in that part of the world, One Pacific Airways will face a unique set of challenges.

Vast distances, relatively small populations and widely dispersed islands will likely make it difficult to build profitable routes.

Many destinations have limited infrastructure, with short runways and only basic facilities, such as the provision of an NDB rather than any VOR or ILS approach.

Fuel, aircraft parts and engineering support can also be expensive and difficult to source.

Заголовок: Asynchronics Raises $3.1M To Boost its Digital-Twin Software
Полный текст:
As a species, aerospace engineers typically give birth to twins: One spacecraft destined for orbit, and another digital replica to test before its sibling flies. As in real life: Twins are expensive.

Polish engineering software startup Asynchronics today announced the closing of a $3.1M seed round to bring more affordable digital-twin software to the market, and grow its virtual catalog of off-the-shelf components to help space engineers more quickly build and test.

b2venture led the round, which included additional participation from Movens Capital, HEARTFELT, and Hard2beat.

Meet Asynchronics: Airbus veterans CEO Adam Chikha and CTO Serge Barral founded Asynchronics in 2023 to bring high-performing simulation software to the startup sector. The idea was to give space startups access to the same quality of simulation tools used by legacy primes, and spur greater competition in the market.

“Smaller companies or mid-sized companies do not have access to this kind of simulation tooling. What we did was we took our vast experience, [and] created something better,” Chikha told Payload. “It lets the smaller companies create better simulations of their missions, and start competing with big industry.”

Asynchronics’ flagship product—NeXosim—is an open-source simulation tool.

• It allows companies to digitally reproduce their spacecraft and missions before launch, to test the performance of components and the overall spacecraft design.

• Sitting on top of this open-source world is Asynchronics’ marketplace, which features a growing list of digitally recreated spacecraft components that spacecraft builders can quickly—and for a small fee—input into their designs.

“The use of the off-the-shelf components in the industry is very common, but the problem there is that they redo the simulation models or the digital twins for all of their missions,” Chikha said. “Since there are components that are available readily off the shelf, there should be their digital replicas that are also available readily off the shelf.”

Into the metaverse: Asynchronics plans to use the new capital to increase the number of components in its catalog. Chikha told Payload the company is aiming to add 50 components in the next two years—targeting the most popular in each category, including reaction wheels, solar array drive assemblies, and power-control-and-distribution units.

Asynchronics plans to more than double its headcount, from about 11 employees today to 24 in the next few years.

The company will also invest in bolstering its software tools—adding visual representations to help engineers see their designs—and developing an AI-model-generation tool to shorten the creation of digital twins from months to days.

Partner up: Although it’s just a few years old, Asynchronics has locked down partners who are using the company’s simulation tools for major missions, such as K2 Space and Infinite Orbits. Asynchronics has also been working with NewSpace Systems, the European components builder, since 2024 to create digital twins of NewSpace Systems parts. Chikha told Payload that in a recent test, the performance of these parts was “identical” to their digital twins.

Space computing company Ramon.Space raised $124M in Series B funding, the company announced today.

Space computing startup Ramon.Space raised $124M in Series B funding, the company announced today, bringing its total amount raised to $180M.

PSG—a growth equity firm traditionally focused on software—led the round, with Micron Technology, Senvest, and Phoenix Financial joining the group of previous investors. Flight heritage: Among orbital data center (ODC) players, Ramon.Space is focused on processing data for satellites in orbit, rather than moving Earth-based computing to space.

• Ramon.Space’s systems are designed to match the performance of ground-based computers while surviving radiation, extreme temperatures, and tight power budgets.

• The company says its technology has been flying for roughly a decade across a few hundred sats.

• An ODC prototype is slated to fly in 2027 under a collaboration with cloud-infrastructure provider Ingrasys, which has been a manufacturing partner with Ramon.Space since 2023.

Ramon.Space argues that as constellations grow and AI workloads move to orbit, every mission will need to process, store, and move data in space.

Scaling up: With the new funds, the company aims to ramp up production of its onboard computing systems, speed up deliveries to customers in its pipeline, and expand into new markets. Its existing customers include satcom-constellation operators, as well as EO providers.

Ramon.Space says it aims to manufacture at a scale that would grow annually “from a run rate of thousands of computing units growing to tens of thousands and beyond.”

Заголовок: Reflect Orbital wants to launch thousands of sunlight-beaming mirrors to space — and the 1st will go up next year
Полный текст:
Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its ambitious plan to place thousands of mirrors in Earth orbit and sell redirected sunlight after dark.

Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its plan to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.

The goal is to extend the hours and output of solar farms globally, "making clean power dispatchable and available when you need it," the California-based startup explains on its website .

Reflect Orbital has made significant progress to date. On Tuesday (Nov. 10), for example, the company announced it had secured $73.5 million in new funding, boosting its total raise to more than $100 million. It has also gotten a formal go-ahead from the U.S. government to try out the concept in space and is currently readying its first test satellite , which is expected to launch in the second quarter of 2027. The identity of the launch provider is being kept under wraps at this time, the firm told Space.com .

The Topaz Solar Farm in California as seen from space. Reflect Orbital's planned space-mirror constellation could make such arrays more productive, according to the company. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Jesse Allen, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey)

Ground-based test

Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.

On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the company explained in an Oct. 14 statement .

The October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.

CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.

Mobile lighting gear was used in a California test to simulate the spot of light that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. (Image credit: Reflect Orbital)

Nighttime demonstration

"Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology."

Mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.

The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.

Reflect Orbital co-founder and CEO Ben Nowack with the company's Earendil-1 demonstration satellite, which is slated to launch to Earth orbit in 2026. (Image credit: Reflect Orbital)

Incremental learning

Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the company operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.

"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.

In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.

Reflect Orbital recently announced the purchase of two launches from Skyroot Aerospace, the first Indian company ever to reach orbit. Seen here is that landmark flight, conducted in July 2026 by the Vikram-1 rocket. (Image credit: Skyroot Aerospace)

Test and learn

In a related development, Reflect Orbital has announced the purchase of two Skyroot Aerospace launches to deploy some of its spacecraft. Skyroot's Vikram-1 launcher is a product of India's private space sector, first flying from the nation's Sriharikota launch site last July. That flight was a landmark success , as Vikram-1 became the first private Indian rocket ever to reach orbit.

"These dedicated launches provide assured schedule and capacity, and complement Reflect Orbital's other planned launches from sites in the United States," Reflect Orbital explained in a different Oct. 14 statement .

Reflect Orbital says its approach is "incremental and test-and-learn." The company has been granted a license from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for one satellite. That mission will test the technology, including built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the sunlight service is delivered.

"It will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites," Reflect Orbital said, "the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions."

Mirror-beamed sunlight can aid agriculture by tailoring growth cycles, extending seasons and boosting yields, according to Reflect Orbital. (Image credit: Reflect Orbital)

Dim view

Reflect Orbital wants to be operating at least 50,000 of its mirror satellites in orbit by 2035. Not surprisingly, many people in the astronomy and stargazer communities have a dim view of this plan , saying it will generate light pollution that significantly degrades the night sky .

Reflect Orbital counters that most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, signoff from local authorities and "Know Your Customer compliance" to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval, the company says, and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.

Reflect Orbital also claims that it can maintain exclusion zones covering astronomical observation sites.

"Our satellites will be default-off when idle and constellation vehicles are designed to stay under +7 stellar magnitude for all non-serving attitudes. We're able to dim the brightness of the service and turn it off at any stage," the company's website states.

Observing campaign

Reflect Orbital also notes that it's an industry member of the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Center for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky.

The company says that it's collaborating with the IAU on an observing campaign for when the service is operational and is also working on a coordination agreement with the U.S. National Science Foundation.

"We've engaged extensively with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other stakeholders," Reflect Orbital stated. "Their feedback has meaningfully informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans. We continue to welcome scientific exploration of how novel technology could deliver a lot of benefits to the world."

Заголовок: Leonid meteor shower: All you need to know in 2026
Полный текст:
Join EarthSky’s Deborah Byrd for a look at the November Leonid meteor shower! We’ll revisit the spectacular Leonid meteor storms of 1833 and 1966, when meteors seemed to rain from the sky, and explore what this year’s shower has in store. Could 2026 bring another storm?

Mid-November meteors … the Leonids

Predicted peak: The peak is predicted** for 0 UTC on November 18, 2026.
When to watch: The midnight to dawn hours — on the mornings of November 17 and November 18 — are likely best. And this year, near the radiant point of the Leonids meteor shower, you’ll spot Jupiter and Mars, separated by only about two full-moon widths.
Radiant: Rises around midnight, highest in the sky at dawn. You’ll see more meteors after the radiant has come over the eastern horizon. Do you need to look at the radiant to see the meteors? No. The meteors will fly from that single point in the sky, but they’ll appear all over the sky.
Nearest moon phase: In 2026, the 1st quarter moon falls at 11:48 UTC on November 17. A 1st quarter moon sets around midnight. So the moon won’t interfere with the Leonids in 2026.
Expected meteors at peak, under ideal conditions: Under a dark sky with no moon, you might see 10 to 15 Leonid meteors per hour.

The 2027 lunar calendar from EarthSky is now available ! See the moon’s phase for every day of the year. Get yours now!

The Leonids stream from a single point in the sky — the radiant point — in the constellation Leo the Lion. And people are always asking how to find the radiant. In 2026, the planets Jupiter and Mars can help! They are close together on the sky’s dome — in the east around midnight — and at their highest in the sky just before dawn breaks. They’re right next to the Leonids’ radiant point in the sky. So look for Jupiter and Mars! Have a dark sky ? Look for the backwards question mark pattern in Leo. It’s known as the Sickle . Chart via EarthSky .

A meteor storm in 2026?

Earth is passing through the Leonid meteor stream in space from October 28 through December 7. You might see a Leonid meteor at any time during that period, especially if you’re out under a dark sky.

The Leonid meteor shower is famous! But why, when the hourly rate is so low, just 10-15 meteors per hour? The Leonids’ fame stems from its periodic meteor storms . The Leonids produced the first major meteor storm of modern times on November 12-13, 1833. It’s often called The Night the Stars Fell . We can’t know the meteor rate exactly. But a widely accepted estimate suggests a rate of up to 2,500 meteors per minute (approximately 150,000 meteors per hour), with some observers reporting seeing up to 20 to 70 meteors per second at the storm’s absolute climax.

Leonids also produced one of the greatest storms in living memory — with rates as high as in the 1833 storm for a period of about 15-20 minutes — on the morning of November 17, 1966. Some who witnessed it reported having a strong impression of Earth moving through space, as our world forded the meteor stream. “I almost felt as if I needed to grip the ground,” one observer told EarthSky.

Leonid meteor storms sometimes recur in cycles of 33 to 34 years. But the Leonids around the turn of the century — while wonderful for many observers — did not match the shower of 1966.

Alas! In most years, the Lion whimpers rather than roars. And scientists don’t expect a Leonid meteor storm this year.

Still, the shower should be fun to watch! Find a dark place to watch at EarthSky’s Best Places to Stargaze page .

Report a fireball (very bright meteor) to the American Meteor Society: it’s fun and easy

Read more: Veteran meteor photographer Eliot Herman’s website: Meteor Photography

The Night the Stars Fell . Engraving by Adolf Vollmy (1889). Vollmy produced this engraving of the 1833 Leonid meteor shower for the Adventist book Bible Readings for the Home Circle . It’s based on a painting by Swiss artist Karl Jauslin, which, in turn, was based on a first-person account of the 1833 storm by a minister, Joseph Harvey Waggoner. Image via Wikimedia Commons .

The parent comet of the Leonid meteor shower

From the late, great Don Machholz (1952-2022), who discovered 12 comets …

Periodic Comet Tempel-Tuttle, officially known as 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is responsible for the Leonid meteor shower. Wilhelm Tempel of Marseille Observatory in France discovered this comet on the evening of December 19, 1865. He found the comet in the northern sky, located in a part of the sky under the North Star near the star Beta Ursae Minoris.

Word of the comet discovery became known throughout Europe. But the news had not yet spread to the United States. Horace Tuttle of Harvard College Observatory picked up the comet 17 days later, on the evening of January 5, 1866. Because this was an independent discovery, Tuttle’s name was added to the comet. Based upon the measurements during this visit of the comet, scientists calculated an orbit of 33.17 years. Astronomers quickly realized that the meteor storm of 1833 — and the annual meteor showers that occurred in mid-November of each year — were the result of this comet.

One would think there’d have been interest in recovering this comet as it came back to Earth’s vicinity in 1899. But there wasn’t much interest in seeing the comet that year. Everyone wanted to see a meteor storm. So, observers missed the comet in 1899. Also missing was a great meteor storm that year.

Scientists expected the next return in 1932. The observatories, using photographic plates with narrow field-of-view telescopes, missed it then too. And again, a major meteor shower did not materialize.

The comet was finally recovered in 1965. The brightest the comet got that year was 16th magnitude , visible only in very large telescopes. But the spectacular meteor storm of 1966 followed!

On the next return, in early 1998, the comet was bright enough that you could see it in binoculars . This pass produced additional impressive meteor showers, which stretched across several years in 1999-2001.

55P/Tempel-Tuttle is due back in early 2031.

Leonid meteor storms in recent history

Most astronomers say you need more than 1,000 meteors an hour to consider a shower a storm. That’s far from the 10 to 15 meteors per hour the Leonids deliver in average years.

The Leonid’s parent comet, Tempel-Tuttle, completes a single orbit around the sun about once every 33 years. It releases fresh material every time it approaches the sun. Since the 19th century, skywatchers have looked for Leonid meteor storms about every 33 years, beginning with the meteor storm of 1833, which witnesses said produced up to 150,000 meteors per hour.

The next great Leonid storms were about 33 years later, in 1866 and 1867. In 1899, a meteor storm did not materialize. In fact, the anticipation of a great meteor storm was so high — and the results so disappointing — that many astronomers felt it was the worst blow ever suffered by astronomy in the eyes of the public.

Not until 1966 did the next spectacular Leonid storm happen, this time over the Americas. In 1966, observers in the southwest United States reported seeing up to 70 meteors per second during a span of 15-20 minutes on the morning of November 17, 1966.

Then came the 1999-2001 showers.

• 1999: Observed rates peaked on November 18 at approximately 3,700 to 4,000 meteors per hour. The peak lasted for a short window and was best seen from Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.

• 2000: Rates dropped considerably in contrast to 1999, but Earth still encountered multiple dust trails. Rates peaked at approximately 130 to 480 meteors per hour, hampered somewhat by bright moonlight.

• 2001: The Leonids returned with a major double peak on November 18–19.

• First Peak: Produced 1,500 to 2,000 meteors per hour, best seen from North America and Hawaii.

• Second Peak: Reached 3,000 to 3,700 meteors per hour, matching or slightly exceeding the peak intensity of the 1999 storm. Best seen from East Asia and Australia.

Leonid meteors viewed from space in 1997. Image via NASA .

The 2026 Leonid meteor shower, seen in sky mode (from the Earth’s surface, looking up). On the late evening of November 17, 2026, the radiant appears to originate inside the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Chart via Guy Ottewell’s Astronomical Calendar .

The view looking toward the east-northeast horizon during the Leonid meteor shower. In 2026, watch after midnight until dawn on the mornings of November 17 and 18. Also, bright Jupiter and the red planet Mars are among the stars of Leo. Image via Guy Ottewell’s Astronomical Calendar 2026 .

Recent days have seen the unusually high deployment of a rare USAF RC-135U Combat Sent surveillance aircraft over the Baltic and Black Seas. Only two of these aircraft remain in service, and their deployment comes during periods of tension with Russia in the twin seas.

AGN reported that the rare RC-135U arrived in the UK earlier this month .

USAF RC-135U Combat Sent returns to Black Sea

The US Air Force RC-135U Combat Sent was seen operating over the Black Sea in a rare deployment of the US spy plane in that area. It was operating with a NATO E-3A Sentry, which stayed closer to the coastline.

The aircraft has been identified as JAKE27 and is an RC-135U (reg. 64-14849). It took off from RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom and flew deep over the Black Sea in international airspace.

The OSINT airplane tracker, Armchair Admiral, showed it was accompanied by a KC-135 Stratotanker that took off from Germany.

Armchair Admiral posted, “JAKE 27 is out of RAF Mildenhall this morning, headed out towards the Black Sea. Their previous two missions of this deployment have focused on the Finnish-Russian border and Kaliningrad.”

US presence in an area now mostly seeing European and NATO aircraft

Italimradar noted, “The mission marks a notable return of visible American intelligence activity in an area where European and NATO surveillance assets have been more prominent in recent weeks.”
