Заголовок: Mars Sample Return: NASA’s new effort to bring samples home
Полный текст:
View larger . | Artist’s concept of the Mars Ascent Vehicle lifting off from the Martian surface, as envisioned in an earlier version of the Mars Sample Return mission. Scientists are eager to have the samples that the Perseverance rover has collected brought back to Earth. Image via NASA / JPL-Caltech.

• Mars Sample Return was NASA’s original plan to bring samples of Martian rocks and sand back to Earth. Scientists would then study them in laboratories, looking for clues about the planet’s wet past and possible signs of microbial life.

• NASA has now proposed a new strategy to bring those samples home. Will it work?

• Previous proposals were considered too expensive, and the estimated time needed to return the samples to Earth was too long.

Are you a moon-watcher? Then you’ll love EarthSky’s 2027 lunar calendar! Order yours today .

Mars Sample Return still alive?

The Mars Sample Return concept was scrapped — and declared dead — due to ballooning costs and a too-long timeframe. But the Mars Perseverance rover has already collected samples. It’s possible they contain evidence of ancient microbial life on Mars. So scientists are itching to have the samples returned to Earth. And now NASA has announced a new plan.

Tiffany Morgan , director of the Mars Exploration Program , detailed NASA’s new Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture on November 9, 2026, during a virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group . The new retrieval architecture provides a framework that NASA could build the actual mission upon. The idea now is to develop “impartial recommendations” for the mission. For example, the architecture will cover proposed mission requirements, review previous lessons learned and evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options.

There will also be a Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture strategy team kickoff in January 2027. A final report will be due in winter 2027-2028.

Leonard David wrote about the new concept for Space.com and Leonard David’s INSIDE OUTER SPACE on November 10, 2026.

NASA’s New Mars Sample Return Effort Detailedwww.leonarddavid.com/nasas-new-ma…

— Leonard David (@ldavid1129.bsky.social) 2026-11-10T19:09:08.202Z

NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. ? ? #PlanetSci

— Dr Space Junk (Alice Gorman) (@drspacejunk.bsky.social) 2026-11-13T07:14:22.855Z

A new strategy for Mars Sample Return

The framework of the new strategy is as follows:

• Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth

• Assess proposed mission requirements

• Review prior lessons learned

• Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options

A previous proposal would have cost an estimated $11 billion by 2024. And the samples wouldn’t have been returned to Earth until 2040. NASA determined that was too long and too expensive.

Another effort would cost $8 billion, with a return to Earth by 2035.

View larger . | Some of the samples, in small tubes, that Perseverance has collected over the years. Image via NASA .

Perseverance rover’s priceless samples

The Perseverance rover has obtained numerous samples from Martian rocks. They are stored in small tubes. Some tubes are kept within the rover for analysis and others are left on the ground, waiting — hopefully — to be picked up later in a sample return mission. The rover had collected 33 samples by 2025.

Meanwhile, Perseverance is still exploring a region just outside the rim of Jezero crater. It still has a few sample tubes left, but not too many.

Read more: NASA’s Perseverance rover on Mars sets off-world driving record

Signs of ancient life?

One of the most important — and exciting — samples comes from a rock called Cheyava Falls. It lies in an ancient riverbed that dried up billions of years ago.

Perseverance found odd rings and dots on the rock that looked like leopard spots and poppy seeds. They highly resembled formations on rocks on Earth created by microbes. Could they be signs of ancient life?

The rover itself can’t determine for sure their origins, however. The samples need to be studied in more advanced labs on Earth. This is the primary reason these samples are so important. They could hold evidence of ancient microbial life. And we can’t bring them home yet.

View larger/full image . | Perseverance captured this view of the “leopard spots” (rings) and “poppy seeds” (smaller dots) on a Martian mudstone rock. Continued analysis of the rover data supports the possibility that the formations involved living microorganisms . It’s a compelling — though still inconclusive — case for ancient life on Mars. Image via NASA / JPL-Caltech/ MSSS.

Risks for future human missions

There is another element to the sample return quest as well. It involves the risks to future human astronauts landing on Mars. There could be compounds in the samples or other rocks or sand that are toxic and dangerous to humans.

Bruce Jakosky of the University of Colorado Boulder and the University of Washington told Space.com:

The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in. This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear.

View larger . | An astronaut examines rocks on Mars in this artist’s concept. Toxic compounds in the rocks or sand could pose a risk to future astronauts. The new sample return strategy calls for the samples from the Perseverance rover to be returned to Earth for study before any human missions begin. Image via NASA/ Wikimedia Commons .

Mars Sample Return 1st, then astronauts

Jakosky explained why it’s important to bring the samples back to Earth before human missions to Mars. This includes astronaut safety as a top priority:

• Identify and characterize known hazardous chemicals to ensure astronaut safety (e.g., perchlorates and chloromethanes), and look for possible additional hazardous chemicals

• Characterize very fine dust particles that could cause respiratory issues in astronauts

• Characterize dust and regolith properties for spacesuit design and wear patterns

• Search in advance of the arrival of humans for evidence of extant life that could interact with terrestrial life

• Enhance astronaut effectiveness on the surface and science return from human missions by providing initial context and analysis

• Demonstrate successful round-trip to Mars

• Demonstrate successful round-trip travel, including entry, descent, landing and ascent from the surface of Mars.

• Demonstrate implementation of planetary protection protocols. While human missions would not use the same approaches, what we learn from doing these would make the approach for humans much easier to plan and implement.

China’s sample return mission

Meanwhile, China is pushing ahead with its own sample return mission. The complex Tianwen-3 mission will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter and an Earth reentry module.

China is looking to launch the mission by 2028 and bring the samples back to Earth by 2031.

Bottom line: NASA has begun a new effort for a Mars Sample Return mission to bring the highly-sought samples from the Perseverance rover back to Earth.

Заголовок: ADA Space Lists on Hong Kong Stock Exchange, Raising Funds
Полный текст:
Over 600 million Yuan has been raised to set up a new production base to build customer and constellation satellites with better capabilities.

This article discusses an initial public offering, stock markets, and select stocks. I am not a financial advisor, and this article is not investment advice; consult a financial advisor before investing.

Team members at ADA Space’s Taizhou facility posing for a photo with the third group of satellites for the Three-Body Computing Constellation in November 2026. | Image: ADA Space

ADA Space (国星宇航), operator of the world’s only in-use space-based computing constellation, completed its initial public offering last week, becoming listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (香港聯合交易所) on November 13th .

The process to go public last week was approved by regulators in late October , following the company’s third submission. After the relevant documents were reviewed and released, it was disclosed that ADA Space was valued at 11.554 billion Yuan (1.733 billion United States Dollars, as of November 16th) prior to the listing.

ADA Space’s first day of being traded was attended by company and exchange executives as well as politicians of the Hong Kong (香港) Special Administrative Region. Company founder Lu Chuan (陆川) sent in a commemorative video for the occasion, as he was busy elsewhere working on future satellites.

In going public, the company raised 750 million Hong Kong Dollars, about 637.32 million Yuan (95.59 million United States Dollars), in new funding, according to Reuters .

A good part of the funds are planned to be used to establish a new satellite design, development, and testing base in Shenzhen (深圳市) 1 by the end of 2028 to boost capabilities to expand the Three-Body Computing Constellation . That facility will work alongside existing ones in Chengdu (成都市) 2 for production, Jiaxing (嘉兴) 3 for thorough testing, Chongzhou (崇州市) 4 for component manufacturing, and Taizhou (台州) 5 for design verification.

Building the new Shenzhen base will be helpful in working through producing 114 satellites currently on order from customers, as of October 20th, and worth about 3.475 billion Yuan (521.154 million United States Dollars). Customers awaiting the delivery of those may be technology giant Tencent (腾讯) and computer vision firm SenseTime (商汤科技) , as both have signed agreements for space-based compute.

The rest of the funds raised will reportedly be used for repaying financing provided by banks, going after relevant strategic acquisitions, and enhancing ADA Space’s satellite capabilities.

In addition to satellites for customers, ADA Space is also deploying those for its Three-Body Computing Constellation, hoped to become a new infrastructure by crunching large amounts of compute in space efficiently. That is being done by many small satellites, able to launch on most of China’s launch vehicles, that could eventually number up to 2,800 in Earth orbit.

So far, only two groups of satellites have been launched for the constellation, in May 2025 and October this year, seeing twenty performing computing tasks in orbit. Those were via the well-established, state-backed Long March 2D and then LandSpace’s Zhuque-2E , a newer commercial option. Despite the small number of satellites, the constellation has demonstrated its ability to perform complex tasks and maintain week-long laser links for joint computation.

In the coming weeks, ADA Space will see the recently completed third group of satellites, at least five in number, being launched for the Three-Body Computing Constellation. That will expand the total amount of compute available, allowing for more complex and compute-intensive tasks to be performed.

At present, ADA Space leads China’s in-space computing efforts, ahead of competitors including Orbital Chenguang (轨道辰光) , Chaozhisuan Beijing Technology Co Ltd (超智算(北京)科技有限公司), and Peng Cheng Laboratory (鹏城实验室), who are actively performing orbital trials . Other computing constellations, like those from STAR.VISION Aerospace (地卫二空间技术) and backed by the municipal government of Shanghai (上海市) , are yet to reach space while planning for thousands of spacecraft. Efforts at state-owned enterprises are underway , with plans being kept behind closed doors, in case they become a new needed infrastructure .

Meanwhile, America’s leader in the field , Starcloud, is still awaiting the launch of its second spacecraft, which may mine cryptocurrency instead of doing something useful. Behind them, Google’s Project Suncatcher is performing technology verifications , and SpaceX’s plans are not yet near liftoff.

Заголовок: Telesat lenders agree to hold off, buying time on December debt
Полный текст:
Telesat said Monday that a group of its lenders has agreed to hold off on collecting the first big block of its debt, due Dec. 6, until Jan. 18, 2027, giving the satellite operator about six more weeks.
The pause, called a standstill, covers lenders to Telesat GEO Inc., the unit that runs Telesat’s older geostationary satellites and owes the debt that’s coming due, according to the company’s announcement.
Those lenders bargain through an ad hoc committee, an informal group of debt holders that negotiates as one. Its members hold Telesat GEO’s term loans and two kinds of bonds: secured notes, which are backed by company assets, and unsecured notes, which are not. In return for the pause, Telesat agreed to keep paying interest.
The term loans and certain secured notes mature on Dec. 6. They are the first $2.4 billion of Telesat GEO debt to come due, according to the company’s third-quarter results.
Telesat said the standstill gives it more time to deal with those maturities. Its goal “remains reaching a fair and consensual resolution,” the company said, and it will keep trying to negotiate in good faith.
Telesat’s lenders have offered a rescue package twice since August, most recently a $3.2-billion plan to repay the December debt. They have also sued the company in New York and Ontario over its 2025 transfer of most of Lightspeed, its low Earth orbit broadband constellation, to a subsidiary outside their collateral. In August, chief executive officer Dan Goldberg ruled out a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing.
Telesat shares fell $2.70, or about 4 per cent, to close at $62.01 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Monday. The announcement came after markets closed.

Заголовок: India’s AMCA decision could create a new combat aircraft force alongside HAL
Полный текст:
The winner of India's AMCA competition will gain responsibility for the country's flagship stealth fighter programme and could establish a rival aerospace ecosystem.

India expects to select within weeks the company that will build prototypes of its first indigenous fifth-generation stealth fighter, bringing a competition involving three private-sector bidders close to a decision.

Defence Secretary R K Singh announced the timeline at the ANI National Security Summit in New Delhi, where he said the evaluation of proposals for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme was nearing completion.

“I hope in about a month, we’ll be ready to announce the winner of that race. Thereafter, we hope it will lead to faster development of the AMCA prototypes and, thereafter, for induction,” Singh said.

Photo: IDRW

The announcement marks an important step in India’s efforts to develop a domestically designed stealth fighter and establish a new manufacturing base for advanced combat aircraft outside the traditional state-owned aerospace sector.

The three competing teams are TASL, bidding independently; L&T in partnership with Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) and Dynamatic Technologies; and Bharat Forge alongside BEML and Data Patterns.

Their technical and commercial proposals are being evaluated before the government selects a development-cum-production partner to work with the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA), the organisation responsible for designing the aircraft.

AMCA bids opened on 1 November

The latest announcement follows the opening of bids earlier this month.

According to a 16 November report in The Times of India , industry sources said the three contenders submitted their proposals on 30 October, the extended deadline, and the bids were opened on 1 November.

The newspaper reported that a high-level committee constituted by the defence ministry was evaluating the submissions for the INR150 billion ($1.6 billion) prototype development programme.

Photo: Indian MoD

Aerospace Global News reported in September that the original 27 August deadline had been extended to 30 October after the shortlisted companies requested additional time to prepare their proposals.

The winner will be responsible for building five flying prototypes and a structural test article, establishing manufacturing facilities and supporting the aircraft’s extensive flight-test programme.

The development plan envisages approximately 1,800 test sorties over seven years to validate the aircraft’s flight controls, stealth characteristics, sensors, radar, weapons integration and propulsion systems.

The competition represents a significant departure from India’s previous combat aircraft programmes, which have relied heavily on Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) for manufacturing.

Why HAL is missing from the competition

HAL, which manufactures India’s Tejas fighter aircraft, participated in the initial AMCA selection process but did not advance beyond the technical and financial evaluation stage.

As AGN reported in February, seven companies and consortia initially expressed interest, but only three qualified for the subsequent bidding stage.

Photo: IDRW

The decision brought private manufacturers to the forefront of India’s most ambitious indigenous fighter programme.

HAL subsequently told AGN that it had received no formal communication confirming its exclusion and was therefore unable to comment on the reports.

The three shortlisted bidders bring different capabilities to the competition.

Tata Advanced Systems has experience manufacturing aerostructures for international aerospace companies and is involved in the Airbus C295 military transport aircraft programme in India.

L&T’s consortium combines defence engineering and systems integration with BEL’s electronics expertise and Dynamatic Technologies’ aerostructures manufacturing capabilities.

The Bharat Forge-led group brings together precision manufacturing, heavy engineering and defence electronics expertise through its partners BEML and Data Patterns.

Selecting a private-sector partner could establish a second major combat aircraft manufacturing ecosystem in India alongside HAL.

What comes next for India’s stealth fighter?

The AMCA is being developed as a twin-engine, approximately 25-tonne fighter with low-observable shaping, internal weapons bays, advanced sensors and integrated avionics.

Its initial Mk1 version is planned to use GE Aerospace F414 engines. A more powerful engine developed through international collaboration is envisaged for the subsequent Mk2 variant.

Photo: GE Aerospace

Engine development remains a separate challenge. Singh said at the summit that a workshop would be held in Bengaluru next month to examine the way forward.

India has been pursuing a high-thrust engine development arrangement with France’s Safran, while Reliance Industries and Rolls-Royce announced a competing industrial proposal in August.

AGN previously reported that the Reliance-Rolls-Royce partnership envisages developing an indigenous combat engine and establishing aerospace gas turbine capabilities in India.

The AMCA programme received government approval for its design and prototype development phase in March 2024.

Earlier planning envisaged a first prototype flight around 2029 and series production beginning around 2035, although those milestones will depend on the eventual contract and development progress.

The Indian Air Force is expected to require approximately six to seven AMCA squadrons, but the final production requirement has not been established.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons

India is seeking to develop the aircraft as China expands its fifth-generation fighter capabilities, including the J-20 and J-35.

Photo: Chinese Navy

The immediate decision, however, is industrial. The company selected next month will have to turn ADA’s design into a flying stealth fighter and demonstrate that India’s private aerospace sector can deliver a combat aircraft of this complexity.

Заголовок: Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)
Полный текст:
Seattle space startup sees its focus on advanced composites as a way to get around a technological bottleneck and create an additional revenue stream.

Radian Aerospace’s prototype composite tank takes shape at the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. (Photo Courtesy of Radian Aerospace)

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems .

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Radian Aerospace CEO Richard Humphrey (Photo via LinkedIn)

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release . “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield , an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034 .

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

An engineer tests thermal protection material at NASA’s Glenn Research Center. (Photo Courtesy of Radian Aerospace)

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center . Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

Заголовок: Look for Mercury this week, farthest from morning sun
Полный текст:
Mercury will reach its greatest elongation - greatest distance from the sunrise - on November 21, 2026. Look east at dawn. Bright Venus will be nearby.

The post Look for Mercury this week, farthest from morning sun first appeared on EarthSky .

Mercury will reach its greatest apparent distance from the sun — in the east before sunrise — on November 21, 2026. Astronomers call it a greatest western elongation of Mercury. Any of the mornings around November 21 are a great time to look. For all of us on Earth, it will lie in the brightening twilight, closer to the sunrise point than brilliant Venus (with the bright star Spica next to it). Mercury will be easiest to see from the Northern Hemisphere. But Southern Hemisphere observers might glimpse it, too! Chart via EarthSky .

Mercury farthest from the sunrise on November 21

The innermost planet Mercury orbits the sun every 88 days. And Earth is moving, too. So Mercury ends up passing between us and the sun about every 116 days. It last did this on November 4, 2026, reaching the point astronomers call inferior conjunction . And since then, Mercury has been speeding ahead of Earth in orbit.

And now Mercury is back in our eastern predawn sky. Look for it in the sunrise direction shortly just as dawn is breaking. Mercury is bright! But it’s nowhere near as bright as Venus, which rises earlier and appears farther from the sunrise point than Mercury.

Mercury will reach its greatest western elongation – its greatest apparent distance from the rising sun, in the east at dawn – on November 21, 2026. This morning apparition – a brief one – favors the Northern Hemisphere. But Southern Hemisphere observers might glimpse Mercury, too, especially while using binoculars to scan for it along the eastern horizon.

From the Southern Hemisphere, Mercury will lie low on the horizon that day when it reaches greatest elongation. Above Mercury, Venus and Spica will be much easier to spot. Chart via EarthSky .

Mercury greatest elongation, November 2026

When to watch: Officially, Mercury emerged the second week of November in the morning sky. Look for it shortly before sunrise. At greatest elongation , Mercury is farthest from the sunrise. In the mornings after that, as it’s edging back toward the sunrise, it’ll brighten a little bit more. That will make Mercury easier to spot in the morning twilight .
Where to look: Look in the sunrise direction as the sky is brightening.
Greatest elongation – marking Mercury’s farthest point from the sunrise glare – is at at 0 UTC on November 21 (6 p.m. CT on November 20). Mercury will shine at magnitude -0.6 on that morning. And it’ll be 20 degrees from the sun on our sky’s dome.
Through a telescope on and around November 21, Mercury appears 62% illuminated and 6.64 arcseconds across.
Note: This will be a long morning apparition for Mercury, for the Northern Hemisphere. After November 21, Mercury brightens a bit to magnitude -0.9 (bright, but competing with the morning twilight) until it slips away later – around mid-month – in the December morning twilight.
Venus is nearby: Also in the morning twilight – but higher is the sky – is bright Venus.

Mercury finder charts

In early November, Mercury will lie low in the east shortly before sunrise. Brilliant Venus, and the star Spica are next to each other and far above Mercury. After the middle of the month, Mercury will have brightened and climbed toward Venus and Spica. By month’s end, Mercury will have begun to descend, and slip away by mid-December . Chart via EarthSky .

Mercury events in 2026

Jan 21, 2026: Superior conjunction (passes behind sun from Earth)

Feb 19, 2026: Greatest elongation (evening)

Mar 7, 2026: Inferior conjunction (races between Earth and sun)

Apr 3, 2026: Greatest elongation (morning)

May 14, 2026: Superior conjunction (passes behind sun from Earth)

Jun 15, 2026: Greatest elongation (evening)

Aug 2, 2026: Greatest elongation (morning)

Aug 27, 2026: Superior conjunction (passes behind sun from Earth)

Oct 12, 2026: Greatest elongation (evening)

Nov 4, 2026: Inferior conjunction (races between Earth and sun)

Nov 21, 2026: Greatest elongation (morning)

Mercury charts from Guy Ottewell

Mercury’s greatest morning elongations in 2026 from the Northern Hemisphere as viewed through a powerful telescope. The planet images are at the 1st, 11th, and 21st of each month. Dots show the actual positions of the planet for every day. Chart via Guy Ottewell’s 2026 Astronomical Calendar . Used with permission.

Mercury’s greatest morning elongations in 2026 from the Southern Hemisphere as viewed through a powerful telescope. The planet images are at the 1st, 11th, and 21st of each month. Dots show the actual positions of the planet for every day. Chart via Guy Ottewell’s 2026 Astronomical Calendar . Used with permission.

A comparison of elongations

Mercury’s greatest elongations are not equal. Indeed, some are “greater” than others. For example, the distance of Mercury from the sun on our sky’s dome varies from about 28 degrees (maximum) to 18 degrees (minimum).

Also, Mercury’s elongations are better or worse depending on the time of the year they occur and your location on Earth. So, for both hemispheres, spring evenings and autumn mornings are best.

As an illustration, the chart below – from a Northern Hemisphere perspective – might help you visualize these differences.

Mercury elongations compared. Here, gray areas represent evening apparitions (eastward elongation). Blue areas represent morning apparitions (westward elongation). The top figures are the maximum elongations, reached at the top dates shown beneath. Curves show the altitude of the planet above the horizon at sunrise or sunset, for latitude 40 degrees north (thick line) and 35 degrees south (thin line). Likewise, maxima are reached at the dates in parentheses below (40 degrees north in bold). Chart via Guy Ottewell’s 2026 Astronomical Calendar . Used with permission.

Heliocentric solar system, November 2026

Heliocentric view of solar system, November 2026. Chart via Guy Ottewell’s 2026 Astronomical Calendar . Used with permission. Plus Guy Ottewell explains heliocentric charts here .

Seasons make a difference

So, in the autumn for either hemisphere, the ecliptic – or path of the sun, moon and planets – makes a narrow angle to the horizon in the evening. Conversely, it makes a steep slant, nearly perpendicular, in the morning. So – in autumn from either hemisphere – morning elongations of Mercury are best. Then, Mercury appears higher above the horizon and farther from the glow of the sun. Conversely, evening elongations in autumn are harder to see.

On the other hand, in the spring for either hemisphere, the situation reverses. Then, the ecliptic and the horizon meet at a sharper angle on spring evenings and at a narrower angle on spring mornings. So, in springtime for either hemisphere, evening elongations of Mercury are best. Meanwhile, morning elongations in springtime are harder to see.

Mercury reaches its largest apparent distance from the sun on November 21, 2026. This is called its greatest western elongation . Chart via EarthSky .

Bottom line: Mercury will reach its greatest elongation – greatest distance from the sunrise – on November 21, 2026. Look east at dawn. It’ll disappear from the morning sky in mid-December. Bright Venus will be nearby.

Полный текст:
Основной экипаж МКС-76 совершил срочные расстыковку и «спуск» на Землю: итоги тренировки по аварийным ситуациям на тренажёрах российского сегмента МКС и корабля «Союз»

Космонавты Роскосмоса Дмитрий Петелин и Константин Борисов, а также астронавт NASA Дениз Бёрнхем проходят цикл тренировок по работе на российском сегменте Международной космической станции (РС МКС). Особое внимание инструкторы в процессе подготовки уделяют действиям космической команды при возникновении нештатных и особенно аварийных ситуаций.

У основного экипажа МКС-76 состоялась тренировка на тренажёрах РС МКС и корабля «Союз». На «станции» космонавты и астронавт отработали все три возможные аварийные ситуации: пожар, разгерметизацию и выброс аммиака на американском сегменте.

«Бригада инструкторов ввела очень интересную, нестандартную нештатную ситуацию, которую можно назвать комбинированной. Сначала у нас случился «пожар» в рабочем отсеке служебного модуля, прогорел корпус и случилась разгерметизация», – рассказал Дмитрий Петелин, командир экипажа.

Обнаружить место утечки атмосферы оказалось непросто, так как измерители потока ИП-1 не сработали, поэтому экипажу пришлось искать проблемный отсек вручную. С этой задачей команда справилась на отлично, после чего на «станции» вновь возникла критическая ситуация.

«Мы отработали действия по выбросу аммиака. Это очень сложная, опасная и коварная ситуация, которая возможна на американском сегменте. В случае такой утечки аммиак распространяется внутри герметичного объема станции, поэтому необходимо действовать очень быстро и чётко. Мы покинули «станцию» и перешли в транспортный пилотируемый корабль (ТПК) «Союз» всем нашим интернациональным экипажем», – пояснил Дмитрий Петелин.

Эта часть тренировки проходила на тренажёре ТПК «Союз». По сценарию, загрязнённый аммиаком воздух распространился и внутри корабля, который составляет со станцией одно целое, поэтому экипаж приступил к срочной расстыковке в ручном режиме, выполнению манёвра безопасного увода корабля от «станции» и спуску, не дожидаясь более удачных условий. При этом необходимо было очистить атмосферу «Союза» от вредных примесей, что возможно только с помощью разгерметизации корабля, а значит, в процессе тренировки Дмитрий Петелин, Константин Борисов и Дениз Бёрнхем надели скафандры.

«По сценарию мы находимся в бытовом отсеке в аварийных масках, и нам необходимо надеть скафандры, чтобы отстыковаться от станции. Это выполняется в два приёма. Помогая друг другу, сначала мы надеваем его фактически до головы, после чего, задержав дыхание, снимаем аварийный респиратор и окончательно надеваем скафандр и его герметизируем, чтобы исключить попадание вредных примесей паров аммиака. И, продувая скафандр кислородом, создаём благоприятную среду для дальнейшей работы. Здесь определенные сложности и нюансы присутствуют. В такой ситуации у нас нет полноценной вентиляции, потому что мы считаем, что атмосфера внутри корабля загрязнена. Охлаждение происходит только с помощью подачи кислорода, и объём подачи несоизмеримо меньше, чем при вентиляции скафандра. Поэтому после таких тренировок, как правило, космонавт выходит буквально мокрый, потому что не хватает теплосъёма», – сообщил подробности Дмитрий Петелин.

В процессе срочного «спуска» на Землю инструктор вводил экипажу дополнительные нештатные ситуации, связанные со сбоями в работе автоматики, чтобы команда контролировала системы корабля на всём протяжении полёта до посадки, при необходимости вручную корректируя работу встроенных программ.

▶️ Дмитрий Петелин, Константин Борисов и Дениз Бёрнхем показали высокий уровень взаимодействия в процессе работы, выполнили все задачи тренировки, справились со всеми нештатными и аварийными ситуациями и благополучно вернулись «на Землю».

Полный текст:
17 ноября 1936 года: испытания макетов «объекта 212» на Софринском полигоне

В этот день на Артиллерийском полигоне в Софрино прошли испытания гружёных макетов «объекта 212» — крылатой ракеты, разрабатывавшейся в РНИИ под руководством Сергея Павловича Королёва.

Макеты массой около 40 кг запускались с помощью отделяемой катапультной тележки, оснащенной пороховым ускорителем с целью изучения взлетных характеристик изделия и параметров его разгона.

Первые испытания завершились неудачно. При старте макеты нормально отделялись, но из-за пологой траектории взлёта сбивались в воздухе тележкой, слетавшей вслед за ними с недостаточно длинных рельсов. В результате они падали и разбивались вблизи катапульты.

Это был один из этапов долгого пути «объекта 212»: полноценные лётные испытания ракеты состоялись лишь в 1939 г., уже без С.П. Королёва. Но именно такие пробы — с макетами, расчётами и неудачами — закладывали фундамент будущей советской ракетной техники.

Sun news for November 17, 2026. Long before cameras could capture auroras, artists did the job. This 19th-century engraving shows the northern lights swirling in great ribbons and rays above a snowy log fort at Sitka, Alaska. On this day in 1882, a powerful solar storm pushed auroras like these far beyond the polar regions, all the way to San Diego. Image via Prints & Photographs Division, Library of Congress .

Sun news November 17: The great aurora of 1882

Today’s top story: On this date in 1882, the sun unleashed one of the strongest geomagnetic storms on record. Beginning on November 17, brilliant auroras lit up night skies far from the poles. In fact, people reported seeing them as far south as San Diego, California!

Meanwhile, the storm wreaked havoc on the high-tech network of the day: the telegraph. According to the USGS , telegraph lines stopped working, equipment melted, and one Western Union office caught fire about half a dozen times. In Chicago and Milwaukee, telegraph offices reported sparking equipment. The storm even induced electric currents in the wires strong enough to light a lamp with no battery connected. Even telephone users heard a strange buzzing and ringing on their lines.

So how strong was it? Scientists estimate that the storm’s Dst index — a measure of how hard Earth’s magnetic field was rattled — dropped to about -386 nanoeslas. That puts it in the same league as the 2003 Halloween storms we revisited last month. Today, a storm like that would threaten power grids and satellites instead of telegraphs. That’s why forecasters watch the sun around the clock!

(11 UTC November 16 – 11 UTC November 17)

Flare activity: Low. The sun fired 17 flares: 13 C-class (common) and four B-class (weak), with no M (moderate) or X (strong) flares.

Sun news November 16: The astronaut who watched a solar flare being born

Today’s top story: Fifty-three years ago today, on November 16, 1973, three astronauts launched toward America’s first space station, Skylab. They became the third and final crew to live aboard Skylab. Gerald Carr, Edward Gibson and William Pogue were all space rookies. Even so, they went on to set a record, staying in space for 84 days.

So what does Skylab have to do with the sun? A lot, actually! The station carried a solar observatory called the Apollo Telescope Mount, with eight instruments aimed at our star. The crew used it to capture about 75,000 new images of the sun in X-ray, ultraviolet and visible light.

Then came a historic first. Gibson was a solar physicist, and he kept a close watch on the telescope controls. On January 21, 1974, his patience paid off. He watched and captured images of a solar flare from the moment it began until it faded away, the first time anyone had ever done that. As a result, scientists learned a great deal about how flares work.

Here’s one more twist. The sun ultimately helped bring Skylab down. Solar activity heats and puffs up Earth’s upper atmosphere, which increases drag on orbiting spacecraft. That extra drag pulled the empty station out of orbit in 1979.

Полный текст:
Dr. Richard Pan, who reshaped California's vaccine laws, plans to restore cuts to Medicaid and rebuild trust in public health as he heads to Congress.

Richard Pan shaped California’s strict vaccine laws. Now he takes on new battles in Congress
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Richard Pan, the California pediatrician who helped enact some of the nation’s strictest school vaccine laws, is heading to Congress with children’s health at the center of his focus.
- His priorities include restoring Medicaid funding and health-insurance tax credits, whose expiration drove Covered California premiums up 50% to 60%, while opposing new federal work requirements.
- Pan also wants Congress to scrutinize federal vaccine policy and pursue universal preschool, expanded support for children with special needs and a restored child tax credit.
Dr. Richard Pan, a pediatrician and former California lawmaker known for reshaping the state’s school vaccine laws into some of the strictest in the nation, is heading to Washington after winning a seat in Congress, where he hopes to pursue universal preschool and reverse federal healthcare cuts expected to affect millions of children and families.
The Sacramento Democrat’s first priority is restoring Medicaid, which has seen funding cuts and an added work requirement under the Trump administration’s tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The challenge of having to navigate the work-requirement rules is expected to leave many still-eligible families without aid.
Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, remains a crucial lifeline to healthcare. Even with fewer people benefiting because of Trump administration policies, Medi-Cal still provides health insurance to nearly 14 million residents, or more than 1 in 3 Californians. Roughly 5 million of those are children and young adults under the age of 21.
Pan also hopes to reinstate federal tax credits that helped families purchase affordable health insurance through Covered California. When those pandemic-era subsidies expired at the end of 2025, enrollees saw their health insurance monthly premiums rise 50% to 60%.
Democrats, in the minority at the time, tried to extend the subsidy. Republicans and the Trump administration, citing the costs, allowed them to expire.
Engage with our community-funded journalism as we delve into child care, transitional kindergarten, health and other issues affecting children from birth through age 5.
Pan’s ambitious agenda also includes challenging the Trump administration’s handling of public health and restoring trust, including in immunization recommendations.
“We just had three deaths this week from measles,” said Pan, who was interviewed in early November. He also pointed to cuts to food-safety oversight, the elimination of a committee in charge of newborn screening recommendations and a vaccine advisory committee whose 17 members were dismissed by Kennedy and replaced with his own appointees, including several who have questioned vaccine safety.
“This all needs to stop,” Pan said. “And if this administration under Donald Trump and RFK Jr. is not willing to stop, then Congress is going to need to hold them accountable.”
More parents are choosing to delay childhood vaccinations, such as the MMR vaccine. Doctors worry toddlers remain vulnerable as measles spreads.
Pan’s win was part of a wave of healthcare providers preparing to take office. They are likely to put a spotlight on the Trump administration’s overhaul of the Department of Health and Human Services under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and vaccine policy, said Dorit Reiss, a professor of law and a health policy expert at UC Law San Francisco.
“There are several people that are very devoted to children’s health that I think will make these issues a priority,” Reiss said.
Trump may be less willing to stand by his health secretary if his policies are less politically popular, Reiss said.
“I think there’s a real question on how much tolerance the administration will have for Kennedy, given the result of the election,” Reiss said.
Other Democratic health professionals joining Congress are pediatrician Annie Andrews of South Carolina and epidemiologist Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, both elected to the Senate. In the House, Pan will be joined by New Jersey’s Adam Hamawy, a former Army surgeon.
Republicans also have had health professionals in their ranks, notably outgoing Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, a liver doctor who lost in the Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, and OB-GYN Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican senator who lost his bid for reelection. Cassidy, a staunch supporter of vaccines, was critical of Kennedy, but ultimately voted in line with other Republicans to support his confirmation. Marshall was a vocal supporter of Kennedy’s health agenda. Two remaining Republican physicians are Sens. John Barrasso from Wyoming and Rand Paul from Kentucky.
Pan, who helped eliminate personal-belief exemptions from California’s school immunization requirements, suggested that Congress could consider taking authority over the federal vaccine advisory committee away from the HHS secretary.
Keeping an unvaccinated child as a patient could give pediatricians the chance to educate families on vaccines but may also expose more kids to preventable diseases.
The child-care crisis, which has emerged as a political talking point for both parties, also is an issue for which he has an agenda to pursue.
As a pediatrician and member of a commission that oversaw early childhood funding, Pan said he has seen firsthand the pressures families with young children face. He wants to strengthen services for children with special needs, restore the expanded child tax credit and work toward universal preschool.
“It’s a critical time in child development,” Pan said. “We need to have the political will to put the resources in.”

Заголовок: NASA's Voyager 1 will soon be so far away that its messages take a day to reach Earth
Полный текст:
On Wednesday, after half a century in space, the Voyager 1 spacecraft will be so far from Earth, it will take a full day for light to travel between it and Earth. It's "a tribute to the engineers who designed something that can last that long," said the last person to lay hands on the spacecraft.

NASA’s Voyager 1 will soon be so far away that its messages take a day to reach Earth
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Somewhere far into interstellar space, NASA’s Voyager 1 space probe is about to reach a lonely milestone.
After rewriting our understanding of the solar system nearly 50 years ago, it already became the most distant human-made object in 1998 as it flew away from Earth at 38,000 miles per hour.
Now, it will break another distance record, reaching one light-day away: At about 16 billion miles, it will take a full day for light to travel between the spacecraft and its home planet. Light, the fastest-moving particle in the universe, is what scientists use to communicate with the probe. NASA expects the record to be broken around 2:16 a.m. Wednesday.
Voyager 1 and its trailing twin Voyager 2 were designed and built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in La Cañada Flintridge. To this day, a small flight control team at the lab monitors the probes and sends occasional commands.
Wednesday morning’s record is a meaningful marker for Alan Cummings, a Caltech senior research scientist who worked on the mission as far back as the Nixon administration, years before its launch.
“It’s not a scientific milestone, but it is an engineering milestone,” he said, “a tribute to the engineers who designed something that can last that long.” Generations of engineers, he said, have kept it going.
The Voyagers explored Jupiter and Saturn in greater detail than ever before. Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune, the most distant planets in our system. The images and data the two sent back depicted worlds much more vibrant and dynamic than scientists expected.
“I looked up at our own moon, and I was thinking in my mind that they would all look like that — all the moons of the other planets,” Cummings said. “The fact they weren’t and they were so diverse was just astounding.”
As the Voyagers sent back their images, “it was exciting to get up every day and see what was going to be next,” he said. At a Caltech auditorium, “there was a picture of Io, the moon of Jupiter. It had volcanoes and it was all orange and black, and my immediate reaction was, ‘No, the Caltech students had pulled a prank.’”
What Cummings really looked forward to, as a scientist, was the moment Voyager 1 reached the sea of cosmic particles zipping through the nothingness that lies beyond our sun’s bubble of charged particles — what physicists know as interstellar space.
Scientists didn’t know exactly where that boundary was. Some calculated Voyager would find it by 1980, Cummings remembered.
Voyager 1 didn’t reach it until 2012.
1. Jupiter from Voyager 2 (NASA/JPL) 2. Saturn storms observed by Voyager 2. (NASA/JPL)
The probe’s pristine measurements of interstellar space — untainted by the sun — gave scientists their first direct taste of the space between stars.
“It was all new information,” Cummings said. “You had to go there to measure it, because you couldn’t deduce any of this from near Earth.”
As Voyager 1 ventures deeper into the frontier, its solitude is defined not just by distance, but also by time. In an era of instantaneous communication, Voyager 1’s one-day time delay is a hard limit imposed by the laws of physics.
To celebrate it, NASA is asking people to flash the Morse code for VGR — the mission’s call sign — into the night sky Tuesday to create a “symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet.”
Despite the distance, Cummings can’t help but still feel connected with the spacecraft.
He helped design and build an instrument to detect the interstellar cosmic particles. The device was so fragile, the team decided to send him up an elevator and many flights of stairs to check on it one last time as it sat atop the rocket.
Consequently, Cummings says he was the last person to ever touch Voyager 1.
As it travels away from Earth, there is virtually no chance any human will touch it again. Scientists expect to lose contact with the probe around 2036 as its radioactive power source fades out. Voyager 1 will then continue drifting through the Milky Way galaxy for millions to billions of years. It could very much outlive Earth, which the sun will consume in about 7 billion years.
On its body, adorned with scientific instruments, Voyager 1 carries a golden record filled with sounds and sights of our science, culture and home planet — should any space-faring beings stumble upon our humble probe.
Although, that likely won’t be anytime soon. The first star along Voyager’s path is more than 17 light years away, or about 6,200 light days.

Заголовок: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns
Полный текст:
More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun , while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap . In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

Satellite trails in front of NGC 457, or the Owl Cluster as seen from a latitude of 51° north, around the same latitude of London, England or Calgary, Canada. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation . Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Полный текст:
Aerodata AG has successfully completed the maiden flight of its AeroForce X long-endurance surveillance aircraft in Brandenburg. Designed as a medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) unmanned system, the aircraft aims to offer up to 40 hours of flight time and a 1,300kg payload capacity for global defense and maritime missions.

Germany’s AeroForce X long-endurance surveillance aircraft has completed its maiden flight, marking a major step towards developing a European-built unmanned platform capable of remaining airborne for up to 40 hours while carrying heavy reconnaissance payloads.

Photo: Aerodata

Developer Aerodata AG said the prototype flew successfully from Strausberg Airport in Brandenburg on 14 November, with engineers completing all the objectives set for the initial flight.

The flight comes five months after Aerodata announced the completion of the prototype and follows an agreement with India’s Dynauton Systems to explore adapting the aircraft for surveillance missions in the Himalayas and the Indian Ocean Region.

Although designed as an unmanned aircraft, AeroForce X is initially undergoing crewed flight trials. Aerodata plans to expand testing before attempting its first unmanned flight, when the aircraft will operate under its own flight-control systems.

The company said the maiden flight focused on assessing the aircraft’s controllability, stability and key onboard systems. All requirements specified for the flight were met, although Aerodata did not disclose its duration, altitude or other performance figures.

The successful test moves the programme beyond ground-based development and systems integration into a flight campaign that will determine whether the aircraft can meet its intended operational requirements.

AeroForce X begins flight testing ahead of unmanned operations

Aerodata is developing AeroForce X as a medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) unmanned aerial system for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) missions.

The aircraft is intended to carry sophisticated sensors and other mission equipment over long distances, allowing military and security operators to monitor large areas without repeatedly deploying replacement aircraft.

Photo: Aerodata

Its planned endurance of up to 40 hours and payload capacity of 1,300kg would allow it to undertake extended maritime patrols, border surveillance and electronic reconnaissance missions.

Those figures remain design targets rather than demonstrated capabilities. The maiden flight was intended to establish the aircraft’s basic flying characteristics, not validate its full operational performance.

“The successful maiden flight is a significant endorsement of the dedicated development work carried out by the entire project team,” said Ole Vorsmann, General Manager Unmanned Systems at Aerodata.

“The fact that we were able to meet all the requirements defined for this flight is a major achievement and an important step towards the AeroForce X being ready for operational deployment.”

Aerodata said further crewed flights are planned as engineers progressively expand the aircraft’s flight envelope and test its systems.

The next stages will also include testing the autopilot, a critical requirement before the aircraft can operate without a pilot onboard.

The first unmanned flight will follow the successful completion of those tests. The company has not announced a date.

Aerodata makes first flight of its own aircraft platform

The maiden flight is particularly important for Aerodata, which has spent more than four decades developing and integrating specialised aviation and airborne reconnaissance systems.

The German company has traditionally concentrated on equipping aircraft with surveillance equipment and mission systems rather than developing complete aircraft platforms.

Photo: Aerodata

AeroForce X represents a move into designing and testing an aircraft of its own.

“Aerodata has been developing highly specialised aviation and reconnaissance solutions for more than 40 years. Now, for the first time in the company’s history, we have flown our own aircraft platform,” said Neset Tukenmez, Chief Executive of Aerodata AG.

“AeroForce X exemplifies our commitment to transforming innovative technologies into high-performance solutions for modern armed forces.”

Tukenmez described the programme as Germany’s first MALE unmanned aerial system development and linked it to Europe’s efforts to build greater technological independence in defence aviation.

“By developing Germany’s first MALE UAS, we are strengthening Aerodata’s position in the field of unmanned aerial systems and contributing to Europe’s technological sovereignty,” he said.

Aerodata has also emphasised the aircraft’s modular design, which is intended to accommodate different surveillance sensors and mission equipment depending on customer requirements.

The company has previously described AeroForce X as an ITAR-free platform, meaning its architecture is intended to avoid dependence on equipment controlled under US International Traffic in Arms Regulations.

That could provide greater flexibility when offering the aircraft to international customers, although export approvals under applicable European and national regulations would still be required.

India partnership could open new opportunities for AeroForce X

The flight also marks progress for a programme that already has an international development partnership.

As previously reported by Aerospace Global News, Aerodata signed a memorandum of understanding with Dynauton Systems, part of India’s Dynamatic Technologies, in April 2026 to explore jointly developing AeroForce X for Indian surveillance requirements.

Photo: Aerodata

The agreement focuses on two very different operating environments: the Himalayan region and the Indian Ocean.

Surveillance over the Himalayas requires aircraft capable of operating in demanding mountainous conditions, while maritime reconnaissance involves monitoring large stretches of ocean, shipping routes and strategically important infrastructure.

Both missions place considerable emphasis on endurance and the ability to carry multiple sensors.

The companies intend to evaluate how AeroForce X could be adapted to meet these requirements, combining Aerodata’s surveillance-system expertise with Dynauton’s engineering and manufacturing capabilities.

At the time of the agreement, Tukenmez said the collaboration would provide a basis for developing the aircraft specifically for ISR missions in the Himalayas and Indian Ocean Region.

Udayant Malhoutra, Chief Executive of Dynamatic Technologies, also described the partnership as an opportunity to build on an existing aircraft design rather than begin an entirely new development programme.

The agreement, however, remains a framework for cooperation. Neither company has announced an Indian procurement contract or a production commitment.

The successful maiden flight gives the partners a flying prototype to evaluate as they consider the aircraft’s suitability for India’s requirements.

AeroForce X enters a competitive long-endurance drone market

AeroForce X is being developed at a time when European countries are seeking greater control over their military surveillance capabilities.

MALE aircraft are designed to operate at medium altitudes for extended periods, carrying electro-optical sensors, radar and other intelligence-gathering equipment.

Photo: Aerodata

Their ability to remain airborne for many hours makes them particularly useful for maritime surveillance, border monitoring and missions where maintaining continuous coverage is more important than speed.

The market already includes established aircraft such as the US-built General Atomics MQ-9 Reaper and Turkiye’s Bayraktar Akıncı, while Europe’s multinational Eurodrone programme is developing another MALE-class system.

Aerodata is seeking to distinguish AeroForce X through its combination of endurance, payload capacity, modular mission systems and European development.

The company has identified continuous surveillance of critical maritime infrastructure as one of the aircraft’s potential applications.

Such missions could involve monitoring offshore installations, pipelines, shipping corridors and other infrastructure where sustained aerial observation is required.

The aircraft’s proposed ability to carry substantial mission payloads could also allow operators to combine different surveillance capabilities on a single platform, depending on the configuration.

Aerodata has not provided a timetable for certification, production or operational entry into service.

Заголовок: Embraer E195-E2 tested with low-sulphur fuel to tackle contrails
Полный текст:
Embraer and DLR are testing whether low-sulphur jet fuel can cut climate-warming contrails, using in-flight exhaust measurements from an E195-E2 research campaign.

An Embraer E195-E2 has operated a series of research flights over Germany to investigate whether low-sulphur jet fuel, combined with modern engines, can reduce the formation of climate-warming contrails.

The IGNITE-X campaign, led by the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) , used a Falcon 20E research aircraft to fly behind the E195-E2 and sample its exhaust plume.

DLR’s Falcon 20E followed the E195-E2 over test areas in Bavaria and Saxony, collecting samples at different stages of plume development.

Embraer announced its participation in the tests, which took place in October and November 2026. Researchers are now analysing the data gathered to establish whether changes in fuel composition translate into fewer ice crystals in contrails.

Why sulphur content matters

Contrails form when hot, moist engine exhaust meets cold air, creating ice crystals. Some crystals can linger and spread into clouds that trap heat and contribute to global warming.

As conventional jet fuel cools in the exhaust, its sulphur content forms sulphuric acid particles that can form ice crystals. While soot is still the main source of the crystals which create contrails, researchers are testing whether low-sulphur fuel can reduce contrails, especially in modern engines that produce little soot.

Photo: DLR

The research used an Embraer E195-E2 equipped with Pratt & Whitney PW1900G geared turbofan engines. The aircraft flew with conventional kerosene and a specially manufactured, certified low-sulphur fuel to allow comparisons under operational flight conditions.

Research aircraft measures emissions in flight

DLR’s Falcon 20E followed the E195-E2, taking exhaust measurements. During close-range measurements, the Falcon flew within 30 metres of the Embraer jet, while other measurements were taken at distances of 10 to 30 kilometres.

The campaign included about four weeks of ground and flight tests. At Manching military airfield, researchers tested each engine separately at settings ranging from idle to take-off power. A probe measured tiny exhaust particles, allowing researchers to compare emissions from both engines under different conditions.

Photo: DLR

“We are measuring the emissions directly within the exhaust plume – this is both scientifically and operationally extremely challenging. The test procedure provides unique insights into the potential for reducing emissions. These innovative and, at the same time, challenging tests with our international stakeholders are the result of an exceptionally committed, trusting and inspiring collaboration between applied research and industry,” said Markus Fischer, DLR Divisional Board Member for Aeronautics.

The international project also involved Pratt & Whitney, Aerodyne Research and Missouri University of Science and Technology. Embraer says its participation will help researchers understand the relationship between fuel characteristics, engine performance and contrail formation.

“The E195-E2 was designed to deliver outstanding efficiency and lower emissions, making it an ideal platform for advancing research into the future of sustainable aviation,” said Cleiton Silva, Vice President of Technology Development and Eletronic Equipments at Embraer. “Through our participation in IGNITE-X, we are working alongside leading research institutions and industry partners to better understand the relationship between fuel characteristics, engine performance, and contrail formation. This collaboration reinforces Embraer’s commitment to supporting science-based solutions that contribute to a more sustainable and environmentally responsible aviation sector.”

Early emissions findings are not yet a contrail result

DLR researchers have reported preliminary indications of low soot emissions from the engines and fewer sulphur-containing liquid particles when the low-sulphur fuel was used. However, the team has not yet completed its assessment of how these changes affect ice-crystal numbers or the climate impact of contrails.

Fewer particles in exhaust do not necessarily mean fewer persistent contrails or less warming. The results also depend on temperature, humidity and how the exhaust plume develops.

This research may help identify ways to reduce contrails, supporting other efforts to cut aviation’s carbon dioxide emissions. If it shows a clear benefit, changes to fuel and engine technology could help limit aviation’s climate impact.

DLR says the flight and ground measurements are now being evaluated.

How IGNITE-X fits into wider contrail research

IGNITE-X is part of a growing effort to understand and reduce aviation’s non-CO₂ climate effects. Earlier research has examined whether changing the fuel itself can reduce the particles around which contrail ice crystals form. In the ECLIF3 programme , Airbus, DLR, Rolls-Royce and Neste tested 100% sustainable aviation fuel on an Airbus A350 and found reductions in both soot particles and contrail ice crystals.

Other studies are looking at where aircraft fly rather than what they burn. In March 2026, AGN reported that American Airlines and Google had tested AI-assisted contrail avoidance across transatlantic operations. Of 2,400 flights assessed, 112 followed suggested avoidance routes and produced 62% less contrail formation than a control group, with no statistically significant difference in fuel burn.

The potential benefit is significant. A September 2026 study by Klima Consulting for Transport & Environment (T&E) estimated that cutting contrail warming by half could prevent around 0.025°C of global warming by 2050 and 0.049°C by 2070. The same research suggested that a small share of flights accounts for most contrail warming, making targeted interventions potentially more effective than trying to prevent every visible trail.

Федеральная комиссия по связи США (FCC) начнет проведение важного аукциона (№ 115) по распределению частот в верхнего C-диапазона для беспроводной связи. Аукцион должен завершиться к 4 июля 2027 года.

Данный спектр частот высвобождается спутниковыми операторами — преимущественно компаниями SES и Intelsat — для последующего использования FCC в целях развития наземных сетей связи, в частности для создания так называемого «супердиапазона» (super band) для технологий 5G. Ожидается, что аукцион принесет FCC миллиарды долларов. При этом спутниковые операторы получат компенсации: SES — около $5,6 млрд, а Eutelsat — $504 млн. Кроме того, операторам будут возмещены «обоснованные и необходимые» расходы, связанные с переходом, включая затраты на модификацию телепортов и приемного оборудования их клиентов. SES также получит от FCC средства на создание и запуск до 7 КА для замены существующих космических аппаратов.

Диапазон частот, выставленных на аукцион, составляет 3,98–4,14 ГГц для операторов беспроводной связи, с защитным диапазоном 20 МГц (4,14–4,16 ГГц), а действующие спутниковые службы (FSS) будут переведены в диапазон 4,16–4,2 ГГц. Заявки на участие в аукционе принимаются с 6 по 20 января 2027 года, торги начнутся 27 апреля 2027 года.

Действующие спутниковые операторы должны полностью освободить указанный спектр частот в сроки до 30 декабря 2030 года — 30 июня 2031 года.

Заголовок: Galaxy Outflows Likely Regulate Star Formation At ‘Cosmic Noon’ NASA’s Webb Reveals
Полный текст:
A galaxy’s ultimate habitability is likely linked to massive gaseous outflows that regulate star formation.

Sitting here on the outskirts of our Milky Way Galaxy, itâs hard to imagine the galactic machinations that led to our goldilocks spot around a very welcoming yellow dwarf star. But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation.
As observations by NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now reveal, massive galaxies have largescale gaseous outflows that greatly quench their star production.
And as the authors of a new paper in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science describe, JWST has observed a link between outflows from a massive galaxyâs central core and the quenching of star formation at so-called âCosmic Noon.â That is, roughly 8-12 billion years ago, when the number of stars forming per unit volume in the cosmos reached its peak.
Outflows are large-scale flows of gas, from inside to outside the galaxy usually caused by either supernovae or energetic outbursts from supermassive black holes.
These JWST observations have revealed that outflows are more abundant and more powerful than we thought, suggesting that the evolution of galaxies is strongly impacted by outflows, Sirio Belli, an associate professor at the University of Bologna, Italy and the paperâs co-author, told me via email.
Normally, galaxies are rich in gas, and when the gas is sufficiently cold, it collapses under its own weight and forms a dense cloud from which new stars form. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.
Growing supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies drive powerful winds, blowing away gas that would otherwise form stars, Rebecca Davies, the paperâs lead author and an astrophysicist at Australiaâs Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne, told me via email. With JWST, we can measure the amount of cold star-forming gas being ejected, Davies told me.
But JWST has also revealed that outflows powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes are linked to the rapid shut-down or âquenchingâ of star formation.
As for what leads to such quenching?
Quenching can happen if the galaxy runs out of gas or the galaxy stops being able to turn the gas into stars because the gas is too hot or turbulent to collapse, says Davies.
A Poorly Understood Process
One possibility is that the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy releases a large amount of energy which removes and/or heats the gas and prevents the formation of new stars, says Belli.
As such massive galaxies age, their AGN become relatively quiescent, not unlike Sag A* --- our own Milky Wayâs supermassive black hole in our galactic center.
The Milky Wayâs black hole had a major flare just a few million years ago, smaller outbursts only a century or two ago, and it still flickers almost every day as hot gas swirls just outside it, says Davies.
A key open question is what triggers outflows powerful enough to quench galaxies.
Outflows are very common in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, but most of these galaxies are not quenching: the outflows simply keep the galaxies in equilibrium and prevent them from converting all their gas into stars too quickly, says Davies. Possible triggers of the most powerful outflows include galaxy mergers, or radio jets launched by the central supermassive black holes, she says.
As for how this stellar quenching might impact the formation of molecular clouds that spawn solar type stars and habitable planetary systems?
When galaxies are quenched, the formation of new stars and planets is shut down, with strong repercussions on the probability of developing habitable systems, says Belli. If the Milky Way had been quenched at Cosmic Noon, it would likely not have formed many new stars in the last 10 billion years, and our solar system which is only 5 billion years old would not exist today, he says.
But star formation can become too much of a good thing.
When star formation is too strong there are other problems, such as the large number of stellar explosions that could negatively impact the habitability of planets, says Belli. The connection between galaxy-scale processes and the habitability of planetary systems is only now being investigated, he says.
