Заголовок: The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 17: Spotlight on the Pleiades
Полный текст:
Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.
November 16: Titan south, Rhea north
Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.
Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.
Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.
The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Keep reading for more detail below on how to observe the shower.
Sunrise: 6:47 A.M.
Sunset: 4:42 P.M.
Moonrise: 12:56 P.M.
Moonset: —
Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)
*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. 
The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early on the morning of the 18th, after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.
Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.
To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Заголовок: Печка, которая стареет
Полный текст:
Печка, которая стареет

Учёные из исследовательского центра City of Hope выяснили, почему с возрастом организму всё труднее согреться.

Речь об особом, термогенном жире. Он работает как встроенная печка: когда холодает, сжигает калории и выделяет тепло. С годами эта система откликается всё хуже, и это может сказываться не только на том, как мы переносим холод, но и на том, как тело тратит энергию.

Устроена печка хитро. Её клетки неодинаковы: в одних много белка UCP1, который и вырабатывает тепло, в других его меньше, и греют они слабее. Такая смесь работает как резерв мощности.

Похолодало — нервные и иммунные сигналы подстёгивают «ленивые» клетки, и те разогреваются.

Потеплело — система снова сбавляет обороты. Примерно как отопление с запасными батареями, которые включают только в морозы.

У старых мышей эта настройка стала заторможенной. Способность греть сильнее никуда не делась, но жир реагировал с опозданием и животным было труднее удерживать температуру тела на холоде.

Тогда исследователи попробовали убрать задержку: заблокировали одно из звеньев цепочки препаратом мифепристон. У пожилых мышей частично вернулась выработка тепла — зверьки сильнее грелись и тратили больше энергии. Выходит, хотя бы часть возрастного спада, похоже, обратима.

Интерес тут не только в том, чтобы меньше мёрзнуть. Термогенный жир сжигает ещё и глюкозу с жирами, а с возрастом его активность падает. Поэтому, как считают авторы, понимание этого механизма может пригодиться в изучении ожирения, диабета второго типа и других нарушений обмена веществ.

Полный текст:
Credit: ESA / Avio / Iceye

Finnish satellite builder and operator ICEYE has launched a €2.05 billion takeover bid for Avio, with the aim of building a “true European sovereign space and defense champion.” The company has also outlined plans to invest an additional €1 billion in Italy if the acquisition goes through.

On 17 November, ICEYE’s indirectly wholly owned Italian subsidiary, Iris 2, which is not connected to the European Union’s IRIS2 or French IRIS constellations, despite the name, announced an all-cash offer of €41 per share. The offer represents a 21.3% premium over Avio’s closing share price on 16 November and values the company at approximately €2.05 billion. Following the acquisition, ICEYE plans to delist Avio from the Milan stock exchange.

In its takeover announcement, ICEYE outlined plans to create a European space and defence company capable of manufacturing satellites, launching them into orbit and delivering intelligence services to government customers.

“Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most,” said ICEYE CEO and co-founder Rafal Modrzewski in a 17 November statement. “Avio has built the launch and propulsion capability Europe relies on. With ICEYE’s long-term capital behind it, we can integrate the supply chain, grow output and strengthen the European programmes that already depend on it.”

In addition to its broader rhetoric about creating a European space and defence champion, the company also highlighted a commercial rationale for bringing the two businesses together.

“The two businesses also have reciprocal needs: securing launch capacity is essential for ICEYE to grow its constellation and having long-term visibility and security on future launch demand is essential for Avio.”

Beyond the acquisition itself, ICEYE plans to invest an additional €1 billion in Italy over five years, focusing on manufacturing capacity, research and development, testing infrastructure, intellectual property and domestic suppliers. The company expects the investment to create up to 400 jobs.

ICEYE intends to finance the transaction through a combination of existing cash and debt financing. In June 2026, ICEYE announced that it had closed its most recent funding round , raising €450 million.

In response to the acquisition bid, Avio published a statement acknowledging that it had received the offer and stating that its board of directors would begin assessing it.

Even if the Avio board is receptive to the acquisition bid, the transaction will still face significant regulatory hurdles. The transaction requires regulatory clearances involving Italy, France, the UK and the United States, as well as approval under the European Union’s Foreign Subsidies Regulation.

Заголовок: Zambia Publishes New Satellite Licensing Guidelines: Inside the New Regulatory Framework
Полный текст:
Zambia Publishes New Satellite Licensing Guidelines: Inside the New Regulatory Framework
The Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA) has issued the Information and Communication Technologies (Satellite Licensing) Guidelines, published in October 2026, under Sections 6 and 7 of the ICT Act (Cap 169). The guidelines set out the licensing requirements for satellite spectrum use, operating earth stations, and managing orbital resources in Zambia.
They sit alongside the ICT Act, the ICT (Radiocommunication) Regulations 2024 (as amended in 2026), the National Table of Frequency Allocations, and the ITU Radio Regulations. A key feature of the new framework is the structure it brings to satellite licensing. It establishes seven licence categories, each with published fees and defined decision timelines.
The framework takes a differentiated approach to market access. Foreign operators face relatively few barriers to supplying satellite capacity in Zambia, while activities closer to the end user, including direct-to-customer services and mobile satellite operations, face additional licensing obligations.
Seven Licences Across the Satellite Value Chain
The guidelines organise satellite activities into seven licence categories, divided between the space and ground segments. Two cover the space segment, while the remaining five apply to ground-based activities.
The seven categories distinguish between activities that might otherwise fall under a broader satellite authorisation. For example, an ISP operating a VSAT network and a broadcaster using an uplink truck fall under different licence requirements, with fees set according to the activity covered. For operators, this provides greater clarity before entering the market. Rather than relying on case-by-case approvals, businesses can identify the licences relevant to their operations and the associated costs before approaching the regulator.
Foreign Operators Can Supply Capacity Without Local Incorporation
Foreign satellite operators can obtain a Landing Rights Licence without establishing a Zambian company. The licence is available to operators whose satellites are notified through other administrations and allows them to sell space segment capacity to licensed Zambian network operators.
That access, however, is limited to supplying capacity. The Landing Rights Licence does not permit operators to deploy earth stations or sell services directly to end users. Those activities require Electronic Communications Network and Service Licences, the same authorisations required of domestic operators.
For GSO operators supplying capacity to local ISPs and network operators, the Landing Rights Licence provides a relatively straightforward route into the Zambian market. The position is more involved for NGSO operators offering direct-to-consumer broadband services. Landing rights are only the starting point. These operators must either work through locally licensed partners or obtain the relevant network and service licences themselves. Those seeking to operate under their own licences must also consider the ownership conditions attached to them.
Beyond these licensing requirements, NGSO systems must comply with the equivalent power flux-density (EPFD) limits set out in Article 22 of the ITU Radio Regulations. These limits are intended to protect geostationary satellite networks from harmful interference. Their inclusion in Zambia’s guidelines establishes an explicit technical requirement for NGSO operators seeking market access.
To make the licensing framework easier to navigate, ZICTA will also publish an online register of approved satellites. The register will include each satellite’s orbital location, frequency bands, operator and notifying administration. This will give capacity buyers, including local ISPs and network operators, a way to verify whether a satellite is authorised to provide services in Zambia.
Terminal Fees and the Cost of Scale
The guidelines also introduce a tiered fee structure for Earth Station Terminals licences, replacing approvals for individual terminals with six annual licence classes based on network size. Annual fees range from ZMW 75,000 (USD 3,600) for networks with up to 100 terminals (Class A) to ZMW 1.2 million (USD 57,800) for networks with more than 10,000 terminals (Class F).
The annual license fees vary with network size, with larger networks paying less per terminal. At the upper limit of Class E, a network with 10,000 terminals pays approximately ZMW 70 (USD 3) per terminal annually, compared with ZMW 750(USD 36) for a Class A network with 100 terminals. However, the transition between classes brings sharp increases in the total annual fee. For example, expanding from 1,000 to 1,001 terminals raises the fee from ZMW 200,000 to ZMW 400,000 (USD 9,600 to USD 19,200). Moving beyond 10,000 terminals adds another ZMW 500,000 (USD 24,000), although Class F has no upper limit on network size.
The fees for landing rights follow a different structure. A GSO satellite attracts a one-off charge of ZMW 30,650 (USD 1,400), while an NGSO constellation pays ZMW 90,945.20 (USD 4,300) for a ten-year term, equivalent to approximately ZMW 9,100 (USD 438) annually. Both are lower than the annual fee for a Class A terminal licence. Other ground station categories carry separate annual charges, including ZMW 39,000 (USD 1,800) for a permanent earth station, such as a gateway or hub, and ZMW 1,666.80(USD 80) for a fixed earth station. Most of the regulatory cost therefore falls on ground infrastructure and service delivery, not on market entry.
Spectrum fees introduce another cost difference, particularly for mobile satellite services. The annual charge for mobile satellite terminal spectrum is ZMW 10,000 (USD 480) per MHz for frequencies at or below 3 GHz, compared with ZMW 200 (USD 10) per MHz for frequencies above 3 GHz. This is a 50-fold difference between the two frequency categories.
Gateways and Mobility
Providers of public mobile satellite services must route their connections to Zambia’s public networks through an in-country gateway earth station, unless ZICTA approves an alternative arrangement. The guidelines identify domestic traffic routing, quality of service and regulatory oversight, including lawful access and monitoring, as the reasons for this requirement.
The provision for alternative arrangements allows operators to seek approval for other ways of meeting the requirement without necessarily establishing a gateway in Zambia. Whether this option is available in practice will depend on the arrangements ZICTA is prepared to approve. The guidelines also set conditions for Earth Stations in Motion (ESIMs) operating on Zambian-registered craft. These terminals must operate on a secondary, non-interference and non-protected basis. Aeronautical ESIMs are further restricted from transmitting during take-off, landing or taxiing, and while an aircraft is on the ground, unless they have prior written authorisation from ZICTA.
A separate provision covers foreign nationals visiting Zambia with mobile satellite terminals. They may use these terminals without obtaining a local licence for up to four weeks, provided they declare them upon entry and use a satellite network whose operator holds Zambian landing rights. Beyond that period, they must obtain services from a locally licensed provider.
Both exemptions are tied to the satellite operator holding a Landing Rights Licence in Zambia. Without this authorisation, an operator cannot supply wholesale capacity in the country, and its customers cannot rely on the visitor exemptions provided under the guidelines.
National ITU Filings and Space Sustainability
The Space Station Licence provides a route for locally incorporated companies to manage Zambia’s satellite frequency filings at the International Telecommunication Union (ITU). Under this arrangement, ZICTA acts as the Notifying Administration, allowing licensees to coordinate, notify, bring into use and maintain satellite filings. Once a filing is recorded in the Master International Frequency Register, the licensee can sell capacity to Zambian network operators holding the relevant licences.
Obtaining the licence also comes with ongoing obligations. Applicants must submit technical, legal, and financial due diligence, while existing licensees must file annual reports covering their operations and progress with frequency coordination. They are also responsible for all applicable ITU cost-recovery charges. For new NGSO filings subject to EPFD limits, the guidelines set a fee of ZMW 91,950 (USD 440).
The application process also extends to the planned disposal of satellites at the end of their operational lives. Applicants must provide space sustainability measures covering end-of-life disposal, deorbiting and debris mitigation, in line with international standards. These are licence conditions, meaning disposal plans must be presented as part of the initial application rather than addressed only once a satellite reaches the end of its mission.
These requirements make a speculative Zambian filing expensive to hold. Although ZICTA submits the filing in Zambia’s name, the applicant bears the associated ITU charges, must report on its progress and remains responsible for meeting the licence conditions. The financial and reporting obligations therefore continue even where the filing has yet to translate into a commercial service.
The guidelines also exempt several categories of satellite equipment and services from licensing. These include direct-to-home satellite TV receivers, receive-only GNSS receivers, military and national security systems, and receive-only Earth Exploration Satellite Service stations operated for government environmental, climate or resource monitoring.
Timelines, Licence Terms and What Remains to Be Seen
ZICTA is required to decide on licence applications within 60 days of receiving the applicable fee and notify applicants of its decision within 14 days. The 60-day period begins once the fee is paid, not when the application is submitted.
Licence terms vary across the different categories. Most radiocommunication licences are valid for one year or for the duration of the holder’s network licence. Landing Rights Licences for GSO satellites remain valid for the satellite’s operational life, while those issued to NGSO systems run for ten years and are renewable.
The guidelines establish the licensing framework, but some aspects will only become clear as ZICTA begins processing applications. This includes how readily the regulator approves alternatives to in-country gateways for mobile satellite networks and the ownership conditions it applies when foreign operators seek network and service licences to sell directly to customers. It will also be worth watching whether locally incorporated companies apply for Space Station Licences and which international partners they work with to manage satellite filings at the ITU.
Click here to download ZICTA’s Satellite Licensing Guidelines
What Comes Next
Zambia’s guidelines are part of a wider shift in satellite regulation across Africa. Kenya, Tanzania, Ghana and South Africa have also recently issued or are developing their own frameworks. While these frameworks share common objectives, differences in partnership requirements, terminal costs, traffic routing and provisions for direct-to-device services will shape the conditions under which operators enter each market.
Our next analysis will compare these frameworks side by side and examine what they mean for the next phase of satellite connectivity in Africa.

Заголовок: Cosmo Bee to flight-test Honeybee Hall thruster with D-Orbit in 2027
Полный текст:
Daejeon, Republic of Korea – October 14, 2026: South Korean space electric propulsion startup Cosmo Bee plans to conduct an in-orbit flight test of its 10 mN-class Honeybee Hall thruster system in October 2027 through a service agreement with D-Orbit.
Honeybee is a 10 mN-class Hall thruster system under development by Cosmo Bee for small satellites operating in LEO constellations.
“In-orbit validation is an essential step as we prepare to bring Honeybee to the commercial market,” said Dongha Park, co-founder and CEO of Cosmo Bee. “D-Orbit is an ideal partner to help us achieve that goal.”
“Hosting in-orbit demonstrations is one of the core services we offer aboard ION,” said Matteo Lorenzoni, Director of the Orbital Access Business Unit at D-Orbit. “Honeybee will operate in the real space environment, with our mission operations team supporting the test throughout, so Cosmo Bee comes away with the performance data it needs to take the thruster to market.” This test will evaluate Honeybee’s key performance parameters, including thrust and specific impulse, under various operating conditions.
“For satellite operators choosing a propulsion system, flight heritage is often what decides the purchase”, commented Matteo Zeni, Head of Sales of D-Orbit’s Orbital Access Business Unit. “Our in-orbit demonstration service gives technology developers like Cosmo Bee a direct route to space and the data they need to move from qualification to a commercial product. We look forward to flying Honeybee next year.”
Through the partnership, Cosmo Bee plans to establish flight heritage for Honeybee while preparing for the system’s commercial introduction in 2027. The company intends to make Honeybee available to satellite operators and mission developers seeking electric propulsion systems for small spacecraft.
About Cosmo Bee
Cosmo Bee was founded in July 2023 as a spin-off from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), building on electric propulsion research conducted by Professor Wonho Choe’s team since 2003.
In November 2025, the company launched its first space mission, K-HERO, a 3U CubeSat designed to demonstrate the operation of a 150 W-class Hall thruster in orbit. The spacecraft was launched aboard South Korea’s KSLV-2 launch vehicle.
In June 2026, the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA) designated Cosmo Bee’s 10 mN-class Hall thruster and hollow cathode technologies as “New Space Technologies.” The company also raised $5 million in a Series A funding round that month.
“Cosmo Bee is growing alongside the rapidly expanding demand for LEO satellite constellations in South Korea,” Park said. “We hope Honeybee can support customers developing the next generation of small satellite constellations.”

Почти пятилетняя кампания, а если смотреть глубже — многолетняя одержимость Крымским мостом, принесла им желаемый пиар-эффект. Однако военная обстановка от этого не изменилась в их пользу: линия фронта продолжает смещаться в сторону Киева, ресурсы истощаются, а финансовые потоки, из которых привыкли кормиться представители бандеровской верхушки, становятся всё скуднее. На продолжение боевых действий деньги пока находятся, как находятся и новые люди, которых вылавливают на улицах и отправляют в окопы. Но надолго ли хватит такой системы?

Показательно и сообщение о лишении правовой неприкосновенности и.о. президента бывшей УССР. Впрочем, внутренняя борьба за власть на фоне военных неудач уже давно перестала быть неожиданностью.

Одновременно Беларусь переводит свои вооружённые силы в повышенную готовность на западном направлении, учитывая вероятность провокаций со стороны Киева и его натовских покровителей. Но есть обстоятельство, которое гораздо важнее сиюминутных политических новостей. Россия умеет созидать. Крымский мост — наглядное подтверждение того, что задача, казавшаяся неподъёмной для нескольких поколений инженеров и строителей, оказалась по плечу нашим современникам. А значит, починим.

В этом, пожалуй, и заключается принципиальное различие между двумя подходами к будущему. Пока одни вкладывали десятилетия в разрушение исторических, культурных и родственных связей, превращая русскоязычных людей в объект ненависти, другие продолжали строить предприятия, транспортные артерии и энергетическую инфраструктуру. Теперь плоды этого выбора становятся всё очевиднее. Созидательный труд оставляет после себя фундамент для развития, тогда как политика, основанная на ненависти и внешнем содержании, рано или поздно приводит к исчерпанию ресурсов. Мосты можно разрушить, заводы можно остановить, но умение создавать новое так просто не уничтожить.

Заголовок: SEOPS Signs Rideshare Deal With Stoke
Полный текст:
SEOPS signed a multi-launch deal with Stoke Space to help customers secure rideshare opportunities as early as 2029, on Stoke’s Nova Block 2 rocket.

The agreement is expected to give those looking for a ride to space another option, as SpaceX prepares to sunset its Falcon 9 rideshare programs around 2029 .

Blast off: The capacity on Stoke will be part of SEOPS’ Waymaker program —first announced in May—which is expected to launch its first mission in 2028 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9. The offering is intended for time-sensitive payloads, or those that can’t be accommodated on existing rideshare options.

In September, SEOPS announced that it had booked five dedicated launches on Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket between 2028 and 2030.

“There’s a real void opening up in the rideshare market, and Nova is built to fill it,” Stoke VP of Business Development Devon Papandrew said in a statement. “A healthy space economy depends on operators being able to get hardware to orbit early and often, and rideshare is how many of them get there.”

New kid on the pad: Unlike both Falcon 9 and Spectrum, Stoke’s Nova rocket has yet to fly. The fully reusable rocket, which is designed to deliver 15 metric tons to LEO, has some critical milestones ahead—and in September, Stoke announced a $1B Series E to make them happen.

• Nova’s Pathfinder vehicle is expected to make its first flight early next year.

• Nova Block 2 is expected to begin flying in 2029.

Another one: SEOPS also announced the purchase of a third dedicated Falcon 9 mission set to fly in late 2028.

Big picture: SEOPS’ Waymaker program is one effort to fill the impending launch vacuum left by SpaceX’s departure from the rideshare market—a reality that has everyone looking for creative solutions.

• Other launch integrators are also looking to expand their pool of launchers, including ExoLaunch signing a contract with Japan’s MHI H3 in September.

• Portal booked a dedicated launch aboard a Falcon 9, securing the space and timeline it needs, and enlisted integrator Maverick to sell off excess capacity.

• Some companies are trying to avoid the issue all together by building their own rides to space, including AST SpaceMobile, which announced its new Blacklift rocket this month.

October 28, 2026

For astronauts on the International Space Station , looking back to Earth at night can be as dazzling as looking outward toward the stars.

In an essay for Air & Space magazine, Donald Pettit, a NASA astronaut and dedicated photographer , described the “spectacular” view of Earth at night visible from the station. Cities and civilization, he wrote, looked “like tendrils outlined with the glimmer of a Broadway marquee.” Intense, colorful lights cast by clusters of fishing boats across darkened oceans reminded him of “a constellation of stars” forming “unfamiliar members of the Zodiac.”

NASA astronaut Sally Ride —the first American woman to fly in space—also marveled at the “indescribable” sights of Earth from orbit. Lightning was among the most spectacular, she noted in an essay for the same magazine . “On Earth, people see lightning from below the clouds. In orbit, we see it from above,” she wrote. “Bolts of lightning are diffused by the clouds into bursting balls of light. Sometimes, when a storm extends hundreds of miles, it looks like a transcontinental brigade is tossing fireworks from cloud to cloud.”

All three phenomena—city lights, fishing fleets, and lightning—were on display when the space station passed over the South China Sea near Borneo at 14:20 UTC (9:20 p.m. Western Indonesian Time) on October 28, 2026. When an astronaut captured this scene with a Nikon Z9 camera , several overshooting tops bubbled up from thunderstorms, including two illuminated by lightning flashes. These tall, domelike protrusions rise above a thunderstorm’s anvil and sometimes into the stratosphere, indicating strong updrafts and intense storms.

The lights of Singapore , a city-state of 6.2 million people , appear on the left side of the image, with the curving Singapore Strait separating the city from Batam and Bintan islands to the south. The cluster of blue lights west of Singapore, reminiscent of the Pleiades , or Seven Sisters, was likely produced by fishing boats using bright lights to attract squid or schooling fish such as sardines or anchovies. Offshore to the northwest, the scattered orange points are likely gas flares .

For many astronauts, it’s the sight of lightning that lingers. “Like fireflies in the night, lightning is my favorite sight from space,” said NASA astronaut Anil Menon in a video of Earth’s darkened limb that he posted on X , where pinpoints of lightning flicker almost constantly. Lightning is hard to capture and share, he added, but the video offers the best representation he’s seen. “It’s unchanged, at real speed, and shows the vast reach of storms and lightning across earth, plus the rapid flashes that dance across the horizon.”

NASA scientists estimate that there are 2,000 thunderstorms occurring on Earth at any one moment, producing nearly 60 flashes per second—roughly 5 million flashes per day.

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-250951 was acquired on October 28, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew . The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the Internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth . Story by Adam Voiland.

Заголовок: Ringing Black Holes Offer Precision Tests of Relativity
Полный текст:
Black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally canât be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star. Adding to their mystery, several types of black holes exist, including free-floating black holes that drift independently throughout space, stellar-mass and are produced from exploding stars, and supermassive black holes that exist at the center of galaxies like our own. But arguably one of the most mind-blowing mysteries about black holes is figuring out what happens when they collide, and even merge.
Now, a team of more than 70 researchers might be one step closer to solving this decades-long conundrum as they used a combination of computer models and a literature review to analyze how black holes behave when they collide, specifically focusing on a well-known âringingâ phenomenon that occurs when black holes collide and merge. In a recent study published in Classical and Quantum Gravity, the primary motivation behind the study was to advance black hole research by establishing a long-known method called black hole spectroscopy from a theoretical concept to a practical one. Black hole spectroscopy involves measuring the gravitational waves that are produced from two black holes colliding and merging, specifically focusing on the âringdownâ phase, or the waves produced from the newly merged black hole.
In the end, the researchers successfully found that hundreds of observed black hole mergersâ âringdownâ behavior match the longstanding Einstein's theory of General Relativity. While the researchers note current observational methods present limitations for providing more accurate measurements, they emphasize how next-generation ground-based gravitational wave detectors could have the necessary technology for more in-depth and accurate observations of gravitational waves.
âBy listening to the ringing of newly formed black holes, we are turning gravitational waves into a tool for exploring some of the deepest questions in physics, from the nature of gravity itself to the possibility of discovering entirely new forms of matter and energy,â said Dr. Gregorio Carullo, who is an assistant professor in the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Birmingham and a co-author on the study.
Introduced in mathematical equations and a longer paper in 1915 and 1916, respectively, Einsteinâs theory of General Relativity challenged the longstanding hypothesis that gravity acted as an invisible force. In contrast, Einstein proposed gravity behaved like a fabric in both space and time, woven together in a phenomenon called spacetime. As a result, massive celestial objects like stars and planets create curves and warps within this fabric, with the mathematical aspect of the theory also predicting the existence of black holes while also proposing the existence of gravitational waves. However, Einstein himself didnât believe they existed and took this belief to his death in 1955. The reason for his disbelief is because he was convinced that matter was not capable of collapsing inward on itself to create such a state where something like a black hole is produced.
It wasnât until 1964, nine years after Einstein passed away, that the first black hole was discovered, which astronomers designated as Cygnus X-1 and is locate about 7,200 light-years from Earth. And it wasnât for another 51 years that gravitational waves were first detected, 100 years after Einstein first proposed their existence in mathematical equations.
Going forward, the researchers of this latest study anticipate that next-generation observatories could unlock longstanding secrets abut black holes, including gaining insight into their formation and evolution, along with continuing to uphold or challenge theories from Einstein and other scientists.
What new insights into ringing black holes will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!
As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

Заголовок: Senate appropriators unveil $1.1T Pentagon spending bill, folding in reconciliation priorities
Полный текст:
Nearly $69 billion in money sought by the White House through reconciliation will be rolled into the base budget under the Senate appropriator’s plan.

WASHINGTON – Senate appropriators are proposing nearly $1.1 trillion in defense spending for fiscal 2027, a historic figure that includes key priorities but still falls well short of the $1.5 trillion figure sought by the Trump administration.
Until tonight’s release of a proposed spending plan, the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee was the last of the four defense committees to put forth a budget offering. Now its $1.1 trillion figure will have to be sorted out with a slightly lower topline from its House counterparts. (The Armed Services Committees in the House and Senate both included a topline $1.14 trillion figure, though it is not directly comparable to that of the appropriations committees.)
The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion ask was split into two categories: $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in a reconciliation bill. So far, lawmakers have not moved out with that reconciliation request that funds big-ticket priorities like Golden Dome, critical munitions and the bulk of a $55 billion push for the new Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG).
The White House has pushed to still pass that $350 billion by reconciliation, but there has been little sign that will happen. According to Punchbowl News, the top Republican in the Senate, John Thune, declined today to say whether a defense-only reconciliation bill is being actively considered.
RELATED: The fight over the FY27 defense budget is on. Here’s 13 key issues for Congress to resolve.
Senate appropriators are not fans of the reconciliation process, as it takes control of the money out of their hands and gives it to the authorizers. That sentiment was seemingly echoed in a statement from Sen. Mitch McConnell, the defense appropriations subcommittee chair who is retiring at the close of this Congress, who wrote, “This bill is a roadmap to sustainably and responsibly delivering generational investments in the national defense … The nature of warfare is changing, and America’s adversaries are working together to threaten us. Deterring these threats is a project bigger than one-time surges of cash.”
Instead, Senate appropriators are now seeking to funnel some of the Trump priorities into items in their proposal.
“Of this $1.1 trillion, nearly $69 billion, that was initially requested as one-time mandatory spending by the administration, is provided as discretionary funds in order to provide stable, sustainable, and predictable funding for critical capabilities across the Joint Force,” lawmakers wrote in a summary [pdf] of the proposed legislation.
For example, their spending bill includes $9.4 billion for Golden Dome and $3 billion for DAWG; both totals fall far short of the Pentagon’s request, but would be enough keep both initiatives going. The proposed bill includes $47.2 billion to buy munitions with the bulk of the funds, $40.6 billion, directed towards multi-year contracts like Advanced Medium-Range Air to Air Missile, Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement and Precision Strike Missile Increment 1 – key agreements that are in place, in principle, with contractors but have yet to be funded.
Appropriators would also move to rescue other high-priority items like F-35 fighter jets amid dim prospects for a reconciliation bill. Noting that the Trump administration banked on reconciliation to fund 53 jets alongside 32 in its base budget request, appropriators would add roughly half that amount, budgeting an increase of $4.1 billion to buy an additional five conventional takeoff and landing F-35As, five jump-jet F-35Bs and 15 carrier-launched F-35Cs.
Under the SAC’s plan, the Army would see an increase in both procurement and research, development test and evaluation funds, mainly for its aviation programs.
The committee recommended increasing the funding for the Boeing-made Chinook CH-47 helicopters from $210.6 million in the president’s budget to $570.6 million. This is also more than the House committee recommended for the program at $456 million. 
The committee also recommended adding $185 million for the Improved Turbine Engine Program which was zeroed out in the president’s budget. The House committee previously recommended $155 million for the program — which aims to field an engine designed to provide a 50 percent increase in horsepower and a 25 percent improved fuel efficiency rate for the service’s Apache and Blackhawk helos.
Regarding counter drone capabilities for the Army, the committee recommended an increase of $150 million for more Coyote Block 2 and Block 3 platforms, but recommended a decrease of $65.6 million for the Enduring-High Energy Laser program, stating it is “ahead of need.”
When it comes to shipbuilding, the Senate panel included $42 billion with $1.9 billion in additional funding for a second DDG 51 destroyer.
To help pay for unforeseen costs, senate appropriators also included $1.7 billion to “mitigate the department’s projected FY2027 fuel shortfall,” along with $1.9 billion in “flexible readiness funding” to address emerging and unfunded requirements.
Next Steps
The Senate spending bill still needs to work its way through the chamber and receive a vote on the floor before Senate and House leaders decide on the next steps for passing a single bill to the president. And Congressional leaders need to sort it all out by Dec. 11, when the continuing resolution funding the government expires; otherwise, they will have to extend the CR or face a government shutdown.
While US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have continued to publicly push for $1.5 trillion to fund the Pentagon this year, in September the department’s comptroller Jules Hurst told Breaking Defense said he is prepared to work with lawmakers to figure out how to shuffle key priorities.
“If we really want to fund those things, then we have an opportunity to go back to the appropriators before they finalize the bill, at least I think we will…. it’s a conversation, obviously,” Hurst said at the time.
“The question would be, what’s more important to have money for in FY27 [or] can it wait for FY28,” he later added. “And, a lot of these technological areas [are] evolving so fast. Some things we need the money right now to invest in change. … Other things we need to do a little more research and development.”

Заголовок: Canada’s Snowbirds retire Tutor jets after 55 years as long grounding begins
Полный текст:
A farewell flypast closes the Snowbirds’ Tutor era as ageing aircraft, costly upgrades and a lengthy wait for PC-21 replacements reshape the team’s future.

Canada’s Snowbirds have brought 55 years of flying the CT-114 Tutor to a close, returning to Moose Jaw for a farewell flypast before their familiar red-and-white jets enter retirement.

The team’s final scheduled public appearance came on November 15, when nine Tutors flew over Calgary’s McMahon Stadium ahead of the 113th Grey Cup, Canadian football’s championship game. Their homecoming flypast on November 16 provided one last farewell to the Saskatchewan community that has supported generations of Snowbirds personnel.

“Every pilot, technician and team member who has worn the Snowbirds patch has called Moose Jaw home,” the team shared.

“You’ve welcomed every new team, cheered us on through every season and stood by us in the hardest moments. It has been an honour to represent Moose Jaw to North America, and to carry your name with us everywhere we flew … Thank you, Moose Jaw, for 55 incredible years. “

The retirement ends more than six decades of Canadian military service for the homegrown jet. It also begins a prolonged absence for the Snowbirds, whose eventual return will involve a different aircraft — and a switch from jet power to propellers.

Snowbirds return to Moose Jaw for final Tutor flypast

On November 15, nine Snowbirds Tutors flew over Calgary’s McMahon Stadium ahead of the 113th Grey Cup, as the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes prepared to contest Canadian football’s championship.

The CFL proudly welcomes the final flight of the iconic Canadian Forces Snowbirds to Canada’s biggest championship celebration – the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary, AB https://t.co/dI40Kt99w3

— CFL (@CFL) September 3, 2026

The flypast marked the team’s final scheduled public appearance with the aircraft, giving the jets a national sporting send-off before their journey home to Moose Jaw.

In a video message shared by the CFL, team leader Major Maciej Hatta thanked the nation for its support of the Snowbirds: “Thank you Canada, for 55 years of support. It’s been an honour serving our great nation.”

Following the final public appearance of the Snowbirds, today the team headed home.

Flying in from Calgary, the team headed straight to Moose Jaw, but took a wide approach from the north, turning due south to fly down the length of Main Street at around 2,500 feet. The Tutors took a wide circuit around the city before heading south to the base.

Data: Flightradar

On approach to the 15 Wing base at Bushell Park, the jets were joined by a pair of PC-21 turboprop trainers, known in Canada as the CT-157 Siskin II, painting a remarkable picture of the past and the future together.

The Snowbirds celebrated the aircraft, saying, “To the CT-114 Tutor: thank you. You’re a Canadian-built jet that has done more than anyone ever asked of you. You carried generations of pilots through thousands of shows, in every kind of weather, from coast to coast to coast. You were reliable, graceful and unmistakably ours. Few aircraft have ever been so loved.”

As the RCAF closes the door on a five and a half decade history with the Tutor, the Snowbirds face an uncertain future, with the team unlikely to return to flying displays before the 2030s.

The Canadian-built jet trainer that became a national symbol

The Tutor began as Canadair’s CL-41, a privately developed jet trainer intended to win an order from the Royal Canadian Air Force. Designed and manufactured in Montreal, it was the company’s first aircraft developed from scratch rather than adapted from an existing design.

Test pilot Ian MacTavish took the prototype into the air on January 13, 1960. Canada ordered 190 production aircraft in September 1961, with deliveries beginning in 1963. In Canadian military service, the aircraft became the CT-114 Tutor.

Photo: Canadair

Its side-by-side cockpit placed instructor and student alongside each other, with matching controls allowing the instructor to demonstrate techniques or intervene. The small, single-engine jet would become a crucial pillar of Canadian pilot training, serving in that role until 2000.

Its public profile grew through aerobatics. Tutors equipped the Golden Centennaires display team during Canada’s centennial celebrations in 1967, before becoming the aircraft of the Snowbirds in 1971. The team has never flown another aircraft type.

One last time. 🇨🇦 After 55 years, nine CT-114 Tutors made their final scheduled public appearance with the Snowbirds over Calgary. To all who made this legacy possible: thank you. Canada is proud of you. #RCAF #Snowbirds55 https://t.co/SXu5pNgXgz

— Royal Canadian Air Force (@RCAF_ARC) November 16, 2026

Canada was not the Tutor’s only military customer. Malaysia bought 20 examples of the armed CL-41G variant, known locally as the Tebuan, or “wasp.” These served from 1967 to 1986, undertaking training and ground-attack duties. Malaysian parliamentary records also describe low-level and photographic reconnaissance missions in support of ground forces.

A handful also reached civilian hands. One notable private owner was actor and pilot John Travolta, whose CL-41 was donated to Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in 2001 for its aircraft maintenance technology program. That gave the aircraft another educational role after its military career.

Why the RCAF Snowbirds are giving up on the Canadair CT-114 Tutor

Keeping the Snowbirds’ six-decade-old Tutors flying has become an increasingly demanding engineering task. Obsolete components, dwindling spares and problems affecting the aircraft’s engines, airframes and escape systems have progressively narrowed the options for extending their service.

National Defence says retired J85 engines have been cannibalised to supply spare parts , while returning stored aircraft to flying condition would require extensive work. Efforts to improve the escape system also encountered significant technical difficulties: one project was cancelled in 2023, and a separate assessment concluded that replacing the ejection seats could not be achieved within the aircraft’s remaining service life.

Photo: RCAF

Canada had nevertheless been investing in keeping the fleet operational until 2030. A modernisation project approved in 2021 introduced glass cockpit displays, cockpit voice and flight data recorders, new transponders, and updated navigation and communications equipment.

In May, National Defence confirmed to CBC News that C$29.3 million had been spent through the upgrade contract. Eleven modernised Tutors were already in service, while two more were awaiting acceptance test flights — even as the government announced that 2026 would be their final display season.

That timing prompted questions about whether public money had been wasted upgrading aircraft so close to retirement. Moose Jaw MP Fraser Tolmie challenged the logic of the expenditure, while earlier engineering assessments cited by CBC had judged the airframes and engines viable until 2030.

The department’s explanation was that continued monitoring had revealed further engineering challenges requiring work that was no longer technically feasible or practical. New cockpit equipment could meet modern operating requirements, but it could not resolve the ageing fleet’s wider mechanical and safety-system limitations.

The spending was not necessarily without benefit. That investment, which enabled further displays and public engagement, still had value, particularly to those who caught one of the final season’s performances.

Photo: RCAF

The decision to stop flying the Tutors after the 2026 season is more about declining confidence in sustaining future operations than flying safely today. National Defence told CBC that the aircraft were certified for this season, but officials were less confident about subsequent years. With airshow bookings made one or two years ahead, the RCAF said it needed to give organisers notice.

Seven of the 20 aircraft originally earmarked for upgrades will not receive them, and approximately C$1.2 million of the implementation budget is being redirected.

Snowbirds face a long grounding and a jet-less future

The Snowbirds’ next aircraft will be the CT-157 Siskin II, Canada’s designation for the Swiss-built Pilatus PC-21.

Announced in May, the transition is expected to restore the team’s demonstration capability in the early 2030s. The Snowbirds will remain based at Moose Jaw, with the government planning an eventual return to their distinctive nine-aircraft formation.

Photo: SkyAlyne

The choice reconnects the display team with the RCAF’s training fleet. Canada has ordered 19 PC-21s under its Future Aircrew Training program, operated in partnership with SkyAlyne, for advanced fixed-wing training and preparation for the jet stream. The Snowbirds’ aircraft will be a separate acquisition using the same type.

But this new steed will fundamentally change the look and sound of a Snowbirds display. The Tutor’s turbojet produces thrust directly; the PC-21’s turbine drives a propeller. The new aircraft also places its occupants in tandem, rather than side by side.

Propeller power does not preclude demanding aerobatics. The Siskin II has a 1,600-horsepower Pratt & Whitney Canada engine, a published maximum speed of 685 km/h and manoeuvring limits of positive 8G and negative 4G. Australia’s Roulettes have performed with PC-21s since 2019.

Photo: RAAF

For Canada, the eventual routine will have to be developed around the new aircraft’s handling and performance. The government’s commitment is to rebuild the nine-aircraft team; precisely how its future display will compare with the Tutor show remains to be seen.

The PC-21 also should not be confused with a complete replacement for Canada’s former jet-training system. The RCAF retired its CT-155 Hawks in March 2024 and now relies on allied arrangements, principally in the United States and Italy, for fighter lead-in training. A separate Future Fighter Lead-In Training program is intended to restore that domestic capability.

Closing a chapter in Canadian aviation history

The Tutor belongs to an era when Canadian manufacturers were developing military aircraft to meet national requirements. Avro Canada produced the CF-100 interceptor and pursued the supersonic CF-105 Arrow, cancelled in 1959. Canadair’s smaller, less glamorous trainer would prove extraordinarily enduring.

Its retirement should not be mistaken for the disappearance of Canadian aerospace. The industry contributed C$33.1 billion to the economy and supported 218,700 jobs in 2025, according to the Aerospace Industries Association of Canada and the federal industry department . Canada remains among the leading countries in civil aircraft, engines and flight simulators.

Aircraft manufacturing continues through programs including Airbus’s A220 in Mirabel and De Havilland Canada’s Twin Otter and DHC-515 firefighting aircraft. Bombardier, which acquired Canadair in 1986, carries forward another part of that industrial heritage through its business aircraft.

Even the Snowbirds’ Swiss-designed replacement retains a Canadian connection through its Pratt & Whitney Canada engine.

Photo: Canadian Forces Snowbirds

What disappears with the Tutor is something more specific: a flying link between Canada’s military aviation industry, the pilots it trained, and the crowds that watched those skills translate into formation aerobatics.

For 55 years, Canadians looking up at the Snowbirds saw their national team flying an aircraft designed and built at home. When the team returns, its identity and precision will endure — but that particular connection will belong to history.

Заголовок: FAA turned down free Starlink offer before nationwide ground stop, Elon Musk says
Полный текст:
Elon Musk says the FAA declined free Starlink terminals before last week's nationwide ground stop.

Elon Musk says the Federal Aviation Administration could have had Starlink backing up its air traffic communications for free, and he is pointing to last week’s nationwide ground stop as proof it was needed. “As I was saying … Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were,” Musk wrote on X Monday.

Musk was quoting his own post from February 2025, when he wrote that “the ancient system that is rapidly declining in capability was made L3Harris,” while a newer replacement system from Verizon was “not yet operational.” The Department of Transportation has not responded publicly to Musk’s account of the offer.

The outage behind the post began at about 3:30 p.m. ET on Friday, November 13. According to the FAA’s own account , its legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding its FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The agency traced the flood to two locations, a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris had been installing a new router.

Instability spread across 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The agency grounded departures nationwide while about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landed safely, and lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. ET. Operators canceled roughly 12,462 flights that day, though the FAA notes not all of those were directly caused by the ground stop. L3Harris blocked the two sites to stabilize the network, and the FAA disabled the same router function on about 60 similar units. Officials found no sign of a cyberattack.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed prior administrations and dated systems, and has called on Congress to fund a $50 billion overhaul of the system.

Musk’s history with the FAA network goes back to early 2025, when he was leading the Department of Government Efficiency. He claimed on X that the system was failing and putting air travelers at risk, initially blaming Verizon before correcting himself to name L3Harris. The FAA confirmed at the time it was testing Starlink terminals, one at its Atlantic City, New Jersey facility and two at “non-safety critical sites” in Alaska. SpaceX said it was providing the kits at no cost and had no intent to take over any existing FAA contract.

Duffy described Starlink then as “part of a solution” rather than a replacement. By July 2025, the FAA told lawmakers it was not considering replacing its L3Harris and Verizon telecommunications contracts with Starlink.

Whether Starlink would have prevented Friday’s disruption is not clear. The FAA described a fault inside its terrestrial network rather than a loss of connectivity, and Musk did not explain how satellite links would have been used. His post does put SpaceX back in the conversation as Washington debates how to pay for the next air traffic control system. SpaceX already supplies Starlink to commercial airlines for inflight connectivity, and United’s rollout required FAA certification for each aircraft type.

Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured this image of a bright, silica-rich rock in the “Idubi” area using its left Mastcam-Z camera on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023) at the local mean solar time of 13:03:53.

NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU

Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University

Date: Nov. 16, 2026

During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area. These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than the igneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated. Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate. Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica.

Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems. As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars’ hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life. Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils. Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life?

When Perseverance previously encountered silica-rich rocks on the inner rim of Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential. Fortunately, the rocks at “Idubi” offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway.

The Chinese Academy of Sciences built the satellite to test key technologies for its planned Origins space science program, CGTN reported. Later that night, at 11:36 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-627 mission from Vandenberg after two postponements. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.
On Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:47 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched Starship Flight 15 from Starbase, Texas, aiming to catch both stages with its launch tower for the first time. SpaceX was unable to catch the Super Heavy booster after its onboard guidance system made the call to abort the attempt. Instead it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico just before reaching the water. The ship, on the other hand, reached orbit, the second Starship ever to do so, and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites.
Then on Saturday afternoon, after 14 trips around Earth, the rocket’s upper stage slowed over Starbase, dropped between the tower’s mechanical “chopsticks,” and was plucked out of the air. The catch was a first for SpaceX and spaceflight in general — no other spacecraft has ever entered orbit and then been caught at its launch site.
Russia launched a mission from the Vostochny Cosmodrome at 8:16 p.m. EST on Friday, Nov. 13. The Soyuz-2.1b carried a pair of high-resolution imaging satellites and a dozen smaller payloads.

At 12:30 a.m. EST, its Electron rocket flew for the 100th time on The Mountain God Rises, lifting off from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. The rocket placed a synthetic aperture radar satellite into orbit for the Japanese company iQPS. Synthetic aperture radar bounces microwaves off the ground to build images, letting it see through clouds and darkness.

Заголовок: Pentagon fails 9th audit, asserts path towards clean books in 2028
Полный текст:
WASHINGTON — Pentagon officials have again failed an annual department audit, but remain optimistic that incremental improvements made this year will pave the path to a clean report by a 2028 target date.
Details of the audit released in a statement today said the effort examined $4.9 trillion in assets and $5.2 trillion in liabilities. This is the ninth year in a row that the Pentagon has failed the audit, although department officials going back to the first Trump administration have emphasized that the department’s myriad systems, built over decades, would be a long project.
The department received 12 clean opinions, adding the Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund to the 11 that were cleared last year. The department says there are four additional agencies — the Navy Working Capital Fund, Defense Information Systems Agency General Fund, Defense Intelligence Agency (classified AFR) and National Geospatial Intelligence Agency (classified AFR) — projected to be clean by February 2027. By the end of that period, the department claims, 56 percent of assets and over 90 percent liabilities will have been declared clean.
Speaking ahead of the audit’s release, Jules Hurst, the department’s comptroller, said that the department is moving out with a “roadmap” and building on what has worked well to date.
“While we have made progress… [with] the most important development is our change in audit strategy,” Hurst told reporters last week. “That shift is what will put us on the path to achieving a clean, department-wide opinion in 2028.”
That shift includes consolidating 25 separate statements into eight and bringing in outside auditors, according to a press release.
In FY27, Hurst hopes to achieve clean opinions for the Defense-wide Working Capital Fund, US Transportation Command, the Air Force, Army and Navy Working Capital Funds, and several smaller defense agencies.
“From there, in FY 2028, we will focus on the Defense-wide General Fund, a roll-up of the remaining Department components, which is a fundamentally different approach from the entire history of the department,” he added. “We also expect the Navy to achieve a clean opinion on its General Fund in FY 2027, which will support our path to a Department-wide opinion greatly in 2028.”

JPEG (13.80 MB)

Description

This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition.

These images were taken by the Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), a camera that is also located on the end of the rover’s robotic arm. Each hole has a diameter of 0.63 inches (16 millimeters).

Curiosity was built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. JPL leads the mission on behalf of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. MAHLI was built by Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego.

Заголовок: Launch Preview: Ariane 6 to launch Amazon satellites, Falcon 9 to launch government missions
Полный текст:
Following a week of busy launch activity, the worldwide launch manifest is set to see six launches this week, with three SpaceX Falcon 9 missions from Vandenberg, two Chinese missions, and an Ariane 6 mission from South America.

SpaceX will launch payloads for the United States Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office, while at least one of this week’s Chinese missions and the Ariane 6 will launch a batch of internet satellites.

Chang Zheng 2D | Unknown Payload

Wednesday, Nov. 18, will see a launch from China, with a Chang Zheng 2D (CZ-2D) expected to launch from Launch Complex 9 (LC-9) at the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center at 22:50 UTC. Official warning notices indicate a southerly launch trajectory, but details of the payload and its intended orbit will not be released until after launch.

The two-stage, 40.77-m-tall CZ-2D is manufactured by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology (SAST). The 2D variant requires no additional strap-on boosters. This flight will mark the 108th CZ-2D to fly, the seventh of this year.

Falcon 9 | USSF-317 (R-6)

SpaceX’s first of two launches this week comes on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at the start of a four-hour launch window that opens at 7:00 PM PST (03:00 UTC on Thursday).

The only mission for the United States Space Force (USSF) this week, the USSF-317 mission will launch from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California, flying southeast to place its classified payload into low-Earth orbit (LEO).

All systems are looking good, and weather is favorable for liftoff. Propellant load is about to begin for Falcon 9’s launch of the USSF-627 mission from California → https://t.co/IdlZbviZZl pic.twitter.com/fKxyN4DIui

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 12, 2026

Booster B1100 will support this mission, marking its eleventh flight since first supporting Starlink Group 11-30 nearly a year ago on Nov. 23, 2025. Eight of the booster’s previous flights supported Starlink missions, in addition to flying NROL-105 and USSF-385. SpaceX’s west coast droneship, Of Course I Still Love You, will be stationed downrange for B1100’s landing approximately eight minutes after liftoff.

Falcon 9 is a 3.9-m-diameter, 70-m-tall two-stage rocket. Nine Merlin 1D engines power the first-stage booster, while the second stage uses a single vacuum-optimized Merlin engine. Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy were the first orbital rockets to achieve regular re-use, with one Falcon booster having flown 37 flights. The two payload fairings are also recovered and reused after flight.

Chang Zheng 8A | SatNet LEO Group

The second Chinese launch of the week is scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, at 11:00 UTC from the Commercial LC-1 pad at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China. A Chang Zheng 8A (CZ-8A) will carry nine communications satellites into LEO, with the satellites owned by SatNet and operated by the China Satellite Network Group.

The CZ-8A rocket features two 3.35-m-diameter stages, with a total height of 50.54 m. The first stage is assisted by two strap-on liquid-fuelled boosters. This flight will mark the 13th overall CZ-8A flight, the seventh of 2026.

Falcon 9 | NROL-136

SpaceX’s second Falcon 9 mission of the week is scheduled to launch on Saturday, Nov. 21, at 4:30 AM PST (12:30 UTC), again from SLC-4E at VSFB in California. The NROL-136 mission will carry an unknown number of payloads into LEO for the National Reconnaissance Office’s (NRO) Proliferated Architecture constellation, built by SpaceX and Northrop Grumman.

The booster supporting this mission will be B1097, flying for the 14th time. This booster first flew on Sept. 3, 2025, and has previously flown eight Starlink missions, as well as NROL-172, Transporter 17, Sentinel-6B, Twilight (Pandora & Others), and USSF-259. Following stage separation, B1097 will conduct a return-to-launch-site landing at Landing Zone 4 (LZ-4), located directly next to SLC-4E.

Ariane 64 | Amazon Leo (LE-04)

Amazon is continuing to put together its constellation of Leo satellites and will add another 36 on Monday, Nov. 23, at 10:12 UTC aboard an Ariane 64. The rocket will launch from Ensemble de Lancement Ariane 4 (ELA-4) at the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana, with the launch window lasting five hours and 27 minutes. Ariane 64 will follow a northeastern trajectory, delivering 22,000 kg of Leo satellites into LEO.

Ariane 64 is a 62-m-tall, 5.4-m-diameter, expendable two-stage rocket built by the ArianeGroup on behalf of the European Space Agency. Both stages are powered by liquid hydrogen and oxygen-fuelled engines. The 64 variant of the basic Ariane 6 utilizes four P129 strap-on solid rocket boosters to provide additional lift-off thrust. This will be the fifth Ariane 6 mission of 2026.

First flight with P160C boosters
Heaviest Ariane payload ever #LaunchingAmbitions #Ariane6 #VA269 @Amazonleo @ArianeGroup @esa @CNES @EuropeSpacePort pic.twitter.com/YLxW60wAo1

— Arianespace (@Arianespace) June 17, 2026

Falcon 9 | USSF-266 (TH-3)

Closing out the week, a Falcon 9 launch is currently scheduled for Monday, Nov. 23, at 8:04 AM PST (16:04 UTC) — the third this week from SLC-4E at VSFB. The classified USSF-266 mission has a four-hour launch window extending to 12:04 PM PST (20:04 UTC).

Falcon 9 will fly due south, indicating a polar orbit for the payload. While the payload is classified, the launch trajectory and other factors suggest that this may be an additional batch of satellites for the USSF’s Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program. These are based on the SpaceX Starshield satellite bus.

The Falcon 9 booster supporting this flight will be B1081, making its 29th flight. B1081 first flew on Aug. 26, 2023, and flew four missions from SpaceX’s Florida launch sites before moving to Vandenberg for Transporter 10, where it has operated since then. The booster will land atop Of Course I Still Love You , stationed approximately 640 km downrange in the Pacific Ocean.

If the current schedule holds, this will mark the 122nd Falcon 9 flight of 2026, and the 273rd orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026.

Заголовок: Relive Starship's historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and 'Mechazilla' tower catch
Полный текст:
See the most epic photos from SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and historic launch tower catch.

STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

The 33 Raptor engines of SpaceX's Starship V3 rocket during its test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II , with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.
