Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review . View Deal

Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas, as a bird passes on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space , while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

Super Heavy (top) performs a boostback burn after stage separation as Ship 42 (bottom) fires its engines on its way to space. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super Heavy descends back toward Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

Super Heavy flies back toward Texas, firing its engines to slow its descnet on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

Super Heavy flies back toward Texas, firing its engines to slow its descnet on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Three-panel image showing Super Heavy's landing burn, engine cutoff and subsequent explosion. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com)

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit , where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites . It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

SpaceX's Starship V3 rocket launches on a test flight from Starbase, Texas on May 22, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

Starship upper stage approaches the launch tower in Starbase, Texas on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

Starship upper stage lowers into the launch tower in Starbase, Texas on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

The six Raptor 3 engines that powered Ship 42's return are seen as the vehicle hangs by the arms of the "Mechazilla" launch tower arms. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

(Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Starship hangs, caught by its launch tower on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Starship hangs, caught by its launch tower on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

Заголовок: This Supernova is 50 Million Light Years Away, But That's Close Enough For Astronomers
Полный текст:
A new supernova has been detected in a spiral galaxy about 50 million light years away. That's close enough for detatiled follow-up observations, which have already begun. It's a type Ia supernova, meaning it's an exploding white dwarf rather than a massive star ending its life in a core-collapse detonation. Astronomers will watch as its light fades and changes over the next days, months, and years to track the changes and learn more about these standard candles. It's close enough for astrophotographers to get in on the action, too.

A new supernova has been spotted in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy about 50 million light years away. That's pretty close for supernova observations, and it's an opportunity for detailed follow-up study. It's not a core-collapse supernova, where a massive star has burned through its fuel and collapses and explodes. It's a Type Ia supernova. That means it's happening in a binary star, where the exploding star is a white dwarf.
In type Ia supernova, a white dwarf, called the accretor star, draws material away from another star called the donor star. Material builds up on the surface of the white dwarf until it breaches the Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.44 solar masses. Then the white dwarf explodes and is obliterated. A type Ia supernova can also occur in a double white dwarf binary, where the two stars merge and explode.
This supernova is named SN 2026ahvu, where the suffix ahvu is a chronological identifier. It signifies that the supernova is the 41,855th transient discovered in 2026. But even though thousands of transients and supernovae have been found this year, this one is still particularly noteworthy for its relative proximity to Earth, and because it was detected early.
SN 2026ahvu was discovered on November 2nd by ATLAS, the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System. ATLAS is designed and optimized to detect incoming near-Earth Objects shortly before they reach Earth, but it can also detect other transients.
New transients are recorded on the Transient Name Server (TNS), a transient registry sanctioned by the International Astronomical Union (IAU). The TNS also hosts AstroNotes, where short notes are posted describing new transients when they're discovered.
The AstroNotes for SN 2026ahvu reads: "ATLAS operates with 4 x 0.5m telescopes in Hawaii (Haleakala and Mauna Loa), Chile (El Sauce) and South Africa (Sutherland), and a fifth unit in Tenerife, Canary Islands. We are robotically surveying the whole sky with a cadence of 1 day between -50 and +50 and 2 days in the polar regions, weather permitting. While carrying out the primary mission for Near-Earth Objects, we search for and publicly report stationary transients to the IAU Transient Name Server."
"We report a new transient source, most likely a supernova in the galaxy NGC 1433. We are submitting AstroNotes for transients that are either within 100 Mpc, or have some other interesting feature to bring to the community's attention, such as bright nuclear transients, slowly rising or rapidly fading objects."
In this case, the SN's brightness is rising, and that's important for observations. It gives astrophysicists an opportunity to observe the supernova from an earlier point in its evolution. When it was first discovered, its apparent magnitude was 17. A few days later, it was at 13.5. (Lower apparent magnitude means the object is brighter.)
The Dark Energy Camera on the VÃctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope captured these images of NGC 1433 before and after SN 2026ahvu exploded. The before images are from the Dark Energy Survey, DECam's primary job. The after image was taken after ATLAS detected the supernova and alerted other astronomers. The orange star below and to the right is a foreground Milky Way star. Image Credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)
When supernovae are detected, astronomers are alerted and other telescopes watch closely. In this case, there are new images of SN 2026ahvu from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Gemini South telescope.
Type Ia supernovae are typically brightest for about 6 months, but their brightness inevitably drops over time. Their peak brightness lasts several days and is powered by the decay of an unstable nickel isotope, Nickel-56 (56Ni.) Then the decay of âµâ¶Co â âµâ¶Fe creates a weaker tail of light.
This simple schematic shows the typical light curve for a Type Ia supernova, relative to the Sun. The peak is primarily due to the decay of nickel-56 (56Ni), while the later stage is powered by 56-Cobalt to 56-Iron, which is stable. Image Credit: By Xenoforme~commonswiki (attribution as on the source page); SVG reconstruction: PJ Geest. - This file was derived from: SNIacurva.png, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/201323073
About 2 or 3 months after the initial explosion, the ejecta will have thinned out and expanded enough to form a nebula. At that point, when astronomers look at the spectra, they're seeing the composition of the entire exploded star, not just its core. It's a fairly well-understood progression, but there's always room for more observations and more refinement.
Type Ia supernovae are important because they serve as standard candles in the cosmic distance ladder. It's the system astronomers use to find distances to celestial objects that are way too distant for more direct measurements like parallax. So the more opportunities they have to study Type Ia supernovae, the more accurate the cosmic distance ladder is.
Beyond their scientific importance, supernova remnants are among the most visually stunning objects that exist.
This is the Crab Nebula, probably the most well-known supernova remnant. The Hubble captured this image of the nebula, showing it less than 1,000 years after its progenitor exploded. So it's possible that our descendants will see something similar when they observe SN 2026ahvu reads a millennium from now. Image Credit: By NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University) - A Giant Hubble Mosaic of the Crab Nebula, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/516106
More images and observations, included detailed study of how the explosion's light changes over time, will follow. The supernova is also within reach of astrophotographers, so there could be some fantastic images arriving soon.

Заголовок: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
Полный текст:
Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions.

One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.

A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.

Finding the centers

The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

Заголовок: Iceye’s Fifth Generation SAR Satellite Built for 11cm Resolution
Полный текст:
Iceye announced its next-generation satellite, designed to provide synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging in as fine as 11 centimeter resolution for sovereign nations, and 16 cm for commercial customers.

This marks the fifth generation, Gen5, of Iceye’s SAR constellation. The satellites are designed to provide faster downlink than the previous generation, at up to 1 Gbps of downlink speed, compared to 700 Mbps in the previous version.

The satellites are also designed to collect more images per pass than the previous version, with 18 images per acquisition, compared to 15 images in the previous acquisition.

Iceye did not state when the first Gen5 satellites will launch, but said that it can deliver Gen5 satellites to customers within 12 months of deal signing.

Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company updates its satellite generations approximately every 18 months, and issues new software releases each quarter.

“Time to decision is everything in space-based intelligence, whether you’re tracking a vessel or responding to a flood. Gen5 shortens it at every step: sharper and more images per pass, and AI analysis that starts in orbit,” Modrzewski commented.

The first satellites in Iceye’s previous generation, Gen4, were launched in March of 2025. In comparison, Gen4 offers resolution up to 16 cm and up to 700 Mbps data downlink with a steerable antenna.

Iceye stated that the new generation will be fully compatible with the ground segment of previous versions, so existing customers can onboard Gen5 satellites without change.

Заголовок: Umbra Secures Launch for Next 7 SAR Satellites WIth Increased Capabilities
Полный текст:
Umbra has secured launches for its next seven synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites as it upgrades its constellation. Umbra also released the first images from its 13th and 14th satellites, which launched in October.

Satellites Umbra-13 and Umbra-14 both launched to mid-inclination orbit in the SpaceX Bandwagon mission on October 20 , and Umbra-14 delivered its first image on October 24, followed by Umbra-13 on October 28.

Umbra CEO David Langan said in a statement that time to first images speaks to the company’s “relentless improvement” on its early operations and imaging.

Umbra has secured rides for its next seven SAR satellites. Spacecraft 15 through 18 are set to launch on the SpaceX Bandwagon-6 rideshare mission, planned no earlier than April 2027.

Then satellites 19 and 20 and a spacecraft for a private demonstration for an unnamed customer will launch on the SEOPS Waymaker-1 dedicated rideshare mission. Waymaker is a new rideshare concept from SEOPS, which booked a full Falcon 9 mission and is providing integration, mission management, and in-orbit services to customers. That mission is targeted no earlier than April 2028.

Umbra said these secured launches enable the company to build spacecraft for a defined schedule “at a time of acute demand for access to space.”

“We design our spacecraft to be compatible with multiple launch vehicles, giving us the flexibility to secure access to space and respond to evolving mission requirements. With launch capacity secured for our next seven spacecraft, we’re positioned to build on that momentum, expand our constellation, and deliver greater intelligence value to our customers,” Langan commented.

Заголовок: Meridian Space Validates Reflectarray Antenna in Space
Полный текст:
Meridian Space has validated its reflectarray antenna technology on the operator’s demonstration satellite, which launched early October.

The First Customer Link (FCL) satellite demonstrated high bandwidth communications, communicating with a ground segment deployed in Toulouse, France, Meridian CEO Massimiliano Ladovaz told Via Satellite.

For Meridian Space, it validated five years of development on the proprietary reflectarray antenna technology, as the company hopes to make Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations economically feasible for governments and regional operators.

“You need this antenna to deliver a constellation at an order of magnitude cheaper than every other system; without this antenna, you couldn’t get there,” Ladovaz said. “We have demonstrated it on the ground. Now we have demonstrated on in orbit. There is no doubt that we can deliver on that, and we can claim very clearly that the antenna is here and now.”

Ladovaz explained that what sets this demonstration apart is that previous reconfigurable reflect arrays are in fixed systems, which are not as useful for telecommunications use cases. And compared to other software-defined communications satellites, the Meridian payload is designed to be much lower power, and support operations on a smaller platform.

Meridian built the communications payload, and Kongsberg NanoAvionics provided the satellite bus.

Now, Meridian will go through a testing and demonstration phase with early customers, particularly governments, regional satellite operators, and telcos.

“We will test everything from fixed applications to mobility applications, maybe some special waveforms for defense applications,” he said. “There are not that many satellites in orbit with those frequencies as well. We have a lot of demand from people that want to test.”

Ladovaz also mentioned that Meridian stuck to the timeline it originally stated when the constellation was announced in April of 2025, to launch the first satellite in 2026.

Meridian Space is a “spin out” of kinetic launch startup SpinLaunch, which is now being separated into an independent company . Ladovaz, who has deep experience in the satellite industry from OneWeb, Eutelsat, SES, and Inmarsat, joined the company in July last year .

Ladovaz said Meridian is focused on scaling up production in Long Beach, California, as well as expanding its presence in Europe. The company is working on the “flat satellite design,” which uses the same payload technology in a compact design to deploy more satellites in a single launch.

Заголовок: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
Полный текст:
Credit: NASA

For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements.

The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position.

“Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.”

The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources.

In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole.

NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time.

The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Заголовок: Vulcan failure deepens concerns over US military launch capacity
Полный текст:
The failed launch could further delay the rocket’s return to national security missions as the Space Force works to expand its launch options.

WASHINGTON — Sunday’s failed launch of United Launch Alliance’s (ULA) Vulcan rocket adds to growing concerns about the Space Force’s hopes to dramatically increase its launch cadence over the next few years.
The Vulcan suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes after liftoff, preventing the rocket from reaching orbit and destroying 40 satellites for Amazon LEO’s planned broadband network for low-Earth orbit. The failure will likely trigger a lengthy investigation that could ground the rocket for months, further limiting the number of US rockets available for both national security and commercial customers.
The incident further cements SpaceX’s near monopoly on US space launch. Aside from Vulcan, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy are the only rockets currently authorized to carry critical payloads under the Space Force’s National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 3 Lane 2 program — given that Blue Origin’s New Glenn also remains grounded following a launch pad explosion in May.
“We can hope that whatever caused this problem gets fixed. We can hope that Vulcan, New Glenn and other medium-lift vehicles come online soon, but this is really the same place we have been for the last several years,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Breaking Defense. “But the launch bottleneck is real and set to get worse.”
While the failed Vulcan mission was carrying a commercial payload, it was also designed to serve as an important step toward the rocket’s return to the Space Force’s NSSL program.
Vulcan was grounded by the service in late February due to persistent problems with its solid rocket boosters. By Oct. 1, the Space Force reassigned six NSSL missions previously manifested on Vulcan to SpaceX.
ULA has yet to publicly announce the cause of the rocket’s failure shortly after liftoff, but the problem appears to have occurred in the booster stage, according to a report in Ars Technica. If the rocket’s BE-4 engines were involved, the failure could also have implications for Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which uses the same engines.
“If the issue is with the BE-4 that is a particularly thorny problem — for the Pentagon, for NASA, for Amazon and for anyone who needs a ride to space,” Swope said.
Meanwhile, SpaceX is making progress with development of its new, fully reusable Starship super-heavy launch vehicle. During a test flight on Nov. 14, the company demonstrated for the first time its ability to capture the rocket’s massive upper stage.
The company plans to shift all of its own launch operations to Starship around 2030, phasing out its Falcon rockets In September, SpaceX stopped taking commercial orders for Falcon rides post 2028. The company has also yet to announce plans to offer Starship launches to commercial or military customers.
Those decisions have caused widespread concerns about a potential multiyear gap between demand for US launch services and available capacity.
“I don’t see a magic wand here. I mean, the only thing that could happen is that somebody persuades Elon to keep Falcon 9 flying until there are viable alternatives,” said Martin Halliwell, of Luxembourg-based private equity firm New Space Capital.

Заголовок: SpaceNukes Opens Los Alamos Manufacture and Materials Facility to Build Its Next-Generation Space Reactor
Полный текст:
LOS ALAMOS, N.M., Nov. 16, 2026 — Space Nuclear Power Corp. (SpaceNukes) opened its Manufacture and Materials Development Facility at 150 Central Park Square in Los Alamos on Nov. 13. The facility is dedicated to manufacture and materials development for the company’s Generation 2 reactor, including additive manufacturing of nickel-based and refractory alloys. No radioactive material is handled in the facility.
SpaceNukes’ next-generation reactor is designed to run much hotter. A hotter reactor needs a much smaller radiator, which makes up most of the mass of a space fission power system. Raising the temperature at which heat is rejected lets the same-size radiator shed roughly six times as much heat. The limit is not the nuclear physics but the materials. Today’s power conversion hardware already sits at the edge of what nickel-based superalloys tolerate over a long mission, so going hotter means moving to refractory alloys of tungsten, molybdenum, tantalum, rhenium and niobium. These metals are difficult to form, and many of the component shapes and materials SpaceNukes needs cannot be bought from any supplier.
“Our next-generation reactor is a bet on temperature,” said Andrew Phelps, CEO of SpaceNukes. “What stands between us and that is not the nuclear physics. The physics is in good shape, and it was proven in 2018. The limit is metal. Our next reactor is a materials and manufacturing challenge before it is a reactor problem, and that is what this building is for.”
The facility is led by Omar Mireles, director of manufacture and materials, who heads the Generation 2 program. Mireles spent 13 years as a research engineer and principal investigator at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, where he led the $25 million Refractory Alloy Additive Manufacturing Build Optimization project.
“Additive manufacturing is used only for specific circumstances,” Mireles said. “You have parts that are highly complex, made from materials that are difficult to form, have a low production rate that won’t benefit from economy of scale, and have the design flexibility that can optimize designs to the manufacturing process. These lessons were learned over the last two decades in the liquid rocket engine community, and we are applying them to the needs of SpaceNukes, which have very similar conditions. We are manufacturing aerospace components at aerospace-quality standards. This building is where we learn to make them.”
The Los Alamos facility complements SpaceNukes’ integration and test facility in Medina, Ohio, led by chief engineer Marc Gibson. SpaceNukes is now building hardware to test components for its Generation 2 reactors at the Ohio facility.
The grand opening featured remarks from Phelps and Mireles, a ribbon cutting and tours of the new facility. Guests included staff from the office of Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; Los Alamos National Laboratory and its Feynman Center for Innovation; the Los Alamos County Council; the Los Alamos County Community Development Department; the Los Alamos Commerce & Development Corp.; the Los Alamos Chamber of Commerce; Century Bank; Merrill Lynch; and space industry partners.
The facility opening follows SpaceNukes’ Oct. 21 announcement of an agreement with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, under its Fast Capacitance (Fat Cat) program, to design, build and ground-test an actively controlled Kilopower reactor with Los Alamos National Laboratory. It comes as SpaceNukes works to fly a nuclear reactor by 2028.
About Space Nuclear Power Corp.
Space Nuclear Power Corp. (SpaceNukes) builds nuclear reactors that power missions in space for government and commercial clients. In March 2018, the team that is now SpaceNukes ran a space reactor at full temperature and power for 28 hours, and it performed as predicted. It was the first time this had been done in the United States in 50 years. The team took it from concept to full power in three years for less than $20 million. Today, SpaceNukes has roughly 15 full-time employees, more than $50 million in contracts and agreements with the Department of War and NASA, two completed Space Force design reviews and a Los Alamos National Laboratory license for the reactor technology its founders invented there. Space Nuclear Power Corp., headquartered in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is committed to delivering safe, affordable, reliable nuclear power wherever people and machines go in space.

Заголовок: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place
Полный текст:
Appeals court ruling rejected grant cancellations on First Amendment grounds.

On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications.

The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision.

The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI , and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search .

Полный текст:
All estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt.

The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.

However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?

The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.

Заголовок: This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?
Полный текст:
Astronomers have found a Long Period Radio Transient about 5,000 light years away that's different from other LPTs. Other LPTs have a white dwarf and a red dwarf, but this one has a white dwarf and a main sequence star. The exact cause of the binary pair's radio pulses isn't certain, but this work narrows it down. It also shows that these binaries could be common progenitors for Type Ia supernova explosions.

Unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves. The sources of many of these signals are well-understood, and in some cases, special spacecraft have been launched to monitor them. But some remain unexplained.
Radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures. Radio astronomy has been around for decades, so many of these are well-understood. But not all of them. Some of them have only been discovered more recently and are awaiting an explanation.
One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours. That's important because it differentiates them from pulsars and their extremely short radio periods. Astronomers have only detected about 15 LPTs in total, and they've had difficulty explaining exactly what they are and how they generate their radio pulses.
There are different hypotheses invoked to explain them. They could be magnetars, which are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields that rotate very slowly. Or they could be something exotic and speculative, like strange dwarf pulsars.
But at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. Astronomers have only been able to confirm the white dwarf's companion in a handful of cases, and in those, the companion is a red dwarf.
Now astronomers have identified for the first time a LPT that consists of a white dwarf with a Sun-like, G-type star as its companion. Their results are published in Nature Astronomy in a paper titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion." The lead author is Dr. Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR.
At the time of this research, there were only 12 detected LPTs, and the ones with identified components favoured WD and red dwarf pairs. "An optical follow-up confirmed that at least 4 (ouf of 12) long-period transients are binary systems comprising a white dwarf and an M dwarf," the authors write. But this newly-detected LPT, named GPM J071507â114153, bucks that trend. "It is a binary system comprising a low-mass white dwarf and a G-type star identified via optical spectroscopy."
âWe detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,â said co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker, Associate Professor at the Curtin Institute of Radio Astronomy.
The MWA detected 214 separate pulses, and the MeerKAT pinpointed its location based on 33 detected pulses. 26 of MeerKAT's pulses were co-detected by the MWA.
The new LPT has a period of only 7.9âminutes, which is almost certainly from its rotation. The properties of its radio pulses, like its polarization, are modulated by a longer period of about 1.3âdays, which the researchers say is the binary system's orbital period.
Follow-up optical observations and spectrometry came from the Keck Telescopes. "The optical counterpart of J0715-1141 was observed with the low-resolution imaging spectrometer on the Keck 1 telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii," the authors write. Those observations were a pair of 1,200 second exposures. They let the researchers determine the nature of the WD's partner star.
This figure from the research shows the optical spectrum of the new LPT, J0715-1141, compared to model spectra from F-type, G-type, and K-type stars. The spectrum most closely matches that of a G-type, Sun-like star. "As a comparison, hotter F-type and cooler K-type stars show distinct spectral features not present in the data," the authors write. The three panels on the right highlight this in three different elements. Image Credit: McSweeney, S.J., Hurley-Walker, N., Bahramian, A. et al. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion. Nat Astron (2026).
In this case, the WD's binary partner is a star like our Sun, which is far more massive and luminous than the M dwarfs (red dwarfs) found in other LPTs. So this rules out the idea that only WD-red dwarf pairs can generate LPTs.
Astronomers and astrophysicists want to know exactly how these radio pulses are generated. Can any of their observations help researchers determine the exact source of the radio pulses? Not exactly, but the clarity of the pulses helps narrow it down.
âThis is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,â said lead author McSweeney.
"We conclude that in long-period transients powered by white dwarf binaries, the coherent radio pulsed emission crucially depends on its interaction with the companion star, which we show can be G-type stars in day-long orbits," the researchers write.
There's another suprise in these findings. The pulses from the WD let the researchers detect stellar flares from the Sun-like star as it passed in front of the WD.
âAs a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a âstellar prominenceâ, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a starâs surface,â Hurley-Walker said. âItâs amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.â
This image shows a solar prominence from the Sun in 2010, with Earth shown for scale. The researchers were able to detect one of these coming from the main sequence star in the pair, as the white dwarf moved behind it. That's pretty impressive for a star that's 5,000 light years away. Image Credit: NASA/SDO
One questions astronomers ask is how these types of binaries form, and the researchers have a hypothesis for that. They say the system could've formed through binary evolution. "One possibility is that the present configuration of the system arises through post-common-envelope (CE) binary evolution," they write. The progenitor of the system most likely had an intermediate-mass primary with a lower-mass companion on a wider orbit. "As the primary evolved off the main sequence and expanded into a giant, unstable mass transfer initiated a CE phase, during which orbital energy and angular momentum were transferred to the envelope, leading to its ejection and substantial orbital shrinkage."
The primary star was left as an exposed stellar core, and evolved to become a WD, creating the situation the astronomers see today: a WD star with a G-type partner, that are still in a binary relationship, but detached from the common envelope they once shared.
As for the system's future, it could hold a cataclysmic explosion.
Binaries like this that have left their common envelopes, and that consist of a WD and a massive main-sequence star, are potential breeding grounds for eventual Type Ia supernovae. This can happen as their orbit decays and the WD accretes material from its companion. Once enough material builds up on the accreting WD, it explodes and destroys the WD. Or they could created a double degenerate WD-WD merger, if the main sequence companion collapses before the binary orbit decays.
Could the radio signals from LPTs be used to find the progenitors of these supernovae explosions?
"Radio detections of LPTs may offer a route to finding cooler WDs around hotter stars at greater distances than traditional ultraviolet and optical surveys," the authors write.
The upcoming Square Kilometre Array could be the key to this.
"In an era of larger and more sensitive radio surveys, such as those to be conducted by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, this may form a new pathway for investigating the progenitors of type Ia supernovae," the authors write.

Заголовок: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
Полный текст:
Voyager 1 is approaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a milestone that highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.

After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth.

This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond.

Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year . Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space.

For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement.

By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth , a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

A NASA visualization showing Voyager 1 looking back towards the solar system as it approaches one light-day away from Earth. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe.

Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977 . Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day.

Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2 , which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035.

As Voyager 1 and, eventually, Voyager 2 continue their journeys through interstellar space , their growing distances from Earth offer a measure of both the reach of human exploration and the communication challenges that come with sending spacecraft ever farther into the cosmos.

Заголовок: As exquisite radars become targets, smaller tactical sensors take on a bigger role
Полный текст:
[Sponsored] Record demand for radars is accelerating investment in manufacturing capacity and a distributed supply chain.

Missile and drone attacks in Ukraine and the Middle East are putting new pressure on the radars that underpin air-and-missile defense, driving demand for systems that can be fielded faster, in greater numbers, and be networked across a wider area.
Breaking Defense spoke with Joe Mollo, senior director of Advanced Programs at Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit (DRS RADA), about surging demand for tactical radars, the push to expand manufacturing capacity, and how a new generation of sensors could change the way air defenses are built.
Breaking Defense: There’s been a lot of attention in Washington on defense-industrial base capacity and resilience, particularly in response to the new threats we’re facing in the CENTCOM region. Summarize what you view as the rapidly evolving threat?
Mollo: The Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran loitering munition has become the poster-child of this new threat environment, and it’s evolving on multiple axes at once. In Ukraine, we’ve seen single-day tactical drone employment exceed 10,000 units along the front line, while the long-range strike variant aimed at cities has simultaneously gone jet-powered – now representing over half of deep-strike sorties, shortening the already challenging warning time of the original propeller-driven design, requiring a defense that detects sooner, engages further, and acts faster.
Against Israel, we’ve now seen three massive, coordinated Iranian state barrages – April 2024, October 2024, and the 12-day war in June 2025 – each launching hundreds to over a thousand ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones directly from Iranian soil. Layer on top of that the grinding, continuous fire from Iran’s proxies: 15,000-20,000-plus rockets, missiles, and drones from Hezbollah and the Houthis. The threat is constant and pervasive, requiring a defense that scales, costs less, and is mobile.
Operation Epic Fury and the parallel Houthi Red Sea campaign showed this threat has outgrown any single theater. Iran demonstrated both the willingness and the reach to strike across the entire Gulf – and, more troubling for us, the ability to take out major US IAMD sensor infrastructure.
Ballistic missiles and low-cost one-way attack drones together damaged or destroyed radar systems in Qatar, Jordan, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, and Kuwait – including a $1.1 billion early-warning radar. Those systems will take years to replace.
This requires a defense that can be produced faster and has a cost that supports dispersed operations for survivability. Such systems need to look at things that are low and slow or low and fast, the cruise missiles, the Group 3 drones. Tactical radars for survivability’s sake and the ability to look low have become a real hot item. If you’re going to have a big radar protecting a geographic area and that’s the first thing that gets hit, well now I need smaller, more dispersed radar capabilities.
The real issue is whether the US industrial base produces sensor and interceptor systems at the quantity and speed that this evolving threat demands in order to protect US and allied interests.
How does this translate to DRS RADA?
As a leading global supplier of tactical radar systems for counter-UAS, air-defense, and missile-defense applications, DRS RADA is feeling the stress of significant demand across both US and international markets. In the United States, demand is increasing from the Department of War and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as through Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Direct Commercial Sales (DCS) to international partners.
DRS RADA also continues to see sustained demand from customers in the Middle East and Eastern Europe served through its non-US operations. This is reflected in record bookings in each of the past two quarters, underscoring both the breadth and urgency of this demand.
Ukraine came in at the end of 2023 with a single order in which they ordered more than we had sold the prior two years. All of a sudden we’re getting this tremendous demand for tactical radars.
Additionally, there is an increased emphasis on robust homeland missile defense, especially in light of the operational lessons demonstrating the vulnerability of our current inventory of long-range sensors. Looking at the Golden Dome concept, these expensive radars, which are necessary for your long-range ballistic missiles, are the first to be hit. And, oh by the way, they take four or five years to produce and cost half a billion to a billion dollars.
In response, we looked at any way we can use smaller tactical radars in a disaggregated way. This would include geographically dispersed sensors that are more affordable and manufacturable at scale, that can be networked to provide the coverage, resilience, and mission performance traditionally associated with a few exquisite systems. DRS RADA’s tactical radar portfolio is well aligned with this shift toward disaggregated, networked sensing.
DRS RADA also supports numerous prime contractors and system integrators that are responding to the same market demand. These customers require close engineering and program support to integrate DRS RADA radar systems into complete mission solutions spanning the detect-to-effect chain. As a result, growth in radar-unit demand is accompanied by increased requirements for product development, systems integration, technical support, and manufacturing resources.
Together, these dynamics – higher demand volumes, shorter delivery timelines, and increasingly challenging customer requirements – are driving substantial investment in accelerated product development and expanded manufacturing and test capacity.
How is DRS RADA addressing the surge in demand?
The 2022 merger with Leonardo DRS has been instrumental in enabling the company to scale in response to growing customer demand. This merger has enabled us to increase R&D investment to accelerate new-product development, capitalize expanded manufacturing and test capacity, and add the technical and business infrastructure needed to build and sustain a global presence.
DRS RADA currently manufactures six radar models spanning a range of sizes, power levels, and missions. We continue to sustain and advance these models through ongoing improvements informed by requirements derived from extensive operational deployments. For example, these changes may support new technical requirements, such as new electronic counter-countermeasures, ECCM, threats and integration requirements.
DRS RADA is releasing two new radar models this month, the result of significant R&D investment and extensive development, integration, and testing over the past several years.
In terms of capital investment, the company has committed to expanding capacity in the communities that have supported our growth, while leveraging its broader international footprint to strengthen the supply chain for critical materials. At our Germantown, Maryland, facility, RADA has expanded its engineering and manufacturing workforce from 30 to 150 employees with 60 more planned for early 2027.
Our footprint has increased nearly 10-fold and our complex test facilities by four times. We are planning another wave of expansion to accommodate our newest product, the cxMHR (RPS-502), which is larger and more complex than any of our other systems, requiring its own dedicated production and test facilitation. And we’ve got another expansion following what we’re doing right now.
We’ve been in Montgomery County for the entire time we’ve been in the US and we wanted to stay there, stay there with the people that have worked with us all that time, stay with the community that supported us. So we’ve made all that investment right at home in Germantown, Maryland.
However, our global development and manufacturing footprint has undertaken expansion across our multiple facilities similar in scale to our US operations. These facilities are located in operational areas of conflict or where regional restrictions require a physical presence. One of the benefits of this distributed manufacturing footprint is that it improves DRS RADA’s supply-chain resilience and cost efficiency by enabling each location to source appropriate materials from its respective regional market, which can then be made available company wide, reducing dependence on any single supplier base or geography.
What does the cxMHR bring operationally?
As I noted earlier, the cxMHR is significantly larger, more powerful, and more complex than our other radar models and represents a major technology step forward that delivers a clear operational advantage in the medium-range tactical radar market.
The cxMHR operates in C-band, which occupies a very useful middle ground. It provides the high-resolution and precision-tracking performance typically associated with higher-frequency X-band systems while offering range and weather benefits similar to S-band.
What is particularly unique and important is that the cxMHR uses a fully digital aperture. Like all of our radars, the cxMHR is a software-defined active electronically scanned array (AESA) system. AESA is the current state of the art for tactical radars, giving users tremendous flexibility to tailor performance for a specific mission or to support multiple missions simultaneously, all through software control. This is particularly important for evolving missions or multi-mission requirements and for resilience against electronic attack.
AESA technology represents a meaningful distinction from both conventional phased-array and metamaterial-based approaches. A conventional passive phased-array radar relies on a centralized transmitter and phase control across the aperture, which provides electronic beam steering, but less independent control over the individual radiating elements and less flexibility to generate or manage multiple, mission-specific functions simultaneously. Metamaterial apertures performance is far less effective in mitigating electronic attack because it is closely linked to the electromagnetic response of the physical surface and requires iterative aperture-specific optimization to achieve a particular use case.
With a fully digital array, the cxMHR takes AESA another step forward. The cxMHR’s fully digital AESA architecture provides true, independent, per-element control across the transmit/receive aperture. This gives the radar exceptional ability to tailor beams, waveforms, power distribution, and radar-resource allocation rapidly and repeatedly via digital control.
The operational advantages are profound. These include: up to 40 times faster volume scan; precision beam pointing, a narrower main beam, less SNR loss, longer detection range, and less multi-path interference; simultaneous search, track, and jammer localization beams; ECCM and EMI performance with less clutter and better jamming suppression; independent element calibration and control for less loss and graceful degradation; and frequency diversity for reduced multipath elevation errors and reduced RCS fluctuation, resulting in a higher Pd.
If it gets shot, you’re not going to take out half of the radar. You’re going to take out maybe one of these elements, maybe four of them. The radar will still continue to work. It’s not a spinner. It gives you the whole 360-degree constant view, and there’s no moving parts in the antenna assembly.
In terms of dealing with jammers and interference from other sources, there’s less clutter and more resistance to jamming.
With true per-element digital control, the cxMHR can make mission-driven adjustments through digital control in a faster, more repeatable, and more deterministic manner.
What are your thoughts on the future of DRS RADA?
DRS RADA is well positioned to help the United States and its allies address the rapidly evolving threats we’re seeing in the CENTCOM region and future battlespaces. Since entering the tactical radar market eight years ago, DRS RADA has consistently invested in technology, product performance, and responsiveness to operational user requirements.
From its first prototype, DRS RADA has designed its radars around gallium nitride (GaN) technology and software-defined AESA architectures. GaN enables higher performance in a smaller, lighter, and more power-efficient package than legacy gallium arsenide based (GaAs) systems. While the US continues to pay for vendors to upgrade its tactical-radar inventory from GaAs to GaN, DRS RADA’s radar portfolio was designed around GaN from the outset.
Equally important, DRS RADA’s products have been shaped by extensive operational experience and direct user feedback. It wouldn’t be out of the realm of possibility to say that more of our radars have been shot than some of our competitors have ever produced. We continue to sustain and advance our radar models through extensive R&D investment, incorporating improvements that address evolving mission requirements and emerging threats.
DRS RADA has always operated under a startup mentality with continuous innovation. It’s served us really well and it continues to serve us really well because our adversaries have that same pace of change.
DRS RADA radars led the way for US capabilities in mobile short-range air defense, counter-UAS, and active protection system missions. Building on that foundation, the company continues to deliver high-performing tactical radars and develop integrated sensor solutions that help warfighters detect, track, and respond to the new and evolving threats they face in battle.

The 2026-2028 Documento Programmatico Pluriennale (DPP) was published late Sunday, and includes national defense plans and investments from the ministry of defense.
The naval launcher will be designed to equip both the FREMM EVO frigates and DDX destroyers classes of warships.

The DPP also outlined plans to acquire two new FREMM EVO frigates, built by Orizzonte Sistemi Navali (OSN), a joint venture between Fincantieri and Leonardo.

Заголовок: 'Maybe the scariest thing I've heard in my life': Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover reveals his toughest challenge before flying to the moon
Полный текст:
For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, one of the hardest parts of traveling to the moon happened before he even left Earth.

TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters.

Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet.

"This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said.

Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1 , 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972.

But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead.

When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space.

"We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained.

Victor Glover speaking at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, 2026. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic/Future)

The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center , toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station . But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home.

Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard.

"You should have this talk with our daughters."

And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have.

"We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard."

The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life , by Chief Tecumseh.

The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking.

"It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. There's a real point to this and there's a reason to take this risk," Glover explained. "This poem helped me to say it in a way that I didn't have words for."

After traveling around the moon and returning safely to Earth, one moment stood out above all others. When we asked Glover in a separate interview at Starmus on Oct. 20, which moment from Artemis II he would most like to relive, he answered immediately.

"Splashdown."

"It's the true, ultimate mission accomplishment. Just 'we did it.' We survived. My family is relieved, and there's just nothing like it," Glover explained. "There's nothing like coming home. There's nothing like returning to Earth."

The UK government has defended the resilience of its satellite-based military communications, saying that while it uses SpaceX’s Starshield service, it does not depend on any single commercial provider for critical communications. The assurance comes amid concerns about reliance on SpaceX after it emerged that restrictions had been placed on Ukraine’s access to the company’s satellite communications services.

The assurance came in response to a parliamentary question from Liberal Democrat MP Helen Maguire, who asked what assessment the Ministry of Defence (MOD) had made of the consequences of losing access to Starlink and Starshield, and how it was ensuring the UK’s strategic autonomy.

Responding on 10 November, defence minister Luke Pollard distinguished between the two services, stating that “Starlink is not used for UK military operations.” He added that the MOD uses Starshield but employs a combination of military and commercial satellite communications capabilities to reduce dependence on any one provider.

In its 2024 report, Ukraine: A Wake-Up Call , the House of Lords International Relations and Defence Committee highlighted the speed and flexibility commercial providers had brought to Ukraine’s war effort. However, it also raised questions about whether companies could be relied upon to maintain continuous service and how they could be held accountable during conflict.

The report cited evidence from RAND space policy analyst Theodora Ogden concerning reported restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starlink, particularly for controlling unmanned systems in the Black Sea.

The issue returned to parliamentary discussions in October during a hearing of the Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy. MP Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi drew attention to the impact of Starlink restrictions on Ukraine during a discussion about threats to space infrastructure.

“We have seen the devastating impact that Starlink being slowed down and restricted for Ukraine has had,” said Dhesi.

In answers published on 16 November in response to a set of three questions tabled by Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary, Pollard said the MOD had access to a substantial number of Starshield terminals, although he did not disclose the specific figure on national security grounds.

He explained that decisions to use Starshield were made based on individual military requirements, with the service operating alongside other capabilities. Pollard declined to list specific applications or provide details of the military’s dependence on the service, citing the sensitivity of operational information. He instead described Starshield as an additional communications capability within a broader strategy, providing “operational resilience through diversity”.

Заголовок: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
Полный текст:
The legend of the Black Knight satellite offers an example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can accumulate into a single conspiracy theory over time.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you."

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the " Black Knight Satellite ," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Odd detections at Colorado Springs

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signal s while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

Unidentified objects in orbit?

Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times .

Retired Marine Corps major Donald E. Keyhoe holds a copy of his book, "Flying Saucers from Outer Space," in which he claims UFOs are spacecraft from another planet and that the U.S. Air Force has secret film recordings proving that they are interplanetary craft. (Image credit: Bettmann/Getty Images)

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well , with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies " resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here ).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper, pilot for the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, during flight test simulations prior to launch. (Image credit: NASA)

"Echoes" from a 13,000-year-old satellite

Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes , proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

The STS-88 mission photographs

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview .

(Image credit: NASA/CC BY-SA 4.0)

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!"

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand."

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

Space Shuttle Endeavour's robotic Canadarm positions Russia's Zarya module above the Unity module during the STS-88 mission while constructing the International Space Station. (Image credit: NASA)

The legend continues

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email , while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!"

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

Полный текст:
Seeking to shorten the timeline from orbital data collection to operational decision-making, Finnish radar satellite manufacturer ICEYE unveiled its fifth-generation synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite system, Gen5, on Monday, Nov. 16.
Marking the company’s fifth spacecraft generation in eight years, the platform introduces finer ground resolution, increased collection agility, and onboard artificial intelligence (AI) processing for defense, intelligence, and emergency response missions.
Higher Resolution and Orbital Collection Specs
Gen5 expands imaging performance across both government and commercial operating modes:
- Government Imaging Mode: Utilizes 1,800 megahertz (MHz) of bandwidth to achieve ground resolution as fine as 11 centimeters (cm), subject to International Telecommunication Union (ITU) regulatory compliance.
- Standard Commercial Mode: Operates at 1,200 MHz with resolution down to 16 cm, supported by higher transmit power and larger incidence angles.
- Collection Agility and Orbit Control: Cuts minimum Image Window Separation by more than 30% and doubles imaging time per orbit compared to prior generations, while upgraded orbit control enables daily passes over the same target from identical viewing angles.
- Onboard AI Processor: Executes automated screening, pre-processing, and tip-and-cue tasking directly on the spacecraft, receiving new capabilities through over-the-air software updates.
Sovereign Deployment Within 12 Months
Building on ICEYE’s 12-month sovereign SAR delivery model, Gen5 operates on the company’s existing ground segment and tasking software, allowing current operators to integrate the spacecraft without retraining personnel. New sovereign customers can field a dedicated Gen5 system—free of U.S. International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) restrictions—within 12 months of contract signing, inclusive of ground infrastructure, software, and operator training.
“Time to decision is everything in space-based intelligence, whether you’re tracking a vessel or responding to a flood. Gen5 shortens it at every step: sharper and more images per pass, and AI analysis that starts in orbit,” said Rafal Modrzewski, chief executive officer (CEO) and co-founder of ICEYE. “With a new generation approximately every 18 months and new software releases every quarter, our customers’ systems keep gaining capability.”

Заголовок: B-21 Raider completes first weapons-release test as bomber enters new phase
Полный текст:
Ahead of entering service in 2027, the B-21 has conducted its first weapons release test from its proving base at Edwards.

The United States Air Force says it has conducted the first weapons-release test of the incoming Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider bomber.

The milestone – announced on 13 November – marked the transition from a flight test platform to a functional weapons platform. In a nod to the B-21’s expanding capabilities, which may eventually include air-to-air missions, the Air Force routinely calls it a “6th-generation long-range, penetrating strike aircraft.”

B-21 releases a weapon for the first time

The B-21 took off from Edwards Air Force Base, California, and released an unidentified “conventional weapon.” The test validated the aircraft’s digital models and the aircraft’s growing maturity.

The Raider is designed to carry a range of conventional and nuclear munitions. At this time, the Air Force has not released any photos of the munitions test.

In a statement, the USAF said, “This test proves the B-21’s strike capability, proves its ability to rapidly onboard new weapons and solidifies its role as the future backbone of the U.S. bomber fleet.”

Image: Northrop Grumman

This comes after thousands of hours of virtual modeling with the B-21’s digital twin. The digital twin is enabling the comparatively rapid development of the bomber and cutting back the amount of physical rework needed after real-world testing.

In July, AGN reported the Air Force had paired an operational test pilot with a developmental test pilot in the same cockpit for the first time to accelerate the bomber’s testing and acceptance schedule.

Able to predict and refine weapons trajectory before taking off

Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said that the test demonstrates the ability to “adapt rapidly” and “hold any target at risk if deterrence fails.” Meink also noted that the Raider is designed to quickly integrate new weapons.

This allows the B-21 Combined Test Force to accelerate weapons integration and “predict and refine” the weapon’s trajectory with “unparalleled precision before the aircraft ever left the ground.”

Image: Northrop Grumman

In its own statement on the test, Northrop Grumman said, “The B-21 is proving in test what it promised on paper: it’s the most advanced bomber in the fleet, and it behaves more like a modern fighter than a legacy bomber when it comes to maintenance turnaround times and cost per flying hour.”
