B-21 Raider remains on track to enter service in 2027

The Air Force reaffirmed that the B-21 remains on schedule to arrive at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027, the first step toward operational service with the bomber force..

In September 2025, the Air Force announced it had received the second test B-21 Raider. The type is in low-rate initial production, and it is unclear how many more have been built or delivered to the Air Force since then.

A 2026 Northrop earnings call revealed it had sold one of its testbed B-21s to the Air Force.

Photo: Northrop Grumman

Currently, the Air Force’s acquisition target remains at least 100 units, but it is expected to formally revise this upward next year.

In 2025, billions of extra funding was allowed to expand Northrop Grumman’s capacity to produce the aircraft at a higher rate. Northrop says it has recently opened the Layton manufacturing facility in Utah (265,000 square feet).

It has also broken ground on an expanded one-million-square-foot final assembly line facility at Plant 42 in Palmdale, California.

Заголовок: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
Полный текст:
3 min read

Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)

Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce.

NASA/Danny Nowlin

The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life.

Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making.

Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA.

“Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.”

His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space.

By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards.

As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe.

Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center.

Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis.

“My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.”

A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue.

This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him.

A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes.

“Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy.

Заголовок: Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026
Полный текст:
The new observatory managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

The comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) discovered by the Euclid mission. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026)

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

What is it?

(Image credit: ESA/Euclid)

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement .

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

An close up view of comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). (Image credit: ESA/Euclid)

Why is it incredible?

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

Заголовок: Часы в двух временах сразу
Полный текст:
Часы в двух временах сразу

Может ли для одного предмета время течь сразу с разной скоростью? Квантовая механика такое допускает, и теперь физики придумали, как поймать этот эффект с помощью атомных часов.

Начнём с привычной относительности. По Эйнштейну, темп времени зависит от скорости движения и силы тяготения. Атомные часы отсчитывают время по точным атомным частотам и чувствуют эту разницу на крошечных высотах: стоит поднять их на несколько миллиметров, где гравитация чуть слабее, и они пойдут быстрее. Самые точные современные часы такой сдвиг уже улавливают.

А теперь квантовый поворот. Движение часов может оказаться в суперпозиции, то есть сразу в нескольких состояниях. Представьте, что одни и те же часы одновременно и стоят на месте, и куда-то едут. Тогда для них должно идти сразу несколько «потоков» времени.

Как это заметить? Движение часов в такой ситуации запутывается с их внутренней энергией — той самой, что задаёт «тиканье». У запутанности есть след: часы теряют часть своих квантовых свойств, и это можно засечь современными методами, объясняет один из ведущих авторов. Получается своего рода отпечаток, который «многослойное» время оставляет на приборе.

Проверять предлагают на часах с захваченными ионами: ион удерживают в ловушке, а лазерная оптика считывает его частоту. Команда учёных из Японии, США, Канады и Швеции придумала, как точнее управлять движением иона, — и это повышает чувствительность к эффекту в 100–1000 раз.

Следующий шаг — эксперимент, который отделит нужный сигнал от неизбежных помех реальной лаборатории. Если всё получится, атомные часы станут инструментом для изучения квантовой природы времени, а заодно, возможно, прибавят в точности. Авторы замахиваются и на большее: проверить, не помогут ли такие часы заглянуть в квантовую гравитацию.

Пока всё это — чистая теория. Зато для проверки не нужно изобретать новую технику: подходящее оборудование уже есть.

Заголовок: China to Launch Asteroid Monitoring Satellite in 2027 for Planetary Defence
Полный текст:
A new piece of information reveals that the first part of a space-based planetary protection system is about a year away from deployment.

A render of NASA’s DART spacecraft on track to hit an asteroid as part of a planetary defence demonstration. | Image: NASA / Jet Propulsion Laboratory

For several years, academics, scientists, and engineers in China have been considering ways to protect Earth from hazardous asteroids, as well as ways to monitor and find them before they cause significant terrestrial damage or, at worst, an extinction event.

On November 13th, an indirect update on those efforts was provided via China’s government procurement portal with the announcement of a successful bid to cover the insurance of an ‘Asteroid Monitoring Satellite (小行星监测卫星)’ under the purview of the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense (国家国防科技工业局). That agency oversees the China National Space Administration, and shares a director, Shan Zhongde (单忠德) , since January 2025.

The announcement and attached documents detailed that the satellite is valued at 360 million Yuan (53.96 million United States Dollars, as of November 14th), and secured an insurance premium of 14.418 million Yuan (2.16 million United States Dollars) to cover any damage should a launch go awry. A launch vehicle was also disclosed in those, naming the Long March 3B/E as the chosen ride into space, flying no earlier than the second half of 2027.

Information useful to the mission ends there, but with the choice of the Long March 3B/E, it indicates that the ‘Asteroid Monitoring Satellite’ could be delivered out to a Sun-Earth Lagrange point 1 while weighing several thousand kilograms. A Lagrange point would provide an excellent vantage point to observe asteroids as they travel through space.

In June, Chinese media reported , citing an interview with Chief Scientist Li Mingtao (李明涛) at the Asteroid Monitoring and Warning Research Center of the China National Space Administration (国家航天局小行星监测预警研究中心), that the country is looking to establish a fleet of asteroid monitoring satellites to keep watch for those that could be hazardous. Those would allow for constant monitoring of the sky, allowing asteroids presently known and unknown to be tracked, from satellites in Lagrange points as well as some orbits of the Earth and Moon.

Space-based asteroid monitors would work in tandem with Earth-based telescopes that already exist and new ones being placed in opportune locations worldwide, Xinhua reported in July , to establish a proper early warning system. That system would protect people on Earth and those exploring the Moon as activity increases into the next decade.

Around February 2025 , the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense began to hire qualified individuals to build China’s planetary defence system and operate it once brought online. In the time since, a consortium of research institutes, university teams, and relevant enterprises has been brought together for the system.

As mentioned, that system will search for asteroids and keep watch of them initially. Potential later parts of it could see protection spacecraft placed high around Earth to deflect incoming asteroids. China plans to prove the capability to do that with a mission starting in late 2027 and slamming a satellite into a harmless target asteroid in early 2029, being watched by a companion spacecraft. That mission will build on experience gained by Tianwen-2 and its many months alongside Kamoʻoalewa, which it will grab samples from soon.

When asked by the media about the planetary defence system, the China National Space Administration and officials state that they are open to working with all countries collaboratively. That includes working as a part of the International Asteroid Warning Network and the Space Mission Planning Advisory Group.

Speaking of international asteroid monitoring work, U.S. space agency NASA is aiming to launch its NEO Surveyor spacecraft for that purpose in September 2027. It may come online around the same time as China’s ‘Asteroid Monitoring Satellite’.

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. SpaceComputer, the Singapore-based in-orbit digital security startup, will fly its Space Fabric secure-compute payload aboard a D-Orbit ION mission next year. The mission aims to test the company’s ability to add a security layer into a satcom network.

How it works: SpaceComputer’s Space Fabric sits on top of a satellite’s compute module and uses cryptographic methods to provide verifiable proof that compute processes run in-orbit were, in fact, run in-orbit.

The module allows for greater security guarantees regarding space-based data operations, and opens the door for multiple digital payloads to safely operate on the same in-orbit compute module—without being exposed to one another.

What’s next: The D-Orbit mission will be one of three missions in 2027 for SpaceComputer, including a mission to GEO on an undisclosed satellite, and a mission with Spacemanic to act as the MVP for the company’s security architecture for compute payloads.

The missions aim to bring to market a new standard for digital security to compute and comms modules in space.

SpaceComputer officials told Payload that security needs on-orbit are on the rise, and not just because of increased threats from a defense-perspective. Satellites today also feature a lot of cross-industry collaboration—where payloads from multiple companies are increasingly sharing a ride on a single satellite. SpaceComputer wants those payloads to be able to share compute and comms resources without exposing themselves to threats.

In a future where orbital data centers are commonplace in orbit, this shared-payload architecture is going to need a security layer to ensure everyone is operating in a protected silo, Bar said.

Заголовок: Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical?
Полный текст:
Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical shapes, such as ovals or pears, depending on composition?
Rich Livitski
Seal Beach, California
Bodies large enough to be considered planets have enough mass that gravity molds them into a roughly spherical shape.
The key word here is roughly — other factors also come into play, such as a planet’s composition (rocky or gassy) and its rate of spin. The faster a planet spins, the more its rotation causes it to bulge outward at the equator. That’s because as a planet rotates, there’s a tug-of-war between the way material wants to fly off the planet due to rotation and the way gravity wants to pull all that planet’s material inward. The battle between these forces is most intense at the equator.
In our solar system, Mercury and Venus are slowly spinning rocky planets; therefore, they are the most spherical of the Sun’s worlds.
Earth and Mars spin a little faster, so they are about 0.3% and 0.6% thicker at the equator than the poles, respectively. This shape is called an oblate spheroid. However, because these planets have a solid surface that is higher in some places than others, they are not perfect oblate spheroids — they are minutely lumpy and bumpy, as data from orbiting satellites have detailed. In fact, the surface area of Earth’s Southern Hemisphere is very slightly larger than its Northern Hemisphere, making Earth marginally pear-shaped. It’s important to note, however, that despite these deviations, Earth is still almost spherical — if you used a basketball to represent the shape of our planet, its deviation from a perfect sphere would be only about 0.03 inch (0.08 centimeter) at the middle.
The gas giants Jupiter and Saturn bulge outward the most — Jupiter is nearly 7% thicker at its equator than its poles, and Saturn is 10.7% thicker around the middle. Ice giants Uranus and Neptune have smaller central bulges, only 2.3% and 1.7% thicker at the equator, respectively.
What about exoplanets, though? Some planetary systems we’ve found experience much more extreme conditions, with large, gassy planets orbiting very close to their stars (called hot Jupiters). One of these hot Jupiters is WASP-121 b, which orbits a blazingly hot star. In fact, this planet orbits so closely to its star that gravitational forces have stretched it out into a football shape. Astronomers believe that if the planet were much closer to its star, it would be ripped apart entirely.
In addition to its stretched-out shape, WASP-121 b and other planets, including WASP-69 b and KELT-9 b, appear to have puffed-up atmospheres and cometlike tails. These tails form as their host stars blast the planets with high-energy radiation, knocking gas particles into space.
As for pear-shaped exoplanets, astronomers haven’t found anything to suggest they exist to the extent you’re likely picturing. Other terrestrial planets likely have deformations similar to Earth’s — or perhaps slightly more extreme — but even “extreme” in this case probably translates to a planet appearing essentially spherical from a great distance.
Alison Klesman
Senior Editor
This question and answer were originally published online October 24, 2020.

Second wave of baby sea turtles hits California waters, this time in Huntington Beach

Less than two days after California’s first native-born sea turtles scuttled into the sea, a second group of 21 olive ridley hatchlings was successfully released Sunday morning in Huntington Beach.
The turtles emerged from eggs laid Sept. 19 on Huntington City Beach.
Those eggs, along with eggs from a second nest laid three days earlier on Seal Beach, were transferred to Long Beach in late September to save them from high tides.
“The hatchlings emerged from their nest behind the scenes at the non-profit Aquarium of the Pacific and were promptly transported back to Huntington Beach for their release,” the aquarium said in a statement.
The young turtles closely followed a first group of 54 olive ridley hatchlings that emerged from 104 eggs laid Sept. 16 on Seal Beach. They were released early Saturday morning in a spot near their original nest.
As of Sunday, 50 eggs from the Seal Beach nest remained in a climate-controlled room at the aquarium and could hatch in coming days, said Dr. Lance Adams, the aquarium’s director of veterinary services. As many as 87 eggs from the Huntington Beach nest could be yet to hatch, though the aquarium could not immediately confirm the number of eggs remaining.
These were the first known sea turtle nests on the U.S. West Coast. A third nest appeared Nov. 1 in Ventura, but cold sand and high tide rendered it not viable.
Olive ridleys are normally found throughout tropical regions of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, with large nesting populations in Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. Before September, the farthest known northern nest was approximately 700 miles south of Orange County in the Mexican state of Baja California Sur.
An extreme marine heat wave and a strong El Niño have pushed Southern California water temperatures closer to those of the turtles’ typical nesting grounds.
Olive ridley nests in the wild have hatch rates of up to 90%. But life as a baby sea turtle is dangerous — and often short. At best, 1% of hatchlings survive to adulthood, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Заголовок: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
Полный текст:
"I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet".

We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.

But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.

"In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule."

As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't."

Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.

130 million pieces of debris are currently estimated to be orbiting Earth. (Image credit: ESA)

In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome , with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth .

Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

What is the Astra Carta?

The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.

Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies . The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.

"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.

The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.

What does the Astra Carta say?

"It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness."

To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.

"If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?"

King Charles III (middle) is photographed in discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield (right) at Buckingham Palace. (Image credit: Photo by EAMONN M. MCCORMACK/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords .

Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.

But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.

From paper to action

Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.

"What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose."

To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.

The Astra Carta seal on display at a UKSA event. (Image credit: Photo by Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX . It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center , Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman , Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.

In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page".

The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.

The Astra Carta seeks to place sustainability at the core of space exploration, protecting Earth in the process. (Image credit: Joshua Stevens/NASA Earth Observatory)

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain"

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the big players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly."

Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the company often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver plans for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today."

A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.

But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.

Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Jeremy Hansen are honored at a gala presented by the Sustainable Markets Initiative. (Image credit: Sustainable Markets Initiative)

"The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cachet of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it."

In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.

"We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet."

However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.

Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.

"If you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.

The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.

Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.

"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full , or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are currently on track for true space sustainability .

Заголовок: Watch: COMAC CE-25A electric aircraft completes first crewed flight in China
Полный текст:
COMAC's CE-25A electric commuter aircraft has completed its first crewed flight in Shandong, China, carrying two pilots and a flight-test engineer.

COMAC ‘s CE-25A all-electric commuter aircraft has completed its first crewed flight, advancing the development of a 19-seat regional aircraft design powered by ten electric ducted fans.

The aircraft flew at Binzhou in Shandong province on 14 November with two pilots and a flight-test engineer aboard. COMAC said the aircraft operated normally and its performance met expectations, according to a report published by China’s Civil Aviation Administration (CAAC) .

The CE-25A spent 16 minutes and 38 seconds airborne, covering 60.4km. The complete test, including ground operations, lasted 57 minutes and 46 seconds.

The first crewed flight follows photos of a full-sized CE-25A demonstrator which first appeared in October, as Aerospace Global News reported.

The CAAC’s latest announcement says the aircraft has been flying uncrewed for months.

COMAC reveals 19 earlier uncrewed flights

COMAC says the CE-25A made its first autonomous, uncrewed flight on 2 February 2026 and completed 19 uncrewed flight validations before Saturday’s flight with people aboard.

Photographs of the full-sized aircraft first circulated widely in late October 2026.

COMAC first unveiled the CE-25A concept at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023.

According to news reports crediting COMAC, the “C” in the name stands for China and COMAC; “E” represents electric power, “25” represents compliance with the CCAR-25 airworthiness regulations for transport category aircraft; and “A” indicates it is the first product of its kind developed in China.

How the CE-25A’s ten electric fans work

The aircraft relies on a distributed electric propulsion system. Five electrically driven ducted fans sit above each wing, replacing the turboprop engines used on conventional commuter aircraft.

Photo: COMAC / Han Lu via X

COMAC lists the aircraft’s maximum take-off weight of 10 tonnes. It has a capacity of 19 passengers, with a cruising speed of 300km/h and a cruising altitude of 2,400m. The aircraft’s range is approximately 400km, which would suit short intercity routes.

The programme involves COMAC, Chinese battery manufacturer CATL, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and other partners. CATL has previously publicised high-energy-density battery technology for aviation , but the cells which power the CE-25A have not been confirmed.

Certification and commercial service remain ahead

The CAAC confirmed it has accepted COMAC’s application for a CE-25A type certificate.

The aircraft was developed to meet China’s CCAR-25 transport-aircraft airworthiness framework. The manufacturer must now prove the design’s safety, battery performance and reliability in various operating conditions before the CE-25A can enter commercial service.

Photo: Heart Aerospace

The CE-25A joins a small group of larger electric aircraft demonstrators. Heart Aerospace ‘s X1 made its first flight in the United States in August 2026 . The company is developing a hybrid-electric regional airliner and unveiled its ES-36 in September , which will carry up to 36 passengers. It would use battery power for shorter routes, with two megawatt-class turbogenerators powered by a compact gas turbine enabling longer routes. JSX has converted its previous letter of intent into an order for 50 ES-36 aircraft, with options for 50 more.

No timeline has yet been established for the CE-25A’s final certification, and no details have been disclosed about possible airline operations. COMAC has not announced a confirmed entry-into-service date.

Заголовок: US Air Force deploys first F-15EX Eagle II fighters to Japan
Полный текст:
As old Eagles are retired, the first two F-15EXs have arrived in Japan, starting a new chapter for Kadena and the defence of the First Island Chain.

In a landmark development for US Air Force posture in Japan, the first two permanently assigned USAF Boeing F-15EX Eagle IIs arrived at the major Kadena Air Base yesterday.

The decision to replace the F-15C/Ds at Kadena was originally announced in 2024. Under the plan, the base’s fleet of 48 F-15C/Ds is to be replaced with 36 F-15EXs. The last of these is expected to arrive in 2028.

USAF’s Kadena AFB welcomes first F-15EX Eagle IIs

The USAF posted , “The Eagle II has landed. Kadena Air Base welcomes its first permanently assigned F-15EX aircraft, advancing our capabilities in the Pacific region.”

The Air Force stated the arrival makes a major “milestone in the 18th Wing’s fighter modernization and the continued strengthening of U.S. airpower in the Pacific region.”

The Eagle II has landed. 🦅🦅

Kadena Air Base welcomes its first permanently assigned F-15EX aircraft, advancing our capabilities in the Pacific region.

Learn more: https://t.co/m2BbgCJXF5 https://t.co/qbPgDKLh4K

— U.S. Air Force (@usairforce) November 15, 2026

Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, said the F-15EX in Kadena strengthens the US ability to “deter aggression” in the region and was a response to “emerging threats.” He also noted it reinforced the US’s commitment to its alliance with Japan.

The 18th Wing’s 44th and 67th Fighter Squadrons are both set to transition to the F-15EX at Kadena.

Importance of Kadena Air Base in the First Island Chain

Kadena Air Base is the largest and most active United States Air Force installation in East Asia and is located on Japan’s southern Okinawa Islands. It is one of the most important military bases in the First Island Chain.

It has become the first overseas USAF base to receive permanent combat-coded F-15EXs and is only the second Air Force installation after the Oregon Air National Guard’s 142nd Wing at Portland Air National Guard Base.

Separately, and adding to the defence of Japan and its southern islands, Japan operates around 200 of the related Mitsubishi F-15Js. These were locally produced Eagles under licence and are set to be upgraded to the F-15EX standard.

Photo: US Air Force

Japan is also purchasing F-35A and F-35B fighter jets (around 47 currently delivered) and has around 85 of the F-16-derived Mitsubishi F-2s in service. Japan is one of the three principal members of the 6th-generation GCAP/Tempest fighter jet program.

Japan is sensitive to the GCAP sticking to the timeline to enter service by 2035 to start replacing its F-2s in order to effectively counter China in the region.

Israel to buy 50 more F-35s and F-15EXs in major fleet expansion
Israel to buy 50 more F-35s and F-15EXs in major fleet expansion

Why the F-15EX is needed to replace the older F-15C/D

F-15EX fighter jets are the latest generation of the long-running F-15 Eagle family. It retains the basic airframe, but it is essentially a new aircraft, with vastly updated computers, sensors, networking, and more.

The fighter jet brings “advanced avionics, modernized electronic warfare systems, and increased weapons-carrying capacity.”

The F-15EX is based on the advanced F-15QA developed for Qatar, incorporating technologies and design improvements from subsequent international F-15 programmes. It was subsequently adapted for USAF requirements.

For the US Air Force, it offers a way to replace ageing fourth-generation fighters while retaining a substantial payload and long-range weapons platform.

Photo: US Air Force

It also complements the limited-in-number F-22 Raptors. Rather than replacing these aircraft, the F-15EX can provide additional weapons capacity, sensors and networking capabilities, particularly when operating alongside 5th-generation fighters.

It also helps to address the practical payload limits on the F-35A (especially limited internal space).

In Kadena specifically, F-15EXs are replacing aging F-15C/D models that were built in the 1980s. These older models would likely struggle in a high-end conflict against China.

Those F-15C/Ds began their phased withdrawal in November 2022 after over four decades of service. Other 4th- and 5th-generation fighters have been rotated through during the transition to prevent a capability gap.

The US has effectively doubled its target F-15EX acquisition from 129 to 267 and is currently investing in ramping up Boeing’s capacity to produce the aircraft to 36 annually.

Заголовок: End of the road: Global Airlines ordered into compulsory liquidation
Полный текст:
Global Airlines has been wound up by the High Court, signalling the end of the all-Airbus A380 venture for the British startup.

The British startup that had ambitious plans to operate an all-Airbus A380 fleet has been wound up by the High Court, signalling the end of a venture that flew just two return passenger flights.

Global Airlines , the British startup that set out a bold ambition to “bring back the golden era of travel” with an all- Airbus A380 fleet has been ordered into compulsory liquidation.

Global Airlines issued winding up order

The London Gazette confirmed on in a notice published on 12 November that the UK’s High Court of Justice issued a winding-up order against the company on 4 November.

The order signals the end of a venture that drew plenty of scepticism from the moment the airline was announced in 2021 .

Founder and CEO James Asquith has repeatedly defended his choice of operating the world’s largest passenger jet. He argued its range and capacity could ease congestion at busy airports by handling a large number of passengers in a single flight. He initially planned to compete on crowded transatlantic routes between the UK and the US (New York and Los Angeles), with ambitions to expand to destinations including the Maldives and Tokyo.

Photo: James Asquith / Global Airlines

The company originally slated a start date for passenger operations back in 2024, but this was pushed into 2025. The a irline ultimately flew only two round trips from Glasgow and Manchester to New York (JFK) with paying passengers. Both flights were operated by Portuguese charter aviation operations company Hi Fly with tickets sold through a third-part provider GA. Flights, powered by Travelopedia.

Global Airlines came under criticism for not having its own operating certificate and never selling a scheduled flight.

In a LinkedIn statement at the time, the airline said: “These flights represent more than just a trip; they signify the beginning of something new, so come and rediscover the magic of flying.”

And as recently as June 2026 Asquith said the airline’s A380 would fly again before the end of the year. He had also spoken of plans to acquire another aircraft and begin operating flights between the UK and the Maldives.

What the ruling means

The order follows a winding-up petition filed on 29 May 2026 by US-based creditor Jessica Huffman Reese . She is represented by a US law firm Vedder Price, which has a specialist aviation finance practice. It was the third such petition in just over a year with two earlier petitions filed in August 2025 and March 2026. The court ruled against the airline after hearings in July.

The ruling means that Asquith and the board no longer run the company, which is now in the hands of the Official Receiver, an officer of the UK’s Insolvency Service. The receiver will investigate the company’s affairs and the conduct of its directors, collect assets and pay creditors from the proceeds. Bank accounts are likely to be frozen, while Global Airlines has 21 days from the ruling being issued to appeal the decision.

If Global Airlines wanted to appeal the decision it would have to do so within 21 days.

What will happen to Global Airlines now?

Global Airlines built its strategy on acquiring and repurposing retired Airbus A380s. Asquith had also quietly teased plans to i ntroduce the A340-300 into Global Airlines’ fleet having unveiled what appeared to be its second aircraft registered 9H-SUN at the end of 2025 .

• Its only operational aircraft the Aregistered 9H-GLOBL previously flew for China Southern Airlines but has been parked at Tarbes-Lourdes-Pyrenees Airport in France since July 2025.

Photo: James Asquith / Global Airlines

The aircraft is now due for a 12-year heavy maintenance check, making it a costly proposition for any potential buyer. Meanwhile its application is limited to operations to and from airports capable of handling the aircraft type, although Asquith has previously said “lots of airports around the world want the A380… we have a whole list of airports asking, offering incentives for us to fly there. Quite a few in the US, West Coast, a few in South America… and then a couple in the Far East as well.”

For Global Airlines, at least, that is no longer an option. Sale for parts or scrapping of its aircraft is the most likely outcome.

Заголовок: FAA identifies suspect router as US flight cancellations continue
Полный текст:
As investigators analyse a suspect router and network logs, airlines continue restoring schedules after a telecommunications failure disrupted US air traffic.

The US Federal Aviation Administration has identified a newly installed router at an Arkansas communications site as one possible source of the network failure that grounded flights across the US on Friday, 13 November . A second site in Texas is also under investigation. The agency has not yet established what caused the disruption.

The grounding lasted almost five hours and left airlines facing thousands of cancellations over the weekend. FlightAware’s early figures suggested far fewer cancellations for Monday, 16 November.

FAA traces disruption to two sites

The FAA said in a statement published on 15 November that its telecommunications network had received bursts of approximately 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The excess traffic destabilised the ageing FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network, interrupting some radar feeds and radio communications. The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop as a safety precaution .

Investigators traced the traffic to a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Contractor L3Harris had installed a router at El Dorado while replacing older copper connections with new fibre-optic links.

The network stabilised after L3Harris blocked traffic from both sites. As a precaution, the FAA turned off a broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers. The router installed at El Dorado was sent to an L3Harris laboratory in Florida for testing.

What is a ground stop and why does the FAA order one?
What is a ground stop and why does the FAA order one?

Timing of router installation in question

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said investigators were looking into whether the router was defective or installed incorrectly.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns router manufacturer Juniper, disputed the suggestion of an equipment fault. It told ABC News the router had operated according to its configuration. The FAA has not announced a finding on the cause.

Duffy also addressed questions on the timing of the upgrade, saying the switchover at the remote location was scheduled for the daytime because it was considered to have a lower impact.

“These smaller locations don’t have that kind of impact—or they shouldn’t have that kind of impact, which is what we saw yesterday. So, there’ll be a reevaluation of when we do this work. But when you look across the country, when the work has been done from copper to fibre, going from analogue to digital, they’ve happened at all times of the day, and so we have to drill in a little further about what happened here,” he said.

Ground stop leaves airlines recovering

The fault affected 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centres and several terminal approach control facilities. The agency halted departures nationwide at about 3:30 pm Eastern Time on Friday and lifted the ground stop at 8:15 pm.

Radar and radio services were not lost completely. Controllers retained some feeds and frequencies, and around 3,500 aircraft landed safely during the disruption, the FAA said. Emergency, military and law-enforcement flights continued to operate.

Over 12,000 flights cancelled on Friday

The FAA recorded about 12,462 cancellations on Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines. It said some cancellations were due to causes other than the ground stop. Airlines still had to move aircraft and crews back into position after the interruption.

On Sunday, FlightAware recorded around 2,100 US cancellations and 9,400 delays, Reuters reported . At 8:28 pm Eastern Time on Sunday, FlightAware listed 88 cancellations for Monday.

Duffy said he expected schedules to return to normal on Monday.

Photo: Markus Mainka | stock.adobe.com

American Airlines said in a Sunday update that its recovery was progressing, with fewer cancellations as it worked to restore its schedule. The carrier extended its travel alert, allowing affected customers to change reservations or request refunds. It advised passengers to check their flight status before travelling to the airport.

Delta Air Lines reported on Sunday that most of its flights were operating normally, although some delays and cancellations remained. The airline extended flexible rebooking through Monday, 16 November, and said it would automatically rebook passengers whose flights were cancelled.

Southwest Airlines said flights had resumed after the ground stop, but warned delays and cancellations could continue as it restored operations. The carrier offered affected passengers options to change or cancel their bookings.

United reported on Saturday that most of its weekend flights were “operating normally” as it worked to restore its schedule. “Some flights will continue to be delayed or cancelled as we position aircraft and crews following yesterday’s prolonged FAA ground stop,” United stated. The airline urged passengers to check their flight status before heading to the airport, and offered a travel waiver for customers who wanted to change their weekend travel plans.

FAA examines network maintenance procedures

The FAA said it had found no evidence of a cyberattack causing the system failure. It described the router installation as routine network work, separate from the wider air traffic control modernisation programme, and said the instability involved legacy time-division multiplexing equipment.

“Now, those of you who are aviation reporters have heard me talk about a decades-old air traffic control system. It’s not just old equipment. We have an incredibly old telecommunication system,” Duffy said.

Photo: Bmurphy380 | Wikimedia Commons

United Airlines chief executive Scott Kirby used a 15 November statement to call for investment in the air traffic control network. “This moment must be a call to action,” he said, urging improvements to the system’s reliability and redundancy. Kirby said he had discussed the disruption with federal aviation officials and congressional leaders.

Duffy said the Department of Transportation would review maintenance procedures, including whether work at remote facilities should be carried out during daytime operations.

The FAA and L3Harris are examining the router and network logs to determine why traffic from the two facilities spread through the national system.

Заголовок: Paratus Expands Starlink Enterprise Connectivity into Lesotho and Malawi
Полный текст:
Paratus Expands Starlink Enterprise Connectivity into Lesotho and Malawi
Paratus Group has expanded its African satellite connectivity solutions into Lesotho and Malawi, introducing Starlink-powered enterprise connectivity services in both markets. The launches, announced on 5 and 12 November 2026, respectively, extend the group’s presence in Southern Africa and add two markets to its regional telecommunications network.
Both operations will initially focus on enterprise customers, combining Starlink’s satellite connectivity with local installation, technical support and customer service. However, the two markets present different connectivity requirements, shaping how Paratus intends to position its services in each country.
Paratus Enters Lesotho Through Local Joint Venture
In Lesotho, Paratus has established a joint venture with local company Real Image Lesotho. The operation, led by Managing Director Makali Lepholisa, will provide high-speed internet services to businesses and organisations across the country.
The launch addresses connectivity challenges associated with Lesotho’s mountainous terrain, where extending conventional terrestrial infrastructure can be difficult, particularly beyond major urban centres. Through its Starlink reseller arrangement, Paratus Lesotho will offer low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite connectivity to organisations in areas where fibre and other terrestrial networks have limited reach.
The local partnership also provides an operating structure through which Paratus can deliver installation, customer support and technical services within the market.
Malawi Launch Targets Enterprise Connectivity Demand
In Malawi, Paratus is initially targeting enterprise connectivity requirements across several sectors, including banking, insurance, agriculture, healthcare, mining, energy, transport and logistics, education, tourism, broadcasting and government.
The operation, led by Country Manager Tiwonge Chirambo, will offer Starlink services as both a primary internet connection for organisations outside major urban centres and a backup service for businesses in Lilongwe, Blantyre and Mzuzu. The latter application is intended to provide an alternative connection where existing fibre or mobile networks experience disruptions.
Paratus Malawi reports that it has already signed several enterprise customers across different sectors. Installations will be carried out through local technical partners, with support from the wider group. The company indicates that installation turnaround times will range from 24 to 48 hours, depending on location and operational requirements. It also plans to expand its local workforce as operations develop.
Extending Paratus’s Regional Network
The two launches form part of Paratus Group’s wider expansion across sub-Saharan Africa. The group says its entry into Malawi brings its network presence to 16 countries in the region.
In both markets, the initial focus on enterprise services provides a route into local telecommunications markets without immediately extending conventional terrestrial networks. The approach combines Starlink’s satellite infrastructure with local commercial operations and technical support.
For Paratus, the launches extend its enterprise connectivity business into two additional markets. For businesses and institutions in Lesotho and Malawi, they introduce another option for accessing internet services, particularly in locations where terrestrial connectivity is limited or where network redundancy is required.

«Огромный словарь, который был нужен нашей области», — так нейробиолог Ана Муньос-Манчадо из Кадисского университета называет новый атлас. И не преувеличивает: сотни учёных из девяти стран описали 25,5 млн клеток базальных ганглиев человека, макак и игрунок и выпустили сразу 26 статей — в Cell, Neuron и ещё четырёх журналах.

Базальные ганглии сидят глубоко в мозге и обрабатывают информацию о движениях, мышлении, настроении и принятии решений, эдакая диспетчерская. С ними связаны болезни Паркинсона и Хантингтона, шизофрения, биполярное расстройство и зависимости. Атлас входит в проект BICAN и станет шаблоном для карты всего мозга человека.

Материал собирали основательно: 21 млн клеток из мозга шести человек, 3 млн — от трёх макак, 1,5 млн — от двух игрунок, плюс готовые карты мозга мыши. Клетки изучали со всех сторон: какие гены в них работают, какими метками помечена ДНК, как они ведут себя электрически и даже как ДНК уложена в ядре. А потом расставили всё по местам — буквально, на карте мозга.

Заголовок: Elon Musk is already planning a bigger Starship, and the Moon may be why
Полный текст:
Elon Musk revealed Starship V4 specs that could reshape how fast SpaceX reaches the Moon.

A day after SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage for the first time, Elon Musk laid out how much bigger the next version will get. “Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load,” Musk wrote on X Sunday evening. “Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.”

The current V3 ship that flew on Flight 15 stands about 52 meters tall with six Raptors, three built for sea level and three for vacuum. V4 stretches the ship and doubles its vacuum engines. Musk first said in August 2025 that V4 would add three engines to “a significantly longer ship” and fly in 2027. Sunday’s post is the most specific look at the ship so far.

The payload jump is the headline for the rest of the industry. SpaceX said in its IPO prospectus that V3 is expected to carry about 100 metric tons to orbit, while future generations could reach 200 metric tons, potentially as soon as V4. For comparison, a reusable Falcon 9 carries roughly 17 metric tons to low Earth orbit.

The bigger impact may be on the Moon. Every Starship lunar mission depends on filling a propellant depot in orbit with a string of tanker flights before the lander departs. A NASA safety panel member put that number at around 22 flights last month, while Musk countered that it would be “more like 6 to 8,” as Teslarati reported . Much of that gap comes down to which ship is doing the hauling. Musk has said a V4 tanker could deliver more than 200 tons of propellant per flight, which by his math brings a lunar refill down to five or six launches.

Fewer tankers per landing means more landings per year. 1988

2026

Curtain Toggle 2-Up

On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers.

Positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “ canaries in the coal mine ,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.

The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by the TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 (left) and in 2026 by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 (right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green.

In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics ( BMKG ). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent . An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said.

The glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn showed a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone.

As the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each new fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice.

“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has tracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”

To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.

As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last. Recent satellite studies suggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by the current El Niño .

Past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than usual , losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year.

Заголовок: Connecting Constellations: The Shift to Real-Time Space Operations
Полный текст:
After years of development and demonstrations, optical communications are reshaping how the space industry approaches mission architectures. Kepler’s optical space data relay constellation gives government and commercial customers opportunities to connect previously isolated systems, strengthen resilience, and move mission data more quickly and efficiently.

For Caitlin Marsh, the recently appointed president of Kepler U.S., that progress marks a turning point.

“The industry has been discussing and planning for optical connectivity for a long time,” Marsh said. “Kepler can do that now; it is real and proven.”

With its first operational optical relay constellation in service and additional launches secured, Kepler is helping customers move from evaluating optical connectivity to reliably integrating it into their missions.

The Interoperability Challenge

Space architectures have historically developed around individual missions, acquisition programs, and operational requirements. Government agencies and commercial operators invested in systems that addressed specific needs.

The result is an ecosystem of highly capable but disconnected systems. Marsh sees this fragmentation as a significant obstacle to faster decision-making.

“Despite advances in technology, operators still have a long data path from collection to the decision-maker,” she said. “The lack of interoperability has historically made the timeline and data movement longer than it should be.”

Solving the problem requires more than a software update. Organizations must address hardware compatibility, communications standards, and different operational requirements across systems.

Kepler helps bridge those gaps with interoperable infrastructure that supports multiple customers and complements existing investments.

Kepler’s network supports Space Development Agency-compatible optical communications terminals, and is designing its future satellites to also support emerging standards from the European Space Agency, creating opportunities to exchange data across participating constellations.

The objective extends beyond moving more data. It’s about shortening the path between collection and operational use.

Resilience by Design

Interoperability also gives operators more ways to maintain connectivity when disruptions occur.

Spacecraft face equipment failures, space debris, radiation, and potential interference from adversaries. In architectures that depend on limited communications paths, losing a critical node can interrupt data delivery.

Interconnected networks provide alternative routes.

“If operators lose a node in their communications path, multiple interconnected constellations can allow data to be dynamically rerouted across the network and still reach the end user,” Marsh said.

“It’s what we do in terrestrial communications,” she said. “Now, we’ve taken those lessons and implemented them into our space architectures.”

The implications extend beyond national security. Consider wildfire monitoring. Satellite observations can help emergency managers track changing fire conditions, but those observations lose value when information arrives too late to inform a response. More persistent connectivity delivers updates sooner, while interoperable networks offer alternative paths if a communications link becomes unavailable.

The example illustrates a broader principle: The infrastructure that rapidly delivers space-based information is as important as the sensors that collect it.

From Connectivity to Operational Value

Kepler’s onboard computing capability complements optical connectivity, allowing operators to process and prioritize information closer to where it is collected.

Rather than transmitting entire datasets for ground-based analysis, onboard processing can identify and prioritize the most valuable information for delivery to the end user.

“You’re decreasing the timeline between collecting data, answering your intelligence question or addressing your operational need, and then delivering that data to the end user in seconds,” Marsh said.

This approach can eliminate processing steps, reduce data transmission volume, and make more communications capacity available for other missions.

It also gives customers a way to evaluate performance.

Marsh said operators have long requested lower latency without necessarily defining quantitative requirements. Now that operational optical networks exist, customers can begin measuring the benefits and determining what performance future missions should demand.

Scaling Infrastructure for U.S. Missions

For Marsh, who joined Kepler as president of its U.S. operations in October 2026, the immediate priority is helping government and commercial customers put the company’s operational infrastructure to work.

That means demonstrating how interoperable optical connectivity can strengthen existing architectures, and helping customers incorporate those capabilities into future mission planning. Kepler partners with customers to build infrastructure that supports and amplifies their existing investments.

The company recently selected Rocket Lab’s Neutron for its first dedicated launch, scheduled no earlier than 2028. Separately, Maverick Space Systems secured capacity for 10 Kepler Tranche 2 satellites aboard Portal Space Systems’ Motus Via Sol mission, targeted for mid-2028 on a SpaceX Falcon 9.

These missions will expand Kepler’s optical relay network with additional communications capacity, onboard computing, and hosted payload capabilities. The next-generation satellites will support optical data rates of up to 100 Gbps.

The launch commitments also give prospective customers greater visibility into Kepler’s planned growth as they evaluate their own deployment schedules and infrastructure needs.

Customers are leveraging Kepler’s hosted payload capabilities as an opportunity to test or deploy new technology without having to develop and launch a dedicated spacecraft.

From Capability to Expectation

The space industry has relied on radio-frequency communications for decades. RF technology is familiar, proven, and deeply integrated into existing systems. Optical communications add substantially greater capacity and new opportunities to connect space systems directly. “We are helping the larger space ecosystem build trust in on-orbit optical technology,” Marsh said.

As customers gain experience with optical connectivity and on-orbit compute, they can begin defining new expectations for performance, interoperability, and resilience. Those expectations, in turn, can influence how organizations design and procure future space systems.

Marsh also sees opportunities that extend beyond today’s established applications. Customers are already exploring different combinations of connectivity, computing, and hosted payload services, and she expects operational experience to reveal uses that neither Kepler nor its partners have fully anticipated.

“We are on the leading edge of optical relay in space and there are endless future applications that we haven’t even considered yet,” Marsh said.

For an industry accustomed to designing missions around communications constraints, optical connectivity creates the potential to move beyond those limitations and design missions around what is operationally possible.

Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk called down to Newfoundland and Labrador from the International Space Station on Nov. 10, answering questions from students and cadets gathered at the Johnson Geo Centre in St. John’s about life in orbit and his two spacewalks this fall.
Elsewhere on the station, astronauts spent the week packing a SpaceX Dragon cargo ship with experiment samples bound for Earth, among them bacterial DNA that Kutryk extracted himself, and cleaning the spacesuits worn on the two spacewalks that finished the station’s solar-power upgrade.
Canada’s week
Kutryk spoke with Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson during the call, along with the young participants. According to the CSA, they asked him what a typical day looks like for an astronaut, what weightlessness feels like and how he prepares for a spacewalk, and he told them what inspired him to become one.
Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon spent the same day studying how bacteria adapt to microgravity, work NASA says could help explain how weightlessness affects antibiotic resistance and lead to ways of protecting the immune system. Menon processed the samples in the sealed Life Science Glovebox in the Kibo laboratory module. Kutryk then carried some of them to the Harmony module, extracted their DNA and stowed it in a science freezer for the trip home, according to NASA’s Nov. 10 update.
Two days later, the pair rearranged and secured the return cargo inside Dragon, spreading its mass evenly to balance the capsule’s centre of gravity for reentry and a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. In its Nov. 12 update, NASA said the crew will finish packing the day before Dragon leaves, when the most critical samples, kept in portable freezers and incubators, go aboard.
Kutryk looked back on working beside Canadarm2 during his second spacewalk, on Nov. 5, in a video the CSA released Nov. 9. “This is an absolute rarity of human experience,” he said. “I feel so lucky, privileged to do this job, but not just to do it as an astronaut, to do it as an astronaut with the Canadian flag on my shoulder.”
NASA astronaut Luke Delaney practised manoeuvres with Canadarm2, the Canadian-built robotic arm, at the robotics workstation in the Destiny laboratory module on Nov. 10.
Science and technology experiments
Delaney set up the Life Science Glovebox in Kibo on Nov. 12 for MVP-Plant-02, a study of how plants respond to disease in microgravity, aimed at learning how to sustain crews on future exploration missions. He then moved to the Quest airlock and cleaned the cooling and ventilation systems in the spacesuits Kutryk and Menon wore on their Oct. 29 and Nov. 5 spacewalks.
In the station’s Roscosmos segment, station commander Pyotr Dubrov studied how to make high-purity semiconductor crystals in weightlessness, then joined cosmonaut Anna Kikina to practise with artificial-intelligence tools that transcribe the crew’s spoken reports for mission controllers. Two days earlier, the pair had serviced three Russian Orlan spacesuits in the Poisk module, cleaning their cooling and ventilation systems.
On Nov. 10, Delaney collected drinking-water samples for safety checks back on Earth, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov set up cameras to photograph landmarks across Southeast Asia and Australia during an automated overnight session.
NASA said Dragon’s return cargo includes 3D-printed blood vessels and, after more than three years of testing, lighting hardware built to mimic natural daylight and help regulate crew sleep.
Looking ahead
In its Nov. 10 update, NASA said Dragon, which docked Oct. 15 with the station’s final roll-out solar arrays aboard, would bring its research samples back to Earth “next week.” Menon and NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins started loading payloads on Nov. 12, but no departure date has been announced.
Watkins had earlier cleared space in Kibo for new hardware and supplies due in a few weeks aboard Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL cargo ship. Cygnus launches no earlier than Nov. 29, and astronauts will capture it with Canadarm2, NASA said in its launch advisory.

Заголовок: ULA Vulcan Centaur Suffers Anomaly During Return to Flight, Losing 40 Amazon Leo Satellites
Полный текст:
United Launch Alliance’s (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an in-flight anomaly on Sunday, Nov. 15, resulting in the loss of 40 broadband satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation.
Designated Vulcan Leo 1, the vehicle lifted off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 12:40 p.m. Eastern Time (ET), or 1740 Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), before failing to reach low Earth orbit (LEO).
Fifty minutes after liftoff, ULA confirmed the mission failure in a statement on X. “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit,” ULA said. “Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.”
Nine-Month Stand-Down and Booster Nozzle History
The Nov. 15 mission marked Vulcan Centaur’s return to flight following a nine-month stand-down. Debuting in January 2024, the successor to ULA’s Atlas V had completed four prior missions, experiencing an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs) during both its second flight in October 2024 and its fourth mission in February 2026. On both occasions, an SRB nozzle burned through and detached roughly 30 seconds after liftoff, though the rocket still delivered its payloads.
Following those incidents, the U.S. Space Force paused national security launches on Vulcan pending corrective upgrades. While the SRBs appeared to perform normally on Nov. 15 following ULA’s nozzle design and process improvements, a separate anomaly 10 minutes into the flight prevented orbital insertion.
Constellation Deployment Footprint
Vulcan Leo 1 was the first Vulcan mission flown for Amazon Leo, the broadband network formerly known as Project Kuiper. Planned to comprise more than 3,200 satellites in LEO, the constellation had roughly 400 spacecraft in orbit prior to Nov. 15 across 15 launches conducted by Atlas V, SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and Arianespace’s Ariane 6.
