By Uyen Nguyen
Photos = Ministry of Gender Equality and Family
"Just because you trim your nails doesn't mean you become a different person."
Park Seonghye, head of the Deletion Technology Team at the National Center for Digital Sexual Crime Response, used this analogy to explain her organization's "video DNA" technology.
Detecting illegal footage through conventional searches based on matching hash values can be difficult when the footage has been altered, such as by flipping the image or adding subtitles or ads. Video DNA technology, however, analyzes a clip's traits to spot illegal footage even after alteration.
Technological advances are also expanding the scope of detection. Artificial intelligence (AI) collects online posts using specific keywords and analyzes their text and images, but in the future, it will go a step further by interpreting the context of conversations.
"You're pretty. How old are you?"
This seemingly ordinary question could be the start of grooming, a tactic used to build trust with a potential victim before gradually steering the conversation toward more personal exchanges. Even if messages appear harmless, warning signs can emerge if the flow of the conversation is examined.
From next year, the center will apply technology that can analyze conversational context to identify attempts to lure children and adolescents into sexual exploitation.
The center on Nov. 10 displayed this know-how at a news conference following a tour for domestic and foreign media at the Women's Human Rights Institute of Korea in Seoul's Jung-gu District.
The Ministry of Gender Equality and Family outlined the center's operations and demonstrated its integrated one-stop service for victims of digital sex crimes. It also showcased the use of AI to proactively detect and respond to sexually exploitative materials involving children and adolescents.
The center provides counseling for victims of digital sex crimes, assists in the removal of videos or content with harmful images, and offers referrals for investigative, legal and medical services. Even after such content is removed, it monitors for any redistribution and helps victims return to daily life.
For child sexual abuse material (CSAM), the center takes a proactive approach by identifying and helping remove such content even without a request from the victim. This helps prevent further harm, especially if a victim is unaware that the material has been distributed or struggles to report it.
Stronger international cooperation seeks to remove the distribution of such content overseas. The center works with organizations such as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children of the U.S. to automate the process for submitting removal requests and verify the results by integrating application programming interfaces.
AI has greatly boosted the speed and processing efficiency of content removal. Previously, staff had to manually search for and analyze online posts, greatly limiting real-time monitoring and large-scale data processing and suffering mental duress due to constant exposure to harmful content.
Today, the center uses about 220 keywords to collect suspicious posts around the clock from 14 online platforms like Google, X and Telegram. AI analyzes texts and images to identify potential CSAM and provide preliminary assessments later reviewed by staff.
From detection to deletion requests, the automated process has slashed the workload to enable employees to focus more on helping the victims.
The center said that from April to September this year, it proactively handled 96,210 cases of removing child and adolescent sexual exploitation material, more than double the 45,438 for all of last year. The daily average per staff member also rose about 9.7-fold, from 20.8 to 202.1.
But AI does not make all the decisions. Staff make the final determination on whether to grant a deletion request and directly verify its removal.
"AI helps identify and connect victims faster to the support they need," the center's director Kim Misoon said. "But understanding each victim's circumstances, determining the appropriate course of action, and supporting their return to daily life remain the responsibility of human staff."
The ministry plans to keep applying the latest technologies, strengthening cooperation among relevant ministries and improving systems to create a safer digital environment, under the goal of tracking the distribution of illegally filmed content to the very end and ensuring its deletion and blocking.

Заголовок: Magellan jumps on results as space index rises 4.1 per cent
Полный текст:
Magellan Aerospace jumped on its third-quarter results and NorthStar Earth & Space fell 36.7 per cent in New York as the SpaceQ Canadian Space Index rose 4.1 per cent to 99.54.

Magellan Aerospace reported on Tuesday that its third-quarter net income rose 57.7 per cent to $20.0 million, on revenue up 17.6 per cent to $300.6 million, and its shares jumped 13.0 per cent the next day. They gave back some of that gain on Thursday and Friday but still finished the week up 8.4 per cent at $34.23.
NorthStar Earth & Space went the other way, falling 36.7 per cent to $US 2.31 on NYSE American in the week it reported its first results as a public company. Its third-quarter revenue rose to $17.2 million from $1.4 million a year earlier, and it kept its forecast of $41 million for 2026, but most of the selling had come before those numbers were out.
For the week, the SpaceQ Canadian Space Index rose 4.1 per cent to 99.54, while the S&P/TSX Composite gained 0.9 per cent. The index rose 5.1 per cent on Monday, when markets rallied on falling oil prices, gave back 3.0 per cent on Thursday as MDA Space, Telesat and Magellan each fell more than 5 per cent, and recovered 2.5 per cent on Friday. Telesat and Magellan each added about a point, but Baylin Technologies, up just half a cent for the week, added the most, 1.7 points. Because the index is recalculated from each day’s percentage moves, Baylin’s 40 per cent rebound from 10 cents on Friday counted for more than its 32 per cent drop on Wednesday.
The board
Magellan’s profit rises 57.7 per cent
Magellan’s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), a measure of operating profit, rose 29.4 per cent to $38.5 million. Its Middletown subsidiary in the United States is still working through the Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection it sought in July, and Magellan said the outcome of that process is uncertain. The company also declared its quarterly dividend of five cents a share.
Magellan has gained 85.8 per cent since January, second on the board only to 5N Plus, which edged up 0.5 per cent this week to $33.71 and is up 90.2 per cent for the year.
Telesat climbs and MDA’s Globalstar satellites pass their first tests
Telesat rose 9.9 per cent to $64.71, the board’s biggest gain for the week. It climbed 8.6 per cent on Monday and 5.2 per cent on Wednesday, then fell 6.5 per cent on Thursday. With its third-quarter results, Telesat said it still has to refinance $2.4 billion of debt in its older geostationary satellite business, which starts coming due in December.
MDA Space said on Tuesday that the first eight satellites it delivered for Globalstar’s 2-R mission have passed initial functional tests in orbit. Its shares rose 8.1 per cent on Monday and fell 5.5 per cent on Thursday, ending the week up 2.7 per cent at $41.25. Calian Group edged up 0.7 per cent to $85.55.
Maritime Launch plans a share consolidation and Baylin pulls its forecast
Maritime Launch Services reported third-quarter revenue of $5.6 million on Friday, level with the second quarter, and net income of $3.5 million. It also plans to ask shareholders early next year to approve a share consolidation, and a day earlier it named Sarah McLean chief operating officer. Its shares fell one cent, or 2.2 per cent, to 43.5 cents. Intermap Technologies lost one cent, or 1.3 per cent, to 76 cents, and C-COM Satellite Systems was unchanged at 84 cents, with its last trade on Wednesday.
Baylin Technologies reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday, withdrew its 2026 forecast and said its lender will not let it make payments of about $10.6 million due Nov. 15 and $2.7 million due Dec. 15 to the former owners of Kaelus, the Swedish radio equipment maker it bought in May. Revenue more than doubled to $35.3 million. The shares fell five cents, or 32.3 per cent, to 10.5 cents on Wednesday and closed at 10 cents on Thursday, a new one-year low. On Friday, when more than five million shares changed hands, they rose four cents, or 40 per cent, to finish the week up half a cent, or 3.7 per cent, at 14 cents.
NorthStar falls 36.7 per cent in New York
NorthStar reported on Thursday third-quarter net income of $7.7 million, against a $6.2 million loss a year earlier. The quarter ended before it completed its merger with Viking Acquisition Corp. I on Oct. 1. NorthStar also said it has signed an agreement to host its space-surveillance sensors on Kepler Communications’ data relay satellites. Its shares had already fallen 22.8 per cent by Wednesday’s close, before the report, and lost another 7.5 per cent on Thursday and 11.3 per cent on Friday. NorthStar has until Nov. 30 to meet the conditions of its approval to list in Toronto.
LUNR Aerospace, a Toronto startup that wants to launch small satellites to orbit by 2029 and listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange on Oct. 27, rose 66.7 per cent to $4.00 on Monday, then fell back to close the week at $2.60, up 8.3 per cent. About 60,000 shares traded all week.
The U.S. board
Rocket Lab sells eight more Neutron launches
Rocket Lab reported record third-quarter revenue of $US 267.8 million on Monday, up 73 per cent, and said it had sold eight more launches of Neutron, the reusable rocket whose first flight it has moved into 2027, for more than $US 515 million. Its backlog rose to $US 3.57 billion. The shares rose 10.9 per cent on Monday, before the results, and 6.5 per cent on Tuesday, ending the week up 15.9 per cent.
AST SpaceMobile reported third-quarter revenue of $US 42.3 million the same day and said Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications will put about $US 1 billion toward J-LEO, a constellation AST is building with Rakuten. AST rose 14.1 per cent on Monday, gave nearly all of it back over the rest of the week and finished up 0.8 per cent.
Three of NASA’s new lunar contractors post double-digit gains
NASA named eight companies on Saturday, Nov. 7, to compete for a decade of lunar cargo deliveries under CLPS 2, a contract with a combined ceiling of $US 10 billion. Three of them are on the U.S. board, and all three rose by double digits on Monday: Firefly Aerospace by 17.1 per cent, Voyager Technologies by 16.3 per cent and Intuitive Machines by 15.0 per cent.
Intuitive Machines added 7.0 per cent on Thursday after it reported record third-quarter revenue of $US 269.3 million and forecast $US 920 million to $US 950 million for the year. Its 24.2 per cent gain for the week was the best among the 20 U.S. companies. Firefly reported on Tuesday that third-quarter revenue rose 259 per cent to $US 110.7 million and that its backlog reached a record $US 1.7 billion. It finished the week up 21.4 per cent, and Voyager gained 12.8 per cent.
Virgin Galactic plunges after its third-quarter report
Virgin Galactic reported after Thursday’s close that it expects its first commercial spaceflight early in the second quarter of 2027, with the first glide flight of its lead spaceship, Apeiron, in January. It ended September with $US 184 million in cash and signed an agreement with Jefferies to sell up to $US 250 million of shares on the open market. The shares plunged 31.1 per cent on Friday to $US 1.84, and their 33.6 per cent drop for the week was the steepest among the 20.
Viasat wins NASA relay work and Planet books Stoke
Viasat said on Monday that NASA had picked it as one of three companies for the first phase of NEXUS, a program to develop commercial Ka-band relay satellites to take over from NASA’s own relay fleet. The contract has a maximum value of $US 460.9 million. Viasat rose 16.3 per cent that day and 5.9 per cent for the week. Planet Labs signed a multi-launch agreement with Stoke Space the same day, rose 14.5 per cent and finished the week up 10.0 per cent.
Satellogic reported on Tuesday that third-quarter revenue rose 342 per cent to a record $US 16.0 million. After the quarter ended, it agreed to sell three satellites already in orbit for about $US 37 million. Its shares fell 5.2 per cent. Spire Global reported that third-quarter revenue rose 42 per cent to $US 18.0 million, and its shares gained 6.5 per cent.

SpaceX rose 5.8 per cent on Monday and 3.6 per cent for the week, to $US 139.11. After Friday’s close it launched Starship’s 15th flight, its first attempt to catch both stages, the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage, with the launch tower. SpaceX called off the booster catch and diverted the booster to the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded just before reaching the water. On Saturday, more than 22 hours after liftoff, the tower caught the upper stage, Ship 42, the first time a Starship upper stage has been recovered.
Among the rest, BlackSky gained 11.6 per cent and Redwire 7.2 per cent. NASA chose Redwire on Saturday, Nov. 7, to supply power generation for a small solar tower on the Moon. Comtech rose 6.2 per cent to $US 1.20, EchoStar 5.7 per cent and Globalstar 2.3 per cent, while Iridium, which Rocket Lab has agreed to buy, gained 4.2 per cent. On the way down, Momentus fell 12.2 per cent and Karman Space & Defense lost 10.9 per cent, including 9.4 per cent on Thursday. Sidus Space fell five cents, or 5.1 per cent, to 94 cents.
In all, 15 of the 20 rose in a week when the Procure Space ETF gained 4.3 per cent and the S&P 500 rose 2.5 per cent.
OHB falls after its nine-month results and Innospace surges
OHB fell 8.9 per cent on Thursday after reporting its nine-month results. Total operating performance, its main measure of sales, rose 10 per cent to €946.5 million, and its order backlog stood at €3.94 billion, about $6.2 billion, but net profit fell 22 per cent to €19.1 million. It kept its forecast for the year. The shares lost another 8.1 per cent on Friday and ended the week down 7.4 per cent at €177.00, about $278.39.
Avio gained 14.0 per cent to €32.97, about $51.86, including 7.7 per cent on Monday. On Wednesday it reported that nine-month revenue rose 16.7 per cent to €409.7 million, about $644 million, while its order backlog fell 8 per cent from December, to €1.99 billion. SES rose 1.4 per cent to €4.56, about $7.17, and Eutelsat fell 4.1 per cent to €1.75, about $2.74.
Innospace, the South Korean rocket developer that has until December to turn its letter of intent with Maritime Launch into a formal agreement to fly from Spaceport Nova Scotia, surged 43.0 per cent to 6,090 won, about $6.51. In Tokyo, ispace, whose U.S. arm was among NASA’s CLPS 2 picks, rose 9.6 per cent to 367 yen, about $3.28. Заголовок: What’s Happening in Space Policy November 15-21, 2026
Полный текст:
Here is SpacePolicyOnline.com’s list of space policy events for the week of November 15-21, 2026 and any insight we can offer about them. The House and Senate are in session this week.

During the Week

It’s tough to top the excitement of yesterday’s Starship “catch” by SpaceX, but there are plenty of great events coming up this week including another milestone that’s really important though in a different way — Voyager 1 reaching the one-light-day threshold in interstellar space.

Tough to top yesterday’s Starship “catch” at Starbase, TX, but lots of interesting events this week. Photo: screenshot from SpaceX webcast.

But let’s start with Congress, which will be busy this week as Republicans try to get as many of their priorities enacted before Democrats take control of both chambers on January 3. As of this morning (Sunday), the Senate will have 55 Democrats (including two Independents who caucus with them) and 44 Republicans, with the Alaska race still uncalled. The House will have 256 Democrat and 169 Republicans, with 10 races uncalled.

From a space policy standpoint, the key tasks for this lame-duck session include passing FY2027 appropriations bills that fund DOD (Defense), NASA and NOAA (Commerce-Justice-Science or CJS), FAA (Transportation-HUD or THUD), and FCC (Financial Services and General Government or FSGG); the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA); and possibly a NASA Authorization Act and a commercial space bill. President Trump is also eager to pass a third reconciliation bill with $350 billion more for DOD on top of the $1.15 trillion requested through appropriations, taking the total for FY2027 to $1.5 trillion. The U.S. Space Force would get $12 billion of that and most of the FY2027 Golden Dome money, $17 billion, also is here. Republicans and Democrats both are signaling $350 billion is too much, however.

Senate Appropriations Committee chair Susan Collins has begun releasing subcommittee recommendations for FY2027 appropriations. CJS was released last week. Defense may come this week.

Of everything that’s on the plate, getting appropriations passed is at the top of the list. Otherwise there’ll be another government shutdown when the Continuing Resolution (CR) expires on December 11. Memories of the disruption caused by last year’s historic 43-day shutdown haven’t faded, but none of the FY2027 bills have been enacted yet.

The House Appropriations Committee cleared all 12 appropriations bills and the House passed three (Agriculture, Milcon-VA, and National Security-State). By contrast, the Senate Appropriations committee hasn’t approved any, but last week seven of the 12 subcommittees, including CJS (NASA/NOAA), released their recommendations. We’ll see if others, like Defense, come out this week. Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), who was defeated in her reelection bid, hasn’t scheduled any full committee markups yet and could decide to negotiate with the House using the subcommittee marks. Or they could simply decide to extend the CR into next year. Or there could be another shutdown. Stay tuned.

The NDAA is considered a “must-pass” bill because it sets priorities and authorizes funding for U.S. military activities. It has passed Congress every year since the first in 1961. The almost certainty of passage makes it a tempting target to add other legislation even if only tangentially related. Although the NDAA traditionally gets broad support from both parties, this year it passed the House in July on basically a party-line vote and Democrats are blocking its consideration in the Senate. They object that it doesn’t place limits on the war in Iran, that the SAVE America voting eligibility bill and partisan provisions on social issues were included in the House version, and that the authorized funding level of $1.15 trillion is too high. The road ahead is challenging, but it still would be surprising if they can’t find a compromise before the end of the Congress.

Joshua Shoemaker, NASA CFO nominee, at his nomination hearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, November 10, 2026. Screenshot.

Meanwhile, on Wednesday, the Senate Commerce Committee will vote on several nominations and bills. Among the nominations are Joshua Shoemaker to be NASA Chief Financial Officer, Robert Steinau to be NASA Inspector General, and Danielle Thumann Severs to be an FCC Commissioner.

Shoemaker and Steinau’s nominations were not controversial during the hearing last week, but Democrats strongly opposed Thumann’s. She is currently Senior Counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. The FCC ordinarily has five commissioners, three from the president’s party and two from the other party. Historically the FCC was independent and presidents could not fire commissioners of independent agencies, but the Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that presidents can fire them at will. The FCC needs three commissioners for a quorum, which is what they have right now: two Republicans and one Democrat. Democrats are worried that if Thumann is confirmed, Trump will fire the one Democrat and only Republicans will be on the Commission. The FCC plays a big role in space activities, assigning the radio frequencies needed by all satellite operators to communicate with their spacecraft, and sets rules on orbital debris. The FCC created its own Space Bureau in 2023 as satellite operations began to boom with the advent of SpaceX’s Starlink and Amazon’s Leo megaconstellations.

Speaking of Amazon Leo, earlier this afternoon the United Launch Alliance launched 40 Amazon Leo satellites on Vulcan, but an anomaly 10 minutes into flight prevented them from reaching orbit. We have a separate article about that. It’s the first total failure for ULA in the company’s history.

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket on the launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, November 15, 2026. Vulcan lifted off, but an anomaly 10 minutes into flight prevented the payloads from reaching orbit. Screenshot.

Lots of other great events this week, including a House SS&T hearing on Space Weather on Thursday, but we’ll highlight just one more — NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft reaching a signature milestone.

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and today continues its journey out into the galaxy. Early Wednesday morning, at 5:16:07 am ET, it will reach a distance of 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth where it will take an entire day — “one light day” — to receive a signal from Earth. It’ll take another day for a reply to be received back here where a team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena, CA monitors and controls the spacecraft. They recently sent energy-saving commands , dubbed the Big Bang, to reduce the amount of power being used by Voyager’s Radioisotope Thermal Generator (RTG) in the hope of extending its lifetime even more.

An artist’s concept depicts one of NASA’s Voyager probes. The twin spacecraft launched in 1977. Credit : NASA/JPL-Caltech

The Planetary Society will hold a virtual event Wednesday evening to celebrate, and NASA will hold another one Thursday at noon ET in-person at JPL and webcast. Members of the Voyager team over these decades will be there to talk about both Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, that’s also in interstellar space, but went in a different direction. The energy-saving commands sent to Voyager 1 were also implemented for Voyager 2. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 flew past those two planets as well as Uranus and Neptune. It’s remarkable that they continue to communicate back to Earth providing data on what’s out there, like the interstellar “hum.”

Заголовок: ULA suffers first outright failure with loss of Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
Полный текст:
In a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the company's new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket carrying a batch of Amazon Leo internet satellites, malfunctioned during the climb to space Sunday, dooming the payload and throwing a costly wrench into the launch schedule of both companies.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan, equipped with six solid rocket boosters, lifts off from Cape Canaveral’s pad 41. A failure 10 minutes into flight resulted in the loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now

In a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the company’s new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket carrying a batch of Amazon Leo internet satellites, malfunctioned during the climb to space Sunday, dooming the payload and throwing a costly wrench into the launch schedule of both companies.

“Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 (at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station) suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit,” ULA said in a statement some 50 minutes after liftoff.

“We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action and return to flight as quickly as possible.”

It was the first outright failure of a United Launch Alliance rocket since the company, a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, was formed in 2006.

It wasn’t immediately known what went wrong, but the Vulcan, the rocket replacing ULA’s fleet of Atlas 5 rockets, will face a potentially significant grounding while engineers review telemetry and implement fixes for whatever caused the mishap.

The six solid rocket booster peel away from the Vulcan first stage booster one minute 35 seconds into flight. Photo: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now.

It was only the fifth flight of a Vulcan rocket and the first in nine months as ULA and booster-supplier Northrop Grumman worked to resolve problems with nozzles used by strap-on solid-fuel boosters that marred two earlier flights.

The solids appeared to work normally Sunday, helping boost the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before burning out and falling away. The two methane-burning BE-4 engines powering the Vulcan’s first stage then continued the climb toward orbit, but they appeared to fire longer than expected based on ULA’s pre-launch timeline.

After stage separation, the Vulcan’s hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage engines took over for a planned 12-minute 15-second burn. According to ULA’s update, something went wrong during that Centaur firing, but no additional details were immediately provided.

Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan flights purchased by Amazon to launch its Leo satellites, designed to compete head-to-head with Elon Musk’s Starlinks and other space-based internet providers. ULA already has launched eight LEO flights using Atlas 5 rockets.

Amazon also has booked 24 Leo launches aboard Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, 24 using the European Ariane 6, and 13 aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9s. More than 3,300 Leo satellites will be needed to complete the constellation. Sunday’s flight would have pushed the total number launched to date to 436.

But it was not to be.

Instead, Amazon Leo will now have to wait on ULA’s failure investigation to run its course before trying again with a Vulcan. The company also is waiting for Jeff Bezos-owned Blue Origin to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after a catastrophic on-pad explosion last May.

That failure was caused by problems with an oxygen valve in one of the New Glenn’s seven BE-4 first stage engines. The BE-4, also built by Blue Origin, powers the Vulcan’s first stage, but the engines used Sunday had been retrofitted with a fix by Blue Origin engineers.

While the cause of the failure is not yet publicly known, “ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action,” the company said.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman promised assistance if needed.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” he wrote on the social media platform X. “The team at @NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

The Vulcan rocket thunders away from Florida’s space coast on Nov. 15, 2026. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now.

The 214-foot-tall Vulcan blasted off from pad 41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. EST, thundering away on a northeasterly trajectory atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust from six Northrop Grummon strap-on solid-fuel boosters and two methane-burning BE-4s.

A launch attempt Friday was scrubbed after problems knocked out a gaseous nitrogen plant that serves multiple launch providers. Another delay was ordered Saturday because of network problems between the Vulcan and ground systems.

On Sunday, launch controllers called a hold at the T-minus 20-second mark because of an unexplained technical issue with the rocket. Re-targeting the end of the launch window, ULA resolved the problem and the rocket roared to life and climbed away at the end of the launch window.

It’s not yet known if the problem that interrupted the countdown played any role in the subsequent failure.

In any case, the strap-on boosters helped propel the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere, burning out and falling away about a minute and 40 seconds after liftoff. But the first stage appeared to burn longer than called for in the company’s pre-launch timeline.

The first stage also appeared to separate from the rocket’s hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage later than expected and telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in the burn.

ULA’s launch commentators, however, did not mention any problems and the launch broadcast came to an end without confirming whether the Centaur’s first planned engine firing went for the full duration.

ULA spent months working to resolve problems with the strap-on booster nozzles that occurred during two earlier flights, one in 2024 and the other this past February. While ULA was free to press ahead with commercial flights, the U.S. Space Force put Vulcan launches of national security payloads on hold pending additional analysis.

“We’ve identified three credible causes (of the nozzle issue), and we have taken positive steps to mitigate all of those,” ULA CEO Mark Peller told Aviation Week & Space Technology magazine in a pre-flight interview.

The boosters appeared to work normally Sunday.

As for the BE-4 engines, Peller said Blue Origin developed a “design improvement” to resolve the valve issue and carried out a “retrofit” on the engines installed on the Vulcan Leo 1 rocket.

“They were down at our facilities probably a couple months ago and implemented that retrofit kit on the engines on this upcoming mission,” Peller said. “And they’re working with us to work through our inventory of engines.”

Заголовок: 30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes
Полный текст:
Sufferin' succotash! The Monstars and Tune Squad interplanetary slam arrived 30 years ago, and it's still a clinic in interplanetary conflict resolution.

You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

While " Independence Day " saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

(Image credit: Warner Bros Pictures)

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly . "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”

It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's " Disclosure Day " from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

Заголовок: Emirates’ stunning premium economy is headed for more European destinations: Here’s how to fly it
Полный текст:
Emirates has expanded its distinctive premium economy cabin to 31 of its 41 European destinations, with Paris the latest addition. Here's what travellers can expect.

Emirates has expanded its premium economy cabin to 31 of the 41 European destinations it serves, making its distinctive cream-leather seats available on more routes this winter. The latest addition is Paris Charles de Gaulle , where a retrofitted Airbus A380 began operating a daily service with the cabin on 25 October 2026.

In its announcement, Emirates said it expects to operate an average of 78 flights daily between Dubai and Europe during the winter schedule.

The expansion gives travellers more opportunities to book the “happy middle” cabin between economy and business class. But with different aircraft and configurations operating across Emirates’ network, a premium economy cabin is not yet guaranteed.

Where Emirates is adding premium economy in Europe

The airline launched its full premium economy service in 2022, introducing the seats on selected aircraft. Its rollout has since become part of a wider investment in refurbishing existing widebody aircraft while adding new A350s.

New Airbus A350s serve some destinations with premium economy built into their factory configuration. Others are served by A380s and Boeing 777s undergoing Emirates’ extensive cabin refurbishment programme.

Photo: Emirates

Paris is the most recent European addition. Emirates introduced the product on daily flights EK071 and EK072 between Dubai and Paris Charles de Gaulle, using a refurbished A380. Its earlier September announcement said this would bring premium economy to all three of its French gateways: Paris, Lyon and Nice.

What makes the Emirates premium cabin different?

The most recognisable feature of the airline’s premium economy is the elegant, quilted cream-coloured leather upholstery, complemented by woodgrain tables and cabin finishes inspired by the airline’s higher-priced premium cabins. It is a marked departure from economy.

Emirates premium economy offers up to 40-inch seat pitch, 19.5-inch seat width and eight inches of recline. Six-way adjustable headrests, calf rests and footrests make longer journeys more relaxing.

Photo: Emirates

The seat also has a fold-out dining table, a separate side table and accessible charging. The 13.3-inch entertainment screen offers access to Emirates’ ice content.

Photo: Emirates

Emirates also offers an enhanced meal service. Premium Economy passengers can enjoy regionally inspired dishes served on Royal Doulton china with stainless-steel cutlery and linen. Amenities include pillows, blankets and, on longer flights, premium economy amenity kits.

A350, A380 or Boeing 777: How Emirates premium economy differs by aircraft

Emirates’ premium economy cabins vary by aircraft type and configuration, including the number of seats available, their location within the aircraft and, on newer Airbus A350s, the seat design itself.

According to AeroLOPA’s Emirates aircraft seating plans , the airline offers premium economy on selected Airbus A350-900, A380-800 and Boeing 777 aircraft. Not every Emirates aircraft in these families has the cabin.

The A350-900 has two premium economy configurations. The 312-seat 359G accommodates 21 premium economy passengers in three rows, while the longer-range, 298-seat 359U has 28 seats across four rows. Both use a 2-3-2 arrangement.

Photo: Emirates

Emirates’ A380 premium economy cabins accommodate 56 passengers in a 2-4-2 layout, but their location depends on the aircraft configuration. On the four-class 388V, 388M and 388Y, premium economy is located in the forward section of the main deck, ahead of economy class. On the three-class, 569-seat 388K, the cabin is instead at the front of the upper deck, ahead of business class. This configuration has no first class cabin.

Selected Boeing 777-200LR and 777-300ER aircraft have 24 premium economy seats in three rows, arranged 2-4-2. These cabins sit between business class and economy.

Emirates’ established premium economy product generally features seats measuring 19.5 inches wide, with around 40 inches of pitch (listed on Aerolopa as 102 cm) and 13.3-inch entertainment screens. The airline’s original A350 specification lists a 39-inch pitch.

New premium economy seat to be introduced on A350s

In September 2026, Emirates unveiled a new electrically operated premium economy seat which will be installed on its newly delivered A350s. The 28-seat cabin retains the 2-3-2 layout, and the seats measure 20 inches wide, with up to 39 inches of pitch.

Photo: Emirates

Each features:

• A full-height, electrically adjustable privacy divider

• Powered seat-position controls

• A Safran U-Dream headrest

• Wireless charging and USB-C power

• A 13.3-inch 4K HDR touchscreen.

Photo: Emirates

The new seats recline forward into a cradle position without intruding on the row behind, so that passengers can relax without disturbing others.

Emirates has invested heavily in its premium economy cabin, including ongoing fleet retrofit programmes and product improvements. While it may not yet be available on every Emirates flight, the airline is clearly committed to expanding access to the luxurious premium economy passenger experience.

Заголовок: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
Полный текст:
On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.

When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.

Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

(Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF)

Why it mattered

When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.

"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus."

The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.

The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF)

During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.

"One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.

Заголовок: Стоит признать, что SpaceX вчера совершила настоящий технологический прорыв: корабль Starship после 14 витков вокруг …
Полный текст:
Стоит признать, что SpaceX вчера совершила настоящий технологический прорыв: корабль Starship после 14 витков вокруг Земли вернулся к стартовой площадке, где его впервые захватили гигантские механические "руки" башни. Ещё один шаг к полностью многоразовой космической системе. Но ещё сегодня, 15 ноября, исполняется 38 лет со дня полёта советского "Бурана", и это хороший повод вспомнить об истории этого мегапроекта.

В 1988 году ракета-носитель "Энергия" вывела в космос 90-тонный орбитальный корабль, который совершил два витка вокруг Земли и впервые в мире полностью автоматически приземлился на аэродром.

Для "Энергии" это был второй полёт, и уже тогда она была рассчитана на выведение более 100 тонн на низкую околоземную орбиту - столько же, сколько заявлено для многоразового Starship нового поколения. В 1990-е годы эту уникальную программу фактически бросили. Но ещё менее известно, что "Энергия" вовсе не задумывалась как конечная точка советской космической программы. У неё было два перспективных, реально прорабатывавшихся продолжения, которые развивались в том числе по замыслу Валентина Петровича Глушко ещё 1970-х годов.

🔹 Первое - "Вулкан". Сверхтяжёлая ракета с восемью боковыми ускорителями вместо четырёх и грузоподъёмностью 200 тонн на орбиту. Вдвое больше базовой "Энергии" и на уровне самых амбициозных планов SpaceX.

🔹 Второе - "Энергия-II", или "Ураган". Полностью многоразовая система, у которой должны были возвращаться и центральный блок, и боковые ускорители. Только не вертикально, как у Starship, а по-самолётному - с крыльями и посадкой на аэродром. Для центрального блока даже прорабатывали изменение геометрии корпуса после выхода на орбиту.

И это были не красивые фантазии конструкторов. По "Вулкану" подготовили подробные технические предложения, прорабатывали двигатели, конструкцию и производство. В 1985 году его разработку закрепили постановлением ЦК КПСС и Совета Министров СССР, а опытно-конструкторские работы намечались на 1990-1995 годы. А по "Энергии-II" провели расчёты, аэродинамические исследования, экономическую экспертизу. К 1989 году проект достиг стадии технических предложений, а на 1990-й планировали выпуск эскизного проекта.

Если бы не распад СССР, к концу 1990-х годов мы вполне могли бы иметь ракету грузоподъёмностью 200 тонн и испытывать собственную полностью многоразовую космическую систему. По ряду характеристик превосходящую даже сегодняшний Starship. Для этого существовал не только научный задел: уже летала "Энергия", работали уникальные двигатели, заводы, испытательные стенды, космодром и огромная кооперация. Сейчас наступило время SpaceX. Но стоит помнить: почти четыре десятилетия назад у нашей страны уже была сверхтяжёлая ракета, а её создатели готовились сделать следующий шаг - к 200 тоннам на орбите и полной многоразовости.

К счастью, наследие "Энергии-Бурана" не исчезло вместе с программой. Созданные школой Глушко двигатели получили продолжение в современных РД. Разработанные материалы, технологии теплозащиты, композиты, решения в области автоматического управления и гиперзвуковой аэродинамики стали частью научно-технического задела, который продолжил развиваться в ракетостроении, авиации, военной технике и исследованиях гиперзвукового полёта. Мы потеряли возможность последовательно развивать одну из самых выдающихся космических программ XX века. Но не потеряли всё, что было создано поколением её инженеров. И сейчас главное наследие "Энергии-Бурана" - технологии и инженерные школы, которые, несмотря на все сложности, продолжают работать на будущее отечественной авиации и космонавтики.

Заголовок: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
Полный текст:
"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."

For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

What is T. Coronae Borealis?

T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare?

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

An animation of T. CrB brightening. (Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab)

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center , told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."

Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."

What will happen when T CrB's nova light reaches Earth?

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude , then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays , light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "

Where can I find the Blaze Star in the night sky?

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

Corona Borealis forms a crown-like pattern of stars between the more famous constellations of Bootes and Hercules. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva)

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

How to find T.CrB near Epsilon Coronae Borealis. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva)

Заголовок: Taikonauts Remain Productive as End of Shenzhou-23 Mission Nears
Полный текст:
Tiangong TV: November 15th 2026.

Despite the conclusion of the Shenzhou-23 mission being no more than a month away, and the imminent selection of a crew member to complete a yearlong stay, Zhu Yangzhu (朱杨柱) 1 , Li Jiaying (黎家盈) 2 , and Zhang Zhiyuan (张志远) 3 continue to busily work aboard the Tiangong Space Station in orbit. This week, as shared via ‘Tiangong TV’ , the trio has been supporting experiments in microgravity biology and taking part in mental health research.

Attached below is a translated transcript of the newest episode:

From midsummer to early winter, the Shenzhou-23 crew’s space mission has entered its sixth month, and the three taikonauts continue to lead busy and productive days aboard the station. What new developments took place on the space station last week? Let’s take a look.

In the field of space life sciences and human research, the fourth exposure experiment for space radiation biology research on the space station has proceeded smoothly. Experimental samples, including nanozymes, actinomycetes, and plant seeds, were brought back inside the station 4 after completing a five-month exposure to the extravehicular space environment. The Shenzhou-23 crew collectively completed the removal, storage, and cleanup of the samples. Once these samples are returned to Earth, they will be used for further research into the long-term effects of space radiation on living organisms.

Last week, the crew conducted a study on the forces exerted on the lower limbs during exercise. Using plantar pressure measurement equipment, they recorded data on foot pressure during a typical workday to analyze the loading characteristics on the lower limbs under various in-orbit conditions.

In the footage, the taikonauts are collecting, labeling, and storing nasal swabs and microbial swabs from environmental surfaces. These samples will be used to study the interactions between viruses and immune metabolism.

Additionally, the crew utilized a computer and specialized software to complete assessments of their emergency decision-making capabilities and tests of their emotional state while in orbit. The results will enable ground personnel to analyze how the taikonauts' emergency decision-making skills and emotional states evolve throughout the mission.

In accordance with the schedule, the crew also completed tasks such as replacing experimental samples in the fluid physics cabinet and replacing filters in the combustion cabinet, ensuring the smooth progress of experiments related to microgravity physics in space.

In terms of maintaining the space station complex, the crew completed a series of in-cabin environmental monitoring tasks, including total volatile organic compound measurements and air purity tests. They replaced components of the regenerative life support system, equipment racks, and the hot-air heating unit in the space kitchen, while also conducting thorough cleaning to ensure the station remains habitable.

Regarding health management, the three taikonauts carried out their exercise routines as scheduled and used equipment designed to counteract the physiological effects of microgravity, such as bone loss prevention devices 5 , to actively combat the effects of microgravity and maintain good health while in orbit.

As time passes and the seasons change, we’ll keep you updated on the latest from Tiangong. See you next week!

Заголовок: Nov. 15, 1988: The Buran orbiter launches
Полный текст:
In 1976, the Soviet Union began development of the Buran orbiter. Concerned that the American space shuttle program might be used for military purposes, the Soviets responded with Buran and its Energia booster rocket, which were capable of carrying antisatellite and antimissile weapons and targeting locations on Earth’s surface. Though the nonmilitary objectives for Buran included ferrying crew and supplies to the Mir Space Station, Buran was also capable of flying unmanned and fully automated.
The Buran program marked several achievements – the development of 230 new technologies, a fully recoverable rocket capable of lifting 220,000 pounds (100,000 kilograms) to orbit, a shuttle that could carry up to 10 cosmonauts. However, it only made a single flight: On Nov. 15, 1988, Buran launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, performed two orbits, and returned to Earth. The 206-minute flight was seamless, and was performed fully under remote control, with no crew members aboard. Despite this success, the colossal expense of the program and the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union meant the end of Buran. In 2002, the roof of a hangar at Baikonur collapsed, killing eight people and destroying the orbiter and its rocket.
Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Полный текст: Humanity is quickly starting to saturate our ability to track all of the satellites we have in deep space. NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN) has been the workhorse for tracking such things for decades, but is quickly being overwhelmed by the number of requests it receives. Which in turn makes it harder to track some of the missions that have been launched recently. A new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv, from Ian Down, James McElreath, and Manoranjan Majji, of Advanced Space, Space Exploration Engineering, and Texas A&M respectively, offer a no-cost solution to that tracking problem - use solar array data from a spacecraft’s eclipse to determine where it is.

Заголовок: Starship capture thrills space fans! And SpaceX makes spaceflight history (again)
Полный текст:
SpaceX has achieved its first Starship capture! The catching mechanism nicknamed Mechazilla grabbed Starship out of the air over Starbase in South Texas.

The post Starship capture thrills space fans! And SpaceX makes spaceflight history (again) first appeared on EarthSky .

Starship capture thrills space fans

Say what you will about Elon Musk. His company, SpaceX, continued to blow the minds of new and old spaceflight fans this weekend with a Starship capture in midair.

SpaceX successfully caught the returning upper stage of its Starship rocket on Saturday, November 14, 2026. It used the giant mechanical tower arms, almost universally called “chopsticks” by SpaceX and spaceflight fans. The “chopsticks” — nicknamed Mechazilla — grabbed Starship out of the air at the Starbase facility in South Texas.

The maneuver capped off Integrated Flight Test 15 ( IFT-15 ). It marked the first time an orbital upper-stage spacecraft has returned from space to be plucked out of the air at its launch site.

The feat occurred at roughly 3:20 p.m. CST (21:20 UTC) on Saturday. The vehicle — designated Ship 42 — descended through overcast skies over Boca Chica, Texas. It fired its engines to hover before settling between Mechazilla’s giant waiting arms at Launch Pad 2.

Starship capture a massive leap forward

About 22 hours prior to Saturday’s amazing Starship capture, Ship 42 lifted off from Starbase on Friday evening, November 13. The spacecraft completed 14 orbits at an altitude of roughly 265 kilometers (165 miles). Then it reentered, putting its upgraded thermal protection tiles to the test against extreme reentry heat.

The mission fell just short of a complete success. SpaceX had hoped to catch both rocket stages during Flight 15. It has already mastered catching the Super Heavy first-stage booster on earlier test flights . But an unspecified anomaly shortly after Friday’s launch forced flight controllers to abort the booster’s return. They diverted the booster over the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded prior to splashdown.

Despite the lost booster, recovering the upper stage represents a massive leap forward. Because an orbital ship travels significantly higher and faster than a booster, surviving reentry and hitting a pinpoint landing target is vastly more complex.

‘Almost magic’

Ditching heavy landing legs in favor of tower catches is central to SpaceX’s goal of rapid reusability. That capability is essential for driving down launch costs and supporting NASA’s Artemis lunar program. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman hailed the catch as:

… Almost magic.

Spaceflight fans agree.

Bottom line: SpaceX achieved another major milestone on November 14, 2026, with its Starship capture. The catching mechanism — nicknamed Mechazilla — grabbed Starship out of the air at SpaceX’s Starbase facility in South Texas.

Заголовок: Exclusive: Düsseldorf’s Asian network ambitions hindered by aircraft delivery delays
Полный текст:
In an interview, SVP Aviation Henning Pfisterer discusses the airport's Asian network ambitions and the arrival of La Compagnie's New York route.

Düsseldorf Airport’s (DUS) long-haul network has shrunk considerably compared to 2019. It has taken steps to rebuild it, with La Compagnie announcing it would introduce an all-business class flight to New York from next spring.

It will use its Airbus A321LRs to fly the service beginning April 2027, capturing higher-yielding premium demand from the region, including from neighbouring countries.

Rebuilding a long-haul network is no easy feat, and adding new destinations is even harder – but talks are progressing well for DUS, SVP Aviation Henning Pfisterer tells Aerospace Global News in an interview. However, he shares that aircraft delivery delays are hindering its network growth ambitions.

Asian growth plans and 777X delivery delays

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Düsseldorf Airport had links to several destinations in Asia. Cathay Pacific flew to Hong Kong, All Nippon Airways to Tokyo Narita, Air China to Beijing and Singapore Airlines to Singapore.

Photo: Düsseldorf Airport

Lufthansa Group’s low-cost branch Eurowings also offered A330 flights to Bangkok. The airline no longer operates long-haul services as these have been shifted to the newly-created Discover Airlines which offers flights exclusively out of Lufthansa’s Frankfurt and Munich hubs.

DUS hopes to recover part of its Asian network, including services to Tokyo Narita. Pfisterer points out that the return of a service to Japan depends largely on slot availability, bilateral traffic rights and capacity constraints at Tokyo’s Narita Airport.

All Nippon Airways continues to prioritise growth from Haneda Airport and will do so through fiscal year 28, it said earlier this year . From FY29, it will take advantage of Narita Airport’s planned expansion which will increase takeoff and landing capacity to 500,000. It hopes to grow by a factor of 1.7x. Aviation Week reports that its focus lies on growing US and Europe flights .

“With deliveries of long-haul aircraft being delayed, there is currently no opportunity to serve this route, but we hope to see it return in the coming years,” Pfisterer said, referencing the airport’s discussions with ANA on the topic.

All Nippon Airways is awaiting deliveries for Boeing 777X aircraft, originally meant to begin service with them in 2021. This would potentially free up lower-capacity jets (such as the 787) for a return to Düsseldorf.

He confirmed that the return of the Tokyo connection was possible with another airline too, but did not comment further. Japan Airlines is the other major long-haul operator out of Tokyo.

ANA Boeing 787-9 at Tokyo Haneda Airport. Photo: Masahiro TAKAGI | Wikimedia Commons

“We also aim to get maybe one or two direct services to the big Asian hubs,” he added. “My vision for the future is that in the coming years we are linked to one, two or three Asian hubs, and from there ensuring connections within Asia, to Australia and the broader Pacific region.”

He confirmed that talks were in progress, but 777X delivery delays were a “challenge”. “There are some talks in progress, but there is still the issue of long-haul aircraft availability. We’re somewhere in the pipeline with a couple of carriers.”

When asked whether he was hinting at Cathay Pacific or Singapore Airlines, he acknowledged that both were natural candidates given their respective networks and the markets Düsseldorf is looking to reconnect with.

The airport also wants to be connected to markets it may not previously have had experience with.

“We spoke with Vietnamese carriers and we see potential for future connections,” he said.

La Compagnie brings New York back to the DUS network

La Compagnie is expanding its network which has historically been focused on connecting France and Italy with Newark with its all-business class configured aircraft. Supported by the arrival of its third A321LR next year, its new Düsseldorf-Newark connection marks its first foray into the German market.

Photo: Düsseldorf Airport

Pfisterer describes the connection as “vital” for the whole region. “New York and Tokyo are basically the most important connections we need to build back,” he said, reflecting on the impact of the pandemic. DUS last had regular flights to the Big Apple until March 2020 with Eurowings, data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. Since 2022, Condor has offered a handful of charter services in September and October each year.

DUS has also previously had all-business class flights to New York with PrivatAir on behalf of Lufthansa in the early-2000s.

“La Compagnie studied the market very intensively and, as a niche carrier with a premium product, identified a lot of premium potential here. Also, we have very strong corporations. We are the economic powerhouse of Europe. We have numerous blue-chip companies in our catchment.”

Düsseldorf Airport’s target market is not limited to Germany. It is actively promoting its position in the Dutch market. Pfisterer expects around 10% of La Compagnie’s Newark customers to come from the Netherlands.

Photo: Düsseldorf Airport

“Currently we have about 1.6 million Dutch passengers per year, and we’re continuing to see strong growth in this market. So Düsseldorf is growing as a departure point for Dutch passengers, particularly from the provinces close to the German border.

Leisure and VFR markets see strong growth

Its catchment area is also what drove its ability to offer new services to Curaçao, a country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. “It gives Dutch travelers a new travel option on a well-established route to a well-established destination, and at the same time it brings a new destination to the German market,” Pfisterer explains.

The Middle East conflict also had a considerable impact on the airport’s network, though Pfisterer assures that this is not a “structural challenge.”

He added: “We have seen demand recovering, and we’re already back in stable operations. What is missing a little bit is cruise tourism, because the Gulf region – Dubai, Doha – used to be ports of origin for German cruise ship operators.”

Instead, there has also been a surge to destinations across the Western Mediterranean, Egypt and Türkiye. Sharm el-Sheikh is returning with TUI, joining Corendon which has a strong Egyptian network using its four based aircraft. Air Cairo, Nesma Airlines and Nile Air are also growing their Düsseldorf services.

Photo: Düsseldorf Airport

Düsseldorf Airport is also maintaining its position as a strong hub catering to Visiting Friends and Relatives (VFR) traffic. It was the first European airport to regain links to Syria (with LEAV Aviation). FlyCham and Eurowings are both expected to begin Damascus flights soon. Pfisterer highlights that it is the only airport in Central Europe with links to two destinations in Libya: Tripoli and Benghazi.

Frankfurt’s proximity and traffic rights pose challenges for long-haul growth from Düsseldorf

Nearby Frankfurt Airport (FRA) is Germany’s largest air hub, home to both Lufthansa and Condor. It boasts an expansive long-haul network with flights to almost every corner of the globe. From Düsseldorf, railway connections are particularly convenient.

Pfisterer concedes that this proximity is “definitely a challenge.”

Photo: Markus Mainka / stock.adobe.com

“We have some leakage, where passengers go by surface transport to Frankfurt and embark on their long-haul flights that are not available from Düsseldorf. Another challenge is bilateral traffic rights. Certain markets cannot be connected with Düsseldorf because of restrictions under bilateral air services agreements,” he continues.

“Certain routes are limited by the number of frequencies and the number of points of entry in Germany. So we are effectively prevented from accessing certain markets that are very important to us, as airlines tend to prioritise the hubs.”

However, he adds that as passengers prefer to avoid surface transportation, there is a desire to grow the number of nonstop connections from Düsseldorf.

Заголовок: Humanity’s 1st intentional signal to space 52 years ago
Полный текст:
The iconic Arecibo telescope is no longer operational. But its legacy lives on. And in 1974, Arecibo sent earthlings' 1st intentional signal to space.

The post Humanity’s 1st intentional signal to space 52 years ago first appeared on EarthSky .

On November 16, 1974, the Arecibo Observatory beamed the 1st intentional signal to space. Look below for the full message and an explanation of each part of the message. Image via Wikimedia Commons .

1st intentional signal to space in 1974

On November 16, 1974, astronomers used the Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico to beam out the first intentional signal to space. It was the most powerful broadcast ever deliberately sent outward. The astronomers said their goal was to contact alien life. And some applauded it, but others didn’t.

On the plus side, it reminded people that Earth likely isn’t the only planet in our Milky Way galaxy where intelligent life has evolved. But others felt — if alien civilizations do exist out there — we shouldn’t call attention to ourselves.

The 2027 EarthSky Lunar Calendar is now available! A unique and beautiful poster-sized calendar. Keep up with all phases of the moon every night of the year. Order yours today!

The message in our signal to space

The message was designed by Cornell astronomy professor Frank Drake with input from other scientists including Carl Sagan . So, the final result was a simple and elegant broadcast. Basically, it consisted of a pattern of binary numbers . This message contained information about the basic chemicals of life and the structure of DNA. Plus, it included Earth’s place in our solar system and even a stick figure of a human.

The Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico broadcast the 1st intentional radio signal into space in 1974. Image via Wikimedia Commons .

Sending the Arecibo message

It took three minutes to send 1,679 bits of information, a snail’s pace compared to modern computer modems. And according to the SETI Institute :

The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo’s megawatt transmitter attached to its 1,000 feet (305 meter) antenna. The latter concentrates the transmitter energy by beaming it into a very small patch of sky.

The emission was equivalent to a 20-trillion-watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo’s.

In fact, the 1974 signal went out in the direction of M13 , a globular star cluster orbiting the center of our Milky Way galaxy. Basically, it was chosen because it’s a large collection of stars and was available in the sky at the time and place of the ceremony.

Also, globular star clusters are very far away. For instance, M13 is about 25,000 light-years from Earth.

And now, the 1974 signal is 52 light-years away from us.

Messier 13 (NGC 6205), a globular cluster 25,000 ly away in Hercules, holds hundreds of thousands of stars. In 1974, the Arecibo message was sent toward it. One of the brightest clusters in the northern sky! #Astrophotography @xipteras @Astro_KPage1986 @jaythegrumpy @AlphaAstro2 pic.twitter.com/Q4pnKtN2Zd

— Rad van Mad (@rvanmad) March 14, 2025

By the way, the Arecibo radio telescope collapsed in 2020 when its 900-ton receiver platform came loose from its cables and fell onto the reflector dish more than 400 feet (120 meters) below.

Read more: Video shows Arecibo telescope crash

Image via Cornell University .

Bottom line: Iconic Arecibo telescope is no longer operational, but its legacy lives on. Fifty years ago, on November 16, 1974, Arecibo sent our first intentional signal to space. What do you think? Should we be advertising our presence in space?
